articles.title: [Rear View] The night they asked Pete Lacaba to sing, and the song that made him cry
articles.summary: The night ended with a rare request. Pete was asked to sing.

blocks.text: My Brother's Moustache Facebook
The night ended with a rare request. Pete was asked to sing.
Pete Lacaba walked into My Brother’s Mustache, a folk house in Quezon City, just as Pat Castillo began her set. It was past eight, and word had gone around that he might not make it.

For a moment no one noticed him come in with his son, Kris. He could have been any silver-haired retiree, come to honor a man whose life and work is being celebrated that night. Then he scanned the standing-room-only crowd, waved at familiar faces, and the room stirred. People came up to greet him. Pete smiled, the fog of memory lifting with a firm handshake, a pat on the back, a familiar face, a name.

Call time had been five. By half past five, the place was nearly full, and extra tables and chairs had to be brought out. Most of the crowd have gone silver: faces behind the bylines, faces you see on television or in movies, faces from one underground meeting or another, faces one had known by other names. It was a mini silver revolution, and Pete’s songs were the background music.

Table talk turned to his work and vignettes from his life. Romy Bohol and Vince Pozon, once advertising’s bad boys and former activists, recalled “Prometheus Unbound,” the 1973 poem Pete slipped past the censors under a pseudonym, published in a crony-owned magazine, its first letters spelling out MARCOS HITLER DIKTADOR TUTA. Romy, then based in Catbalogan, asked for a copy of the magazine from a news vendor. “Wala na. Kinumpiska ng military (There’s none left. The military confiscated it.),” was the reply. Photographer Lito Ocampo, detained for five years during martial law, volunteers that he shared the same detention center with Pete, at Camp Crame. Nick Joaquin made Pete’s release a condition for accepting the National Artist award from Marcos.

blocks.caption: [Rear View] What were you doing in the 90s? Sweating, grumbling, and watching the start of the Marcos Restoration

blocks.text: Salinawit – from salin, to translate, and awit, song – began asa simple idea. Jazz standards and a few pop hits rewritten in Filipino, as adaptations rather than literal translations. Pete would have the lyrics photocopied and given to friends. With Pete, these translated songs, part of the typical piano bar boomer playlist, became classics in their own right, performed in Salinawit gatherings held, on and off, since 2007.

Some of the singers who had carried those songs came back to sing them again. OPM icons like Leah Navarro and Castillo. Navarro sang Pete’s adaptation of “One Note Samba” and “Love Me Tender.” Castillo sang two original compositions from Pete, Sangandaan and Aling Pag-ibig Pa, both from the Mike de Leon movie Sister Stella L. which she originally recorded for the soundtrack. Pete sang along to Sangandaan, and when it ended, Pete wiped away the tears from his face.

Cooky Chua, a Salinawit regular, sang “Kulay-Rosas,” Pete’s take on “La Vie En Rose.” Bayang Barrios joined her for “Kahapon Lang” (“Yesterday”), then sang S’ya (“She”) alone. Mitch Valdez sang “Yun Lang” (“That’s All”). Joey Ayala and Noel Cabangon closed the program’s musical set.
Between the songs came the other Pete Lacabas.

Jackie Lou Blanco read from Sister Stella L., which Pete co-wrote with De Leon, about a nun, played by Vilma Santos, who leaves the convent’s quiet for the picket line. This was Lacaba the screenwriter.

Atom Araullo read from Days of Disquiet, Nights of Rage, Pete’s classic reportage on the First Quarter Storm of 1970. This was Lacaba the journalist, taking you inside the tempest. In this book, compiling articles he wrote for the Asia-Philippines Leader magazine, Pete breaks the old-school rule that a reporter should be a passive, neutral observer. With each demonstration he covered, his convictions surface and harden on the page.

Cooky Chua, Jo-Ann Maglipon and the writers who had been long-time friends with Pete and his late wife, Marra Lanot, helped him choose the songs. Princess Nemenzo sang “La Vie en Rose” in French while Pete answered in Filipino. Those in the room who had shared piano bars and karaoke nights with Pete had heard him sing countless times, but never because someone asked. This evening belonged to him. – Rappler.com
Joey Salgado is a former journalist, and a government and political communications practitioner. He served as spokesperson for former vice president Jejomar Binay.

articles.title: ICC prosecutors seek to present 5 witnesses' prior testimonies in Duterte case
articles.summary: Prosecutors at the International Criminal Court have asked judges to admit the recorded testimonies of five witnesses in the crimes against humanity of murder case against former president Rodrigo…

blocks.text: October 17, 2026 | 10:19am

MANILA, Philippines — Prosecutors at the International Criminal Court (ICC) have asked judges to admit the recorded testimonies of five witnesses in the crimes against humanity of murder case against former president Rodrigo Duterte, saying their accounts could help establish an alleged policy of killing suspected criminals.
In a public filing dated October 16, the prosecution asked Trial Chamber III to admit the testimonies of witnesses identified as P-1087, P-1151, P-1158, P-1161 and P-1204.

The witnesses' accounts cover alleged killings during police operations, the implementation of Operation Double Barrel, the use of a list of suspected criminals during Duterte's presidency and public statements that prosecutors say contributed to a culture in which killings were normalized.
“The Prior Recorded Testimonies of P-1087, P-1151, P-1158, P-1161, and P-1204 are relevant, reliable, and probative,” the prosecution said.

“As [REDACTED], the Five Witnesses provide evidence on [REDACTED]. As such, their evidence is particularly relevant to the policy to 'neutralise' through violent crimes, including murder, alleged criminals in the Philippines and to [REDACTED] to implement this policy,” it added.

The filing, signed by Acting Prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang, seeks to introduce the transcripts of the witnesses' previous interviews and related materials under Rule 68(3) of the ICC's Rules of Procedure and Evidence.

Prosecutors also asked permission to conduct limited follow-up questioning of each witness in court, saying this would shorten their direct examinations and save court time. The estimated time savings were redacted from the public filing.
The application is the prosecution's second request under Rule 68(3) to introduce previously recorded witness testimony in the case.
Witnesses discuss alleged killings

According to the filing, witness P-1087 questioned the accuracy of Philippine National Police reports on killings during police operations and described how killings were allegedly normalized under Duterte.

The prosecution said the testimony included an account of how the President Rodrigo Roa Duterte list, or PRRD list, allegedly gave police officers a sense of impunity. The witness also described Duterte's speeches as contributing to a culture in which killings became normalized.

P-1151's testimony covers alleged killings by police, Operation Double Barrel and the PRRD list. The witness also discussed an alleged reward system, including monetary payments for police officers involved in killings, and Duterte's appointments of personnel to positions prosecutors considered crucial to the alleged crimes.
Prosecutors said these accounts could help establish the alleged policy behind the killings, Duterte's individual criminal responsibility and his alleged knowledge and intent.

The testimonies of P-1158 and P-1161 also concern the alleged policy and Duterte's responsibility. P-1161's account includes information about Duterte's alleged involvement in the PRRD list, although parts of both witnesses' testimonies remain redacted in the public filing.
Witness P-1204 described changes within the PNP after Duterte assumed the presidency and provided hearsay evidence about other killings that prosecutors said reflected a similar pattern.
The prosecution argued that the five accounts were consistent with one another and supported by other evidence it expects to present during the trial.
Defense can cross-examine witnesses

Prosecutors argued that admitting the recorded testimonies would not prejudice Duterte's right to a fair trial because his defense team would still have the opportunity to question the witnesses in court.

“The introduction of the Five Witnesses' Prior Recorded Testimonies into evidence would not be prejudicial to or inconsistent with the rights of the Accused, as the Defence will have ample opportunity to cross-examine them,” the filing said.

“The Defence have been notified of the Prosecution's intention to call these witnesses pursuant to rule 68(3) since 31 August 2026 and have adequate time to prepare for their cross-examination,” it added.

Under the proposed arrangement, each witness would be asked whether they consent to having their recorded statements introduced into the case record. The defense, prosecutors, victims' legal representatives and judges would also have the opportunity to question the witnesses and observe their demeanor during their court appearances.

The prosecution said the interviews were conducted during the ordinary course of its investigation under Article 55 of the Rome Statute and Rule 112 of the ICC's Rules of Procedure and Evidence. According to the filing, all five witnesses were informed that their interviews were voluntary, understood their rights and agreed to proceed.
Prosecutors asked the chamber to grant the application, subject to the other requirements under Rule 68(3).
The ICC has ruled that Duterte is fit to stand trial, clearing the way for proceedings to begin as scheduled on November 30.

The chamber also recently rejected the defense's request to limit the prosecution's evidence to 10,000 items, after the defense argued that the volume of materials disclosed ahead of trial would hamper its preparations.
Duterte faces three counts of crimes against humanity involving alleged murders and attempted murders committed in the Philippines between November 2011 and March 2019.
The case stems from the ICC’s investigation into alleged crimes against humanity linked to killings during Duterte’s anti-drug campaign.
Duterte was arrested in Manila in March 2025 and surrendered to the ICC on March 12, 2025. He remains detained at the ICC Detention Centre in Scheveningen, The Hague, Netherlands.

articles.title: EA producer confirms the return of Wing Commander
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – A panel at the Portland Retro Gaming Expo on game preservation revealed that the master tapes containing high quality source video for Wing Commander III were located. The…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – A panel at the Portland Retro Gaming Expo on game preservation revealed that the master tapes containing high quality source video for Wing Commander III were located.
The contents of these tapes will now undergo restoration and preparation is at work for a new release of the game, tentatively called Wing Commander III 30th Anniversary Edition.
For a certain generation of gamers, somewhere above the age of 30, this is big news. Wing Commander III, subtitled ‘The Heart of the Tiger’ launched way back in 1994.

It was one of the first and most successful games to incorporate full motion video cutscenes alongside its polygonal 3D combat. For these sequences, developer Origin Systems enlisted Hollywood actors such as Mark Hamill, Malcolm McDowell and John Rhys-Davies.

blocks.caption: Wing Commander III stars Ginger Lynn Allen, Mark Hamill and Jennifer MacDonald via Wing Commander CIC

blocks.text: It was all part of a broader trend – one I refer to as ‘the multimedia era’ – in video gaming to flex the storage capacity of CD-ROMs and the growing audiovisual muscle of desktop PC hardware.

This was before specialized 3D hardware became commonplace, so the answer to that was frequently big production values comparable to Hollywood movies, a medium that video games continue to emulate to this day, for better or worse.
Many of these attempts are now historical curiosities at best, willfully forgotten mistakes at worst.
For every The Beast Within: A Gabriel Knight Mystery there is a Psychic Detective and for every The 7th Guest there was a Tender Loving Care.
Today, games like Alan Wake 2 and Immortality are better at incorporating live action performances, making artistic use of them rather than as storytelling crutches.
RELATED STORY: Yu-Gi-Oh! Tag Force GX brings a PSP classic into a new era
The challenge of 30 year old technologies and file formats
Jim Vessella, the senior producer at EA, who hosted the panel, said that the remaster of Wing Commander III will involve brushing off video compression.
He also mentioned features such as “Kilrathi Saga Integration,” and the inclusion of community enhancement patches.
Attendees report that the uncompressed original footage is set to ship with the upscaled version, with a toggle allowing players to switch between them.

blocks.caption: EA senior producer Jim Vessella at Portland Retro Gaming Expo via Wing Commander CIC

blocks.text: Wing Commander III was originally shot on tape with the footage being reduced to 320×240 videos and encoded in an obscure but primitive format known as ‘Xanmovie.’
By comparison, the sequels Wing Commander IV and Wing Commander Prophecy were shot on 35mm film and eventually received limited releases as DVD games with slightly better compression.
The masters for Wing Commander III were believed lost when EA closed Origin in 2004.
Vessella was a producer on this year’s Star Wars: Zero Company, and he also helped lead the charge on a similar remaster, 2020’s Command & Conquer: Remastered Collection.
Vessella’s panel at the Portland Retrogaming Expo has him listed not just as a producer, but as a “driving force in Electronic Arts’ game preservation effort.”
This role has allowed for the digitization of archival assets and the release of source code for classic titles.
RELATED STORY: Why are we playing games that make us work?

articles.title: Mimicking populists will not ease cost of living or boost productivity, Mathias Cormann warns
articles.summary:
Former minister and OECD head urges Australia not to adopt migration caps, with research showing migrants boost employment among Australian-born workers

  • Get our

blocks.text: Australia’s mainstream political parties are being warned not to adopt populist policies such as migration caps to address voters’ grievances over the cost of living.
Instead, Australia’s longest-serving finance minister Mathias Cormann is urging politicians to deliver housing, real wage growth and lower energy costs by boosting productivity.

Now the secretary general for the influential Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), Cormann will deliver an address to the Centre for Independent Studies on Saturday night spruiking productivity as the only way to reliably lower the cost of living over the long term.

Though not directly named in his address, One Nation – which largely runs on an anti-immigration platform – has surged in popularity since the 2025 federal election, with its primary vote reaching 25%, according to the latest Guardian Essential Poll, rising above the Coalition’s 22%.

While populist parties may have gained popularity by speaking to real grievances over rising energy bills, homeownership and real incomes going backwards, Cormann is expected to warn Labor and the Coalition not to follow suit.

“Mainstream parties that respond to a populist surge by adopting its economics do not recover their voters. They lose twice: once to the original, which the electorate will always prefer to the copy, and once to the centre, which has nowhere else to go,” he will say in his address.
“The lesson is consistent: deliver homes, lower energy costs, real wage growth and a credible budget, and the populist tide recedes.
“Mimic the populists, and you simply confirm that they were right all along. The way to defeat populism is to solve the problems it feeds on.”
Cormann will point to “arbitrary migration caps” imposed regardless of their effect on business, hospitals, aged care, or universities.
He will acknowledge more Australians now than any time in 20 years say the migration intake is too high and may support such policies, with many attributing their concerns to housing.
But the answer is to address housing supply, infrastructure, services and the composition of the migration intake, he will say.

According to OECD research across Australia’s regions, in places where more migrants arrived, employment among Australian-born workers grew faster, not slower, with no measurable effect on their wages.
Without migration, Australia’s working-age population would decrease as the number of older people grows.
after newsletter promotion

“An ageing country that chooses to shrink its working-age population while promising to spend more on health, care and defence has not developed a plan – it has put forward a contradiction,” Cormann will say.

Tariffs, which have been imposed by US president Donald Trump and proposed by One Nation, would also fail to address the cost of living and could instead raise costs for farmers, miners and builders, Cormann says.
He believes Australia can only grow its way out of the issue through productivity.
“There is no shortcut to a lower cost of living. There is no populist shortcut, through tariffs and caps and state banks,” he says.
“There is only the long way round: an economy that produces more, competes harder and grows faster than its costs… anyone offering you a quicker route is offering you a poorer country.”

articles.title: Ride-hailing app taps AI to improve customer, driver experience
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – Ride-hailing app, inDrive, wants to use artificial intelligence (AI) to improve mobility in the Philippines while keeping passengers and drivers in control of their choices. The…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Ride-hailing app, inDrive, wants to use artificial intelligence (AI) to improve mobility in the Philippines while keeping passengers and drivers in control of their choices.
The company is exploring how AI can address practical challenges such as traffic, passenger safety and driver earning, in line with its push to make travel decisions more convenient and informed.

“We can transform inDrive from being a mobility platform to being an intelligent movement system where customers are able to make the best choices, aided by technology,” said Mantri during a media roundtable in Makati on October 16.
Mantri said that the challenge is to use AI to improve user experience without removing the human decisions that defined the platform.
He added that inDrive must also adapt its technology to the needs of individual markets like the Philippines.
AI should support decisions, not replace them
inDrive uses AI for several functions, including pricing, vehicle verification and customer support.
Rather than automating decisions, the company uses technology to help both passengers and drivers make informed decisions.
Mantri mentioned that the company’s approach to technology keeps their “super mission” of “challenging injustices” by fair pricing and peer-to-peer model.
For pricing, the platform analyzes historical trends, current demand and available driver supply to help balance the marketplace.
Mantri said AI also accelerates vehicle-image processing, with the technology handling almost 67% of vehicle images processed in driver operations.
This includes making processes for switching from one vehicle to another faster rather than doing things manually.
Globally, he added, generative AI handles around 40% of customer support tickets, allowing human agents to focus on more complicated concerns.
“We’re using AI to help human beings make better decisions. We’re not taking the decision-making authority away from them,” he said.
Mantri described the approach as making advanced technology accessible while adapting it to local conditions.
“We take the best technology available, we democratize it, and we adapt it locally to the super unique, hyper-local needs of markets such as Philippines,” he said.
RELATED STORY: Google partners with DepEd, CHED, TESDA to upskill teachers in AI
Product development starts on the streets
For Mantri, understanding those needs of passengers and drivers, and their challenges they face when using the platform, requires more than studying app data.
He said members of inDrive’s product organization, including himself, must complete at least one field immersion every quarter to observe how passengers and drivers use the service.

“The only option is that my team, including me, we need to spend a considerable amount of our time being out there in the streets, in the dust, in the traffic, and actually observing and studying how our customers are using the product,” he said.
The company also gathers feedback directly from drivers.
Direct remarks, as Mantri claimed, helped the company determine what needs improvement and communicate its responses to the people using the platform.
At a recent driver wellness event in the Philippines, inDrive said around 50 drivers joined discussions with the product team.
Mantri described the process as “closing the loop”: collecting feedback, identifying problems the company can address, and updating drivers on solutions and upcoming features.
The data generated by rides could also help passengers make better-informed choices about routes, travel times and costs.
Autonomous vehicles remain a long-term ambition

inDrive is also exploring how electric and autonomous vehicle technology could work in developing markets, where road conditions, trip distances and affordability differ from those in cities already adopting autonomous mobility.

Mantri acknowledged that autonomous vehicles could replace some driving tasks but said the company does not believe the technology must eliminate drivers’ livelihoods. Instead, he said, inDrive wants to explore ways for drivers to become entrepreneurs as mobility evolves.
The company’s plans remain long-term. Mantri estimated that adapting autonomous mobility for developing markets could take around five to six years, rather than being an initiative for next year.
RELATED STORY: Anthropic sought religious views on AI consciousness

articles.title: The uncertain future of Canada's 30 rescued belugas
articles.summary: An international rescue operation for the last 30 captive whales in Canada made headlines. Then five of them died.

blocks.text: Tofino approached each of his handlers in turn as they knelt in shallow water and stroked his sides.

Shortly after, a crane hoisted the more than 1,500kg beluga whale into a lorry to be shipped out of Canada to his new home, SeaWorld San Antonio - the last of 30 belugas and four dolphins to leave Marineland, a shuttered sea park near Niagara Falls.

Marineland needed to find a new home for its whales. But when the Canadian government rejected its plan to sell them to China over concerns about animal welfare, the park's operations said they would have to be euthanised.

That spurred an international rescue operation by several aquariums, leading to the largest ever transfer of captive whales this summer. But hopes that the animals were headed to a better life have been dampened by a number of deaths in the group.
Photographer Carlos Osorio documented the move, which involved whales being flown to Chicago, Atlanta, San Diego, San Antonio, and even Valencia, Spain.
Osorio recalls watching footage from a drone overhead as Tofino appeared to say his own goodbyes.
Tofino was the last captive whale in Canada. The country banned cetacean captivity and breeding seven years ago, and Osorio felt the weight of the moment.
"This is the last one to happen, and it's never going to happen again," he says.
Despite the rescue operation, tragically, five of the belugas have since died, as well as one dolphin.

Chicago's Shedd Aquarium has seen the most deaths. Peekachu, 23, Rain, 20, Orisis, 26, and Caspian, 27, were all transferred from Marineland, while longtime Shedd resident Beethoven, 34, also died after eight Marineland belugas were brought there over the summer.
Necropsies found chronic inflammatory disease in the gastrointestinal systems in Peekachu and Rain.
Foreign objects were also discovered in their stomachs, including feathers, large rocks and flecks that appear to be paint – objects Shedd believes were ingested before they were moved to Chicago.
Osiris's preliminary examination identified chronic liver disease.

Europe's largest aquarium, Oceanogràfic València in Spain, recorded the death of one beluga, Jelly Bean, and one dolphin, Echo. The dolphin arrived with "serious vision problems" and other health issues, it said, and "began having difficulties swallowing and respiratory problems" in the hours before she died.

Experts say it is too early to judge the outcome of the transfers, especially considering the whales were facing euthanasia and had been living in an ageing facility. According to a tally by the Canadian Press, about 20 whales died at Marineland between 2019 and September 2025.
Once the country's most popular amusement park, Marineland closed in 2024 after years of animal welfare concerns and financial woes, and following the death of its longtime owner.

Public attitudes towards keeping whales in captivity have also changed drastically since Marineland opened in 1961. Like Canada, more countries are moving to ban or restrict the practice, including France and Mexico.

Melissa Matlow, a spokeswoman for World Animal Protection Canada, says that worldwide there are about 3,600 captive cetaceans – a group of marine mammals which includes whales, dolphins and porpoises.
But there are few alternatives for whales raised in captivity without the skills to survive in the wild.
Matlow says that leaves a "growing animal welfare crisis on our hands".
Still, her organisation had concerns about the relocation of the Marineland whales.
"If an animal was not healthy enough to withstand the stress of transport, it should not have been transported," she said in a statement.
In early October, Shedd said it knew some of the Marineland belugas "could have substantial, longstanding medical needs".

Assessments before the move "informed our planning but could not reveal every underlying condition or predict how each whale would respond to the transition. The rescue offered a path to continued, specialised care".
They said the remaining rescued belugas show positive signs, including eating well.

World Animal Protection Canada had suggested two alternatives: repurpose Marineland into a hospice-style facility for the remaining captive whales and dolphins, or fast-track development of a proposed seaside sanctuary in Nova Scotia, the Whale Sanctuary Project.

As they can't be released, "the next best thing we could do is provide sanctuary for them, where they can at least live in the ocean, and they can have back their autonomy", says Lori Marino, a neuroscientist behind the Whale Sanctuary Project, which she hopes could eventually house about 12 to 15 whales.
"I look at it as an exit ramp," she adds.
The project was initiated a decade ago, she said, but construction only began in the last two months. Fundraising is continuing and needs an additional C$6m ($4.2m; £3.1m).
But offshore sanctuaries have yet to be proven a successful solution for retiring performing whales.
One offshore facility for belugas is being created in Iceland, but in July organisers determined that more work was needed, and delayed the introduction of two whales until next summer.

"They are kind of more theoretical and aspirational at this point," says Michael Weiss, research director at the Center for Whale Research in Washington state, who adds that they would definitely "improve the welfare of the animals" compared to concrete tanks.
"It's a very old idea," he says, noting that net pens have been used to rehabilitate injured wild whales, or temporarily used while re-introducing captured orcas back into the wild.

Many critics note that Canada's law banning captivity also banned the breeding of whales - but the places where they were sent do not have the same laws, and some are likely to breed them, perpetuating whale captivity.
Jason Jones, senior curator of animal well-being at Georgia Aquarium, says "breeding is a natural part of an animal's life".
"Breeding is part of good animal welfare, and so we want to make sure that they get the opportunity to do so."
Georgia Aquarium recently took in two male Marineland belugas, named Balor, 10, and Zephyr, 7. They joined the four females already in their care.
They arrived "bright, alert and responsive" and quickly began "vocalising to the females on the other side of the gate", he says.
"There was a little bit of a meeting and greeting period, but afterwards they were all kind of swimming together in a big group."

"They were exploring their new habitat, coming over and participating in sessions, eating and interacting with enrichment. So those were all really positive signs from the get-go, and we've just seen progress since then."
Phil Demers, a former Marineland handler, like many people who the BBC spoke to, said the end of Marineland is "bittersweet".

He's grateful to see the facility shut down, and hopes that Canada's ban will inspire changes in other countries. But for now, the ban won't mean the end of captivity for the Marineland whales, only a change of habitat.
He says for people curious about whales, they should join a whale-watching tour, or watch a nature documentary on TV.
"I'd rather see a whale fart in the wild than do a triple backflip in a tank," he says.

articles.title: There’s a village behind every Likhang Habi piece
articles.summary: ‘It's really about the people behind every craft that we create. It represents the sacrifices, the hard work, the time and effort that they have put into the piece.’

blocks.text: Lists of “slowly dying” traditional art forms almost always include handwoven products as the rise of fast fashion has eclipsed traditional crafts the past decades.
But inside the bustling halls of the 16th Likhang Habi Market Fair, it showcased how younger hands have been trying to revive Filipino weaving traditions.
Algene Fernandez, a 21-year-old weaver, shares that she’s among the young artisans proudly helping keep the tradition alive.
“Ako po, pang-apat na generation na ako sa family namin in this industry (I’m already the fourth generation from our family in this industry),” Algene said.
“It’s really about the people behind every craft that we create. It represents the sacrifices, the hard work, the time and effort that they have put into the piece.”
The market fair, organized by HABI: The Philippine Textile Council, really intends to encourage more young creatives to promote local Filipino art.

“When HABI started, weaving in the Philippines was dying,” said Rambie Lim, a founding member of HABI and a vendor representing the Rurungan Collective. “But through the years of HABI, we’ve really seen the growth and the interest from weavers who are younger.”
​”I think more and more of the younger generation is appreciating it, and the older weavers as well see it as something that they can pass on,” Rambie added.
“In the beginning of HABI, a lot of weavers would say, ‘Ay, hindi, weaver lang ako (No, I’m just a weaver).’ And they didn’t feel that they could or would pass on their skills.”
In recent years, that hesitation has turned into pride.
“Nowadays, that’s what people are looking for: something that’s made by human hands,” shared Adelaida Lim, HABI president emeritus.
“We should value that, and not say that they’re just farmers who do that work. No, they’re also artisans, they’re creatives, and they’re Filipinos.”
This human element is exactly what the market fair bridges. When buyers interact directly with the artisans, a transaction transforms into an education.
“From the customer’s side, they realize, ‘Ah, ang hirap pala gawin (Oh, it’s hard to do),’” Adelaida said. “When the buyer realizes that, they appreciate the product.”

blocks.caption: Accessories, Bag, Handbag

blocks.text: Beyond the labor, buyers also learn about the stories, skills, memories, livelihood, culture, and communities behind these traditional products — and how every piece represents an entire village.

“Weaving is part of the culture, and it expresses what their history was,” said HABI president Mia Villanueva. “It’s a living history. A lot of the things in the textile have symbolism, so the young people have to learn that.”
Aside from the market fair, Likhang Habi recently launched the Lourdes Montinola Piña Weaving Competition for weavers under 30 years old. One of the winners was as young as eight years old.
“Ever since we started the competition, so many new techniques have been revived,” Adelaida shared. “It raised the level of excellence.”

blocks.caption: Furniture, Plant, Crib

blocks.text: For Rambie, young Filipinos can also learn more about their roots through textile.

“​I think people should look back to where their parents are from and see, because if we ask the elders, we’ll find out we also have a weaving tradition that was like forgotten,” Rambie said. “I grew up in Lipa, Batangas, and there are two groups now that are actually pushing forward and will be part of HABI.”
“​So there’s a lot. And I think our challenge is to come to HABI and explore — explore your own identity as Filipinos through the textile.”
Toni Rose Jazmin, who collects woven fabrics from different provinces, said they’re “worth every thread.”
“For me, every thread has a story; every thread is a story. So I just want to showcase that woven fabric in the Philippines is very beautiful,” shared Toni Rose.
“Behind it, the people, the artisans — they are amazing and talented. Especially the ones I’m working with from Bicol weavers, Camarines Sur, from Abra, from Kalinga, and from Bukidnon.”

blocks.caption: Home Decor, Linen, Accessories

blocks.text: Environmentally, the revival also comes at a critical time as the global textile industry relies heavily on cheap, synthetic fabrics like polyester, which clog landfills and pollute waterways.
In contrast, traditional Philippine weaving promotes sustainability as local weaving communities stick to indigenous, natural fibers like cotton and abaca.
“The polyester that they blend with cotton creates all kinds of pollution and garbage,” said Adelaida. “Whereas if they were to stay with cotton, it goes back again to the environment.”
“The weaving industry in the Philippines is actually something that’s very sustainable if it gets going,” she added. “It has a role to play in climate change.”
This advocacy also draws in a new demographic: the more environmentally conscious youth.

“​I really hope that the next generations take it on, because it’s not just a leadership role, it’s a responsibility,” said Adelaida. “You can’t just be responsible to us Filipinos; you’re responsible to the whole of the environment.”

blocks.caption: Blouse, Clothing, Lace

blocks.text: Looking forward, HABI hopes to expand its grassroots footprint by supporting young artisans through various programs and activities.

“It starts with interest, exposure — exposure generates interest,” said Maribel Ongpin, chairman emeritus of HABI. “Young people immediately embraced it. Then suddenly, fashion designers joined. And once that started, it became a mass movement, in a sense.” – Rappler.com
Angel Camille Dio is a Rappler intern studying BA Journalism at Polytechnic University of the Philippines.

articles.title: Baligod, 4 ex-bodyguards of Zaldy Co post bail
articles.summary: Lawyer Levito Baligod and four former bodyguards of ex-lawmaker Zaldy Co posted bail and were freed on Friday after their arrest in San Juan City.

blocks.text: Published October 17, 2026 8:55am
Lawyer Levito Baligod and four former bodyguards of ex-Ako Bicol party-list Representative Zaldy Co posted bail and were freed on Friday after their arrest in San Juan City.
They were freed after 5 p.m., according to a report by GMA News reporter Jun Veneracion.
Ten other former bodyguards of Co meanwhile were not able to post bail in time on Friday before office hours ended.
San Juan City Police chief Police Colonel Anthony Gantang earlier said Baligod and the others were arrested at the San Juan Hall of Justice at around 9:30 a.m. Friday.
Baligod was at the Hall of Justice to attend a court hearing.
The arrest warrant was reportedly issued by the Iba, Zambales Regional Trial Court Branch 69, which set the bail at P10,000 each.
“Doon po sa warrant of arrest niya, ang nakalagay po ay, ang kaso ay unjust vexation, in relation to RA 10175. ‘Yun pong Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012,” Gantang said.
(The warrant of arrest states that the case is unjust vexation in relation to RA 10175, the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012.)

To recall, the bodyguards previously claimed that they delivered suitcases of cash to President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr., Leyte Representative and former Speaker Martin Romualdez, and other individuals. Marcos, Romualdez, and others have denied the allegations.
However, in August, four of the 18 signed affidavits recanted their allegations. They said they just wanted to live quietly, adding that there are threats to their lives. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: A thousand slogans echoed here - but it could be the end for iconic Delhi protest site
articles.summary: Jantar Mantar, an 18th Century site almost synonymous with demonstrations in Delhi, has been denotified as a protest site.

blocks.text: A thousand slogans echoed here - but it could be the end for iconic Delhi protest site

blocks.caption: Image caption, The "cockroach" demonstrations over the summer of 2026 could well become the last time Jantar Mantar was home to a sustained protest movement

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
The "cockroach" demonstrations over the summer of 2026 could well become the last time Jantar Mantar was home to a sustained protest movement
BySharanya Hrishikesh
BBC News, Delhi
What is the point of a protest?
To raise your voice against injustice? To draw attention to a cause? Or to make those in power uncomfortable enough to listen?
For more than three decades, Indians have tried to do all three in a narrow, tree-lined road near Jantar Mantar, an 18th Century astronomical obervatory in Delhi.
But that may now be coming to an end.
This week, Delhi Police said Jantar Mantar, located close to parliament, would no longer be a designated protest site.

The decision comes months after the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - not a political party but a collective which began as a joke - led a massive protest there demanding the resignation of federal education minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Tens of thousands turned up and Pradhan subsequently resigned.

Police barricaded Jantar Mantar soon afterwards, preventing further demonstrations. Last week, an attempt by CJP supporters to march there, this time demanding the resignation of India's election chief, ended in a police crackdown.

Protesters have now been directed to three other sites. Two are far from parliament, while the third, the sprawling Ramlila Ground, is often booked months in advance. Unlike Jantar Mantar, which is free, all three charge tens of thousands of rupees a day.

Delhi Police says, external it acted after the Supreme Court suggested identifying alternative sites with adequate infrastructure. But critics say the move could push protests beyond the reach of ordinary Indians, further from the seat of power and into venues many cannot afford.

Over the years, Jantar Mantar has witnessed everything from mass movements that shook governments to small, lonely demonstrations by people desperate to be heard. Farmers, students, grieving parents and ex-soldiers have gathered under its trees, holding placards and shouting slogans. Not every protest made headlines, but for many, it was a place to turn to when other doors had closed.
This week, when the BBC visited, those scenes seemed a distant memory.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Jantar Mantar is an 18th Century astronomical observatory in Delhi - the protests were held not in it, but in the road next to it

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Jantar Mantar is an 18th Century astronomical observatory in Delhi - the protests were held not in it, but in the road next to it
Yellow barricades blocked both ends of the road, with hundreds of paramilitary personnel standing guard, batons in hand.

In a nearby lane, uniformed men sat in shops drinking tea or scrolling through their phones. At one of the few shops without policemen, the shopkeeper folded his hands and said he did not want to answer any questions.
Built by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II in the 1720s, Jantar Mantar was once better known as a tourist attraction than a place where a thousand revolutions were imagined.
Its story as a protest site began in 1993, when the then-Congress government stopped allowing demonstrations at the Boat Club lawns opposite the old parliament.
Historian Harleen Kaur has traced how, from the 1960s onwards, successive governments brought in new rules that shifted the site of protest in Delhi further away from parliament.

"Jantar Mantar, situated 3km (1.86 miles) from the Parliament House, [allowed the government] to contain protesting crowds at some distance from the Parliament House and PM's residence," she wrote in a 2023 paper, external.
Yet, the road saw countless spirited protests over the years.

Rachna Dhingra, an activist with the Bhopal Group for Information and Action, an advocacy group for survivors of a 1984 gas leak disaster, camped at Jantar Mantar with hundreds of others for around five months in 2008, trying to get the government to agree to demands including setting up a commission to allocate resources for rehabilitation schemes.

Through a scorching summer, they held press conferences, met politicians and even chained themselves to railings opposite then Prime Minister Manmohan Singh's residence to draw attention to their cause.

It was also where she formed solidarities with others - Tibetans protesting against China, activists opposing the displacement of people over large dam projects and even just lone protesters who caught a train from their home towns with nothing but a placard and a grievance.
"It can be lonely to protest but that place became a home for so many of us. We shared each other's stories, struggles and victories," says Dhingra.

blocks.caption: Image caption, In 2008, Rachna Dhingra and other activists camped for months at Jantar Mantar demanding justice for survivors of the deadly 1984 gas leak in Bhopal - when it rained, they sheltered under tarpaulin sheets

blocks.text: Image source, Courtesy Rachna Dhingra

In 2008, Rachna Dhingra and other activists camped for months at Jantar Mantar demanding justice for survivors of the deadly 1984 gas leak in Bhopal - when it rained, they sheltered under tarpaulin sheets

Dipa Sinha, an academic associated with the Right to Food campaign, has seen ground-breaking laws - a landmark rural jobs guarantee scheme, the National Food Safety Act and Forest Rights Act - take shape at Jantar Mantar.
"It was a place where you could discuss issues with people who came to Delhi from across the country," she says.

Protesters would demonstrate outside government offices, including the erstwhile Planning Commission and the agriculture ministry, where they were often detained by police, before returning to Jantar Mantar to "gather, discuss and strategise".
But sustaining a protest for months was not easy.
Dhingra says they sheltered under tarpaulin sheets when it rained, used public toilets near the site and went to nearby gurdwaras to freshen up.
In 2017, the National Green Tribunal cited the lack of infrastructure, along with complaints from locals, to have Jantar Mantar shut down for protests.
A year later, the Supreme Court overturned this, citing the rights to free speech and peaceful assembly guaranteed under the constitution.
When asked whether the proximity to parliament made a difference to their cause, Dhingra quoted the reactions of her co-protesters who had come to Delhi for the first time.
"That's the president's house? Does the prime minister live there? How can they not listen to us when we are at their gates?" she remembered them saying.
Sinha points out that Jantar Mantar was also near institutions like the Press Club and Constitution Club, making it easier to get media coverage, and for politicians to drop by and meet protesters.
It was a simpler time - sometimes they would ask for permission from police only on the morning of the protest.
Those rules have become much stricter, external now.
In recent years, when Dhingra tried to protest at Jantar Mantar, she was told no-one could stay the night.
"Where do you go with hundreds of people who have travelled all the way to the capital to protest?" she asks.

blocks.caption: Image caption, In 2006, Narmada Bachao Andolan (Save the Narmada river movement) leader Medha Patkar (grey sari), sat on a 20-day hunger strike at Jantar Mantar

blocks.text: In 2006, Narmada Bachao Andolan (Save the Narmada river movement) leader Medha Patkar (grey sari), sat on a 20-day hunger strike at Jantar Mantar

blocks.caption: Image caption, In 2015, retired soldiers held protests at Jantar Mantar against the delay in the implementation of a pension scheme

blocks.text: In 2015, retired soldiers held protests at Jantar Mantar against the delay in the implementation of a pension scheme
While Jantar Mantar has its supporters, others share memories of an even more vibrant protest culture.

Mary E John, a gender studies scholar who lived in Delhi both as a student and as an academic, says that before 1993, she attended protests at the Boat Club on issues ranging from workers' rights and women's issues to topics of international significance.
"We lived in a climate where protest was part of life. In fact, we took it for granted," she says.
When the spacious Boat Club lawns made way for Jantar Mantar, it actually felt "claustrophobic", she said.
She pointed out that they, and others before and after them, protested at multiple sites - universities, colleges, streets - instead of just at Jantar Mantar.
She sees signs of that in protests by farmers who camped at Delhi's borders for months, and people who sat at the Shaheen Bagh neighbourhood demanding the repeal of a controversial citizenship law.
Even the 2012 anti-rape protests, she points out, were not restricted to Jantar Mantar but almost reached the Indian president's heavily guarded complex and beyond into other parts of Delhi.
It's not clear what Jantar Mantar's future is - the Supreme Court is hearing pleas challenging its removal as a protest site.
Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and CJP leaders have said that Jantar Mantar belongs to the people and will be "reclaimed".
As the debate rages on, Jantar Mantar is the quietest it has been in decades - will it hear slogans again?

articles.title: [Vantage Point] When a paycheck runs out before payday
articles.summary: True economic recovery means that families can reliably meet ordinary expenses, systematically repay their debts, and still retain something for unforeseen emergencies

blocks.text: Rising prices and a persistently weaker peso are actively squeezing household budgets across the country, creating a quiet but mounting financial strain. Alongside these pressures, there is growing evidence of trouble with credit-card repayments which raises a difficult and urgent question: how much of today’s consumer spending can families afford without compromising their future financial stability?
A national economy can easily maintain its outward momentum even when its individual households are running dangerously short of cash.
Day by day, groceries still reach the kitchen table, children still manage to get to school, and fuel still goes into private and public vehicles for the daily commute.

However, when everyday expenses outlast the payday cycle, spending continues only as financial strain accumulates behind the scenes. Today’s retail purchase undeniably supports current economic activity, but the resulting financial obligation ruthlessly follows the family into the next month.
When assessing the true health of the economy, it pays to look beyond the usual headline forecasts for Philippine economic growth, inflation, and currency valuation.

A far more revealing question is whether families earn enough to sustain their current spending habits, or whether they increasingly need to rely on high-interest credit to bridge the widening gap between their stagnant incomes and escalating daily costs.

While aggregate banking figures cannot identify every individual borrower’s specific grocery or utility purchases, they clearly show when repayment troubles begin to grow faster than the credit supporting those transactions.

Recent data from the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) for universal and commercial banks, as presented by Estella Dhel Villamiel, First Metro Securities department head for institutional research, illustrate this trend.

Speaking before the bi-monthly forum of the Monday Circle Group at the Westin Manila, Villamiel says credit-card receivables reached P1.294 trillion in June, a notable increase from P1.229 trillion in March.

Over that exact same period, non-performing card receivables—the balances going unpaid—rose from P61.07 billion to P68.28 billion. These quarterly increases represent an overall portfolio growth of approximately 5.3%, but a much steeper 11.8% jump in bad debts.

Because troubled balances grew more than twice as fast as the overall lending portfolio, their total share was lifted from 4.97% to 5.28%. Although these figures represent amounts owed rather than the absolute number of distressed borrowers, the aggressive upward direction warrants immediate attention.

To be clear, this data does not definitively establish a full-blown household debt crisis. Card usage naturally expands as more consumers enter the formal financial system, transition away from cash-based transactions, or simply utilize convenient payment terms for routine shopping.

Furthermore, outstanding receivables temporarily include affluent customers who reliably settle their statements in full each month. While aggregate figures do not strictly prove that families are swiping their cards just to buy basic food or fuel, they establish the defensible and narrow finding that repayment stress is noticeably increasing within an expanding credit portfolio.

The broader economic environment makes this subtle warning much harder to dismiss. September inflation reached a punishing 7.2%, up significantly from 6.1% in August. Every family’s individual burden depends heavily on their specific basket of purchases, but consumers with little discretionary money left after buying essentials have far fewer ways to absorb these higher prices.

Each of the options available to them—cutting back on consumption, depleting emergency savings, seeking exhausting additional work, or borrowing—carries a heavy toll. Borrowing simply shifts that cost, with interest, into another month.

Global oil prices and the weakening peso compound this pressure through nearly every ordinary transaction. Expensive imported fuel inevitably raises overhead costs for motorists, transport operators, and logistics businesses moving goods across the archipelago.

Simultaneously, a weaker peso directly inflates the local cost of all dollar-priced imports. Families feel these relentless pressures through rising transport fares, delivery charges, and the inflated cost of goods transported over long distances, even if they do not own a car or purchase imported luxury items.

While access to credit softens the immediate blow of these price shocks, carrying a rollover balance creates an entirely new monthly expense. Consider an illustrative P20,000 balance charged at a standard 3% for just one month: the interest alone would be P600, calculated before any other applicable late fees, charges, and adjustments.

Actual billing depends on specific card terms and payment timing, but once interest permanently enters the household budget, a portion of the next paycheck is automatically hijacked to pay for past spending rather than putting anything new on the family table.

It would be convenient for analysts to blame these repayment difficulties entirely on careless or financially illiterate borrowers. However, making that assumption requires concrete evidence, in the same way that claiming every unpaid balance represents genuine economic hardship does.

blocks.caption: [In This Economy] Should Filipinos’ ‘consumption culture’ be blamed for the weak peso?

blocks.text: A serious examination must carefully distinguish between frivolous discretionary spending, sudden income disruption, and the desperate cycle of repeated borrowing. It must also recognize that cardholders represent only a fraction of the wider population. Millions of families outside the formal credit market face severe financing pressures that banking tables simply cannot capture or measure.
Labor market data reflect this underlying fragility. In August, the national unemployment rate hit 5.3%, compared to just 3.9% a year earlier, while underemployment reached 11.9%, up from 10.7%.

While both metrics showed slight improvements from July, they remain worse than the previous year’s readings. Simply having work and having enough work to pay the bills are entirely different household experiences. The consistent availability of sufficient income matters just as much as its baseline purchasing power.

Villamiel provided this critical macro research: The snapshot included forecasts from the DBS Bank (formerly the Development Bank of Singapore) projecting inflation to average a painful 6.5% in 2026 and 5.5% in 2027, with the peso heavily depreciating to P64 per dollar by the end of 2027. These sobering projections strongly suggest that household financial pressure could stubbornly persist even as overall macroeconomic growth improves.

This dynamic is already visible in the national accounts. Household consumption managed to grow by 2.8% in the second quarter, and Gross Domestic Product (GDP) expanded by 2.3%, but gross capital formation alarmingly plummeted by 9.2%.

Because capital investment is the crucial engine that builds the business capacity and employment necessary for future income generation, its severe contraction should shift the national economic discussion well beyond merely encouraging consumers to spend more. Debt and credit cannot indefinitely substitute for the robust economic foundation that makes consumer spending truly affordable.

The BSP now faces a highly difficult balancing act. Implementing a firm monetary policy can theoretically contain runaway inflation and stabilize currency pressure, but these tighter financing conditions weigh heavily on both retail borrowers and corporate employers. (READ: [Puso at Diwa] BSP monetary policy: When steady is not really steady)

Furthermore, existing credit card charges do not automatically change with every policy-rate adjustment: a lower BSP rate would not retroactively erase the crushing balances already accumulated by households.
Genuine financial relief will require dedicated attention to real incomes, essential living costs, and repayment capacity alongside strict monetary stability.
Moving forward, commercial banks must closely monitor retail affordability and deteriorating accounts with the exact same vigilance they apply to portfolio growth.

Meanwhile, the government must aggressively work to restore financial breathing room by ensuring reliable food supplies, building efficient transport and energy systems, encouraging productive capital investment, and strengthening consumer protection.

Aggregate consumer spending can often look incredibly resilient on paper while individual family budgets simultaneously become dangerously fragile. The ultimate test of economic health is whether families can comfortably cover their essential needs without repeatedly carrying yesterday’s expenses into tomorrow.

While the upcoming surge in Christmas purchases may soon offer artificially reassuring signs of retail activity, the inevitable credit statements arriving in January should be watched with equal, if not greater, interest.
True economic recovery means that families can reliably meet ordinary expenses, systematically repay their debts, and still retain something for unforeseen emergencies.
When the paycheck consistently runs out before payday, securing a higher credit limit merely postpones the inevitable reckoning. It does not repair the broken household budget. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Trump 'completely wrong' to restrict support for Ukraine, Italian minister tells BBC
articles.summary: Defence Minister Guido Crosetto tells the BBC the US risks prolonging Russia's full-scale invasion rather than helping to end it.

blocks.text: Italy's defence minister has said it is a "complete mistake, a major mistake" for the US to limit access to satellite systems and intelligence used by Ukraine to defend itself against Russian attacks.

In a BBC interview, Guido Crosetto warned that any such move by US President Donald Trump's administration "makes absolutely no sense" and risked prolonging Russia's full-scale invasion rather than helping to bring peace.

US officials have said Trump has not asked for the slowdown of internet speeds the US provides to Ukraine and which are vital for its war effort. Trump has also denied that the US has stopped sharing early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks with Ukraine.
Crosetto's comments continue Italy's sharpening criticism of the US.
Earlier this week, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called Trump's deal to buy diesel from Russia a "very risky choice", and said it would "grant Russia legitimacy" as it bombed cities in Ukraine.
Trump agreed the deal with Vladimir Putin, blaming Kyiv's own attacks on Russian refineries for rising fuel prices.
Meloni, once considered so close to the US president she was dubbed a "Trump whisperer", said the move ran counter to efforts to bring Putin to the negotiating table.
"Peace will come when Putin is convinced there is a stalemate, that he cannot advance any further," her defence minister told the BBC at his ministry building in Rome.
Crosetto was a co-founder of Meloni's hard-right Fratelli d'Italia party, which has led a right-wing government coalition since 2022, shortly after the start of Russia's full-scale war.
"If [Putin] sees weakness on the Ukrainian side – and if the US deprives Ukraine of resources, that creates weakness – then he will believe he can win. So he will continue the war," Crosetto warned.
"I think that is completely wrong."
Despite widespread public scepticism, Meloni's Italian government has been a strong ally of Ukraine from the start, sending both military and humanitarian aid.
The specifics of those deliveries have always been classified.

In our interview, the defence minister vowed that Italian military support would continue "for as long as this government is in place", though he warned that getting parliament to approve further deliveries would be "more difficult" as elections approached.
The vote has to take place by the end of 2027 and opinion polls currently put a new far-right party, Futuro Nazionale, ahead of all Meloni's coalition partners.

That party's leader, former general Roberto Vannacci, is openly sympathetic to Russia and opposes aiding Ukraine, arguing that Europe is wasting its money as Russia's military "continues to advance" on the ground.
At a recent event in Tuscany, he described himself as "neither pro-Putin nor pro-Russian" but "pro-Italian".
Crosetto brushed off questions about Vannacci, including on whether his views reflected those of many Italians, saying he had more "serious matters to deal with".
But, perhaps to underline the difference, he was unequivocal on Russia.

"When one state crosses another state's border with tanks, when it bombs hospitals and schools, kills civilians and bombs power plants, and has been doing so for four years, I can only describe that as evil," he said.
But Italians, like many Europeans, are seeing prices go up, driven by the high cost of energy.
During street protests in Rome on Friday, where firecrackers were thrown, secondary school students complained that resources were being diverted to arms, instead of education.
Some chanted: "We want more classroom, not more bombs."
In southern Italy, truckers have begun blocking roads complaining at the hike in fuel prices.

Polls here regularly show that a majority of Italians want an end to military aid for Ukraine. One, conducted for the Ixè institute in September, put support for continuing to supply arms at just 18%.

There are many factors behind that, from a long-standing pacifist tradition to a history of strong business ties to Moscow. Unlike Poland or the Baltic states, Italy feels physically distant from the danger, too.
But the defence minister also blamed an active campaign of disinformation by Moscow – targeting, he said, "certain political figures... and narratives to weaken the political climate against Russia".
"In some way they shift public opinion," the minister argued.

"It's very hard to explain to a citizen who's having trouble at the petrol pump that we can't give any concessions to Russia right now. But that's the only way to defend the future of that very citizen who's complaining."
Italy has not been targeted for major acts of sabotage, unlike other allies of Ukraine in Europe.
The minister said a fire at an arms depot outside Rome in August was not arson, but "human stupidity".
A report last month that Russia was planning to launch drone attacks at Italy, France and Spain from the container ships in the Mediterranean was not proven, Crosetto also told us.
But cyber-attacks, which he linked to Russia, were now routine - "there are hundreds every day" - and he believed Europe had been too weak in its response.
"You can't win a war... if you don't fight back," the minister said.
With additional reporting from Rome by Davide Ghiglione.

articles.title: Homes burn in Southern California amid fast-moving fire, prompting evacuation orders
articles.summary: A fast-moving fire burned at least four homes in Southern California as hot, windy weather gripped the region Friday, prompting evacuations and power outages. TV footage showed homes burning in San…

image.caption: Flames are seen in San Juan Capistrano, Calif., on Friday. (Patrick T. Fallon/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

A fast-moving fire burned at least four homes in Southern California as hot, windy weather gripped the region Friday, prompting evacuations and power outages. TV footage showed homes burning in San Juan Capistrano in Orange County, flames engulfing them.
Wildfire started in the coastal city of San Clemente
Aerial footage from TV crews showed firefighters spraying two-storey suburban homes with flames leaping out of their roofs. Black smoke billowed over tennis courts and backyard swimming pools.
The Orange County Fire Authority said four homes have burned in the Norte Fire and that two evacuation shelters have opened. It asked those under evacuation orders to "leave now."
The wildfire started in the coastal city of San Clemente and was driven by the wind into San Juan Capistrano.
Multiple fires in region

The Norte Fire was one of several fires burning in the region that was hit by dry, warm and gusty northeast winds known as Santa Anas, which blow from the interior of Southern California toward the coast and offshore.
The strongest winds were expected through Friday afternoon, but conditions that increase the fire risk were expected to last through Saturday night.
Firefighters attempt to save structures in San Clemente, Calif., while battling the Norte Fire on Friday. (Paul Bersebach/The Orange County Register/The Associated Press)
The fires have led to evacuations and tens of thousands of people in the state are without power after their electricity was turned off.

The cities are in southern Orange County near the coast and surrounded by hillsides. San Juan Capistrano, a city of 35,000, is known for horse trails while nearby San Clemente, which is home to 62,000 people, is known as a "Spanish village by the sea" and popular with beachgoers and surfers.
Fire 'right up on the city'
Victor Cabral, a city council member in San Clemente, said schools have been closed and activities cancelled, and thousands were being asked to evacuate.
Traffic is seen moving along Interstate 5, toward the Norte Fire, in San Juan Capistrano, Calif., on Friday. (Patrick T. Fallon/AFP/Getty Images)
"The fire is right up on the city," he said. "It's on the perimeter of our homes on the north end."

A blaze in Malibu, Calif., a coastal town west of Los Angeles, prompted evacuation orders and warnings for a large swath of the Santa Monica Mountains. A large cloud of black smoke over the hilltops could be seen on nearby cameras and kilometres away.
Winds from 32 km/h to 56 km/h were expected Friday, with gusts forecast to reach 80 km/h to 112 km/h in some areas, the U.S. National Weather Service said.
With humidity levels dropping, "this will favour a critical fire weather threat," the service said early Friday.
Hundreds of firefighters battle Bryson Fire

More than 400 firefighters battled the Bryson Fire overnight, which was at 100 hectares on Friday morning. It had threatened a Los Angeles County juvenile detention and rehabilitation facility, which was evacuated Thursday night.
A firefighting helicopter is seen dropping water on the Bryson Fire on Thursday. (David Swanson/Reuters)

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who faced criticism for her city's response to deadly fires in 2025, directed the fire department to deploy personnel and equipment ahead of the winds. The fire department also requested assistance from the state's office of emergency services.
"It's a pretty widespread event of elevated fire weather, so the whole SoCal region should really be on alert," said Rose Schoenfeld, a meteorologist with the U.S. National Weather Service.

The Santa Anas could reach 32 to 64 km/h, with gusts from 80 to 113 km/h, in the San Gabriel mountains in Los Angeles County and the Santa Susana mountains, which are mostly in Ventura County, Schoenfeld said. Elevated, though brief, critical fire weather conditions were also forecast for portions of the Santa Lucia mountains in San Luis Obispo County.
Several blazes in Southern California
Firefighters on Friday worked to contain two other fires that had sparked Thursday afternoon and triggered evacuation orders in the city of Azusa, Calif., and Camp Pendleton, near San Diego.
More than 175,000 customers in northern, central and southern California were without electricity as of Friday, according to poweroutage.com.

Some of California's worst wildfires have been sparked by power equipment, and utilities in recent years have begun proactively shutting off power during dry, windy weather in an effort to prevent blazes.
A wind-driven fire in Azusa, Calif., burned over 16 hectares on Thursday. (Jae C. Hong/The Associated Press)

A wind-driven fire in Azusa, Calif., burned over 16 hectares on Thursday and briefly prompted evacuation orders for a neighbourhood in the foothills of the San Gabriel mountains. Forward progress on the blaze had been stopped by midafternoon.
Farther south, a fire at Camp Pendleton threatened buildings. Evacuation orders were issued in the Las Flores area of the military base and lifted by evening, military officials said in a statement.
