articles.title: Brush fires set homes ablaze in southern California as it braces for more hot weather
articles.summary:
Hot, windy weather stokes fires in southern California with mandatory evacuation orders in place for many

A fast-moving fire has spread into neighborhoods in southern California as the…
articles.byline: Lois Beckett and Gabrielle Canon in Dana Point, and agencies

blocks.text: A fast-moving fire has spread into neighborhoods in southern California as the region braces for more hot, windy weather that will amplify fire dangers through Saturday.

Several homes could be seen ablaze in video footage captured by local news helicopters as firefighters worked to wrangle the more than 465 acre Norte fire, which erupted in Orange county on Friday. Damage and destruction estimates have not yet been released by officials, but Orange county fire authority captain Steve Concialdi told KTLA that the fire had impacted at least six homes.
Photos taken by the local TV news station showed a row of houses at the end of a cul-de-sac reduced to blackened debris. Others were coated red by fire retardant.

Tens of thousands in the coastal communities of San Juan Capistrano and San Clemente were under mandatory evacuation orders by Friday afternoon. Flames aggressively ripped across the brush-covered hillsides, shrouding the sky in thick smoke. Sirens wailed through the city streets, as the hum of helicopters and aircraft echoed from above.
Nine schools in the area dismissed early , as the Orange county fire authority urged all residents under the order to leave quickly.
Just to the south, a blaze dubbed the Henderson fire, which erupted in San Diego Marine Corps training base Camp Pendleton on Thursday, swept across more than 2,000 acres by Friday afternoon

blocks.caption: Evacuation orders in place after wildfire breaks out in California - loop

blocks.text: Videos of the incident shared by the California department of forestry and fire protection showed a wall of flames that thrashed in the strong winds alongside the Interstate 5. The major highway was closed in both directions by California Highway Patrol as plumes of thick black smoke clouded visibility.

A blaze in Malibu, west of Los Angeles, covered roughly 146 acres and was 17% contained on Friday. Evacuation orders and warnings for a large swathe of the Santa Monica Mountains were still in effect.
More than 285 firefighters battled the Bryson fire overnight, which threatened a Los Angeles county juvenile detention and rehabilitative facility.

Facing daytime highs of up to 92F (33C) with wind gusts reaching up to 65mph, fire officials said “crews will continue to protect structures and build containment” in a morning update, adding that fire progression and flare ups could occur under increasing winds.
More than 7,200 structures remained under threat, but none have been reported damaged or destroyed by the Bryson fire.

Lindsey Horvath, the Los Angeles county supervisor, thanked firefighters “who held the line to make sure that despite these challenging winds, no lives or structures were put in harm’s way” by the blaze. asked local residents to keep roads clear to make it easier for emergency responders to operate.

There were “only minor injuries” to the more than 400 firefighters working to contain the Bryson blaze, Anthony Morrone, the Los Angeles fire chief, said during a press conference held on Friday morning.

The blazes broke out during a high wind event that has increased fire risks across southern California. Dry, warm and gusty north-east winds known as Santa Anas, which blow from the interior of southern California toward the coast and offshore, could continue through Saturday, according to the National Weather Service, and the potential for extreme fire behavior and rapid spread may still rise.

blocks.caption: Firefighters battle the Bryson fire, a wind-driven wildfire in the hills east of Malibu, California, on Thursday. Photograph: David Swanson/Reuters

blocks.text: “It’s a pretty widespread event of elevated fire weather, so the whole SoCal region should really be on alert,” said Rose Schoenfeld, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service.
Fire hazards typically rise in southern California during this time of year, and risks are expected to remain high into November. If there aren’t significant rains, they could extend longer.
Because some of the state’s worst wildfires in recent years have been sparked by power equipment, utilities proactively shut off power to more than 150,000 customers across the state.

In Los Angeles, the mayor, Karen Bass, who faced criticism for her city’s response to deadly fires in 2025, directed the fire department to deploy personnel and equipment ahead of the winds. The fire department also requested assistance from the state’s office of emergency services.

Schoenfeld said the Santa Ana winds are not going to be as strong as those that fueled a deadly firestorm in early 2025, that destroyed thousands of homes and killed more than 30 peoplewhen gusts reached up to 100mph.
But she still urged residents to be ready.
“We are still in red flag conditions through 8pm [Saturday] evening,” Horvath said . “It’s important that we stay vigilant and stay prepared.”

articles.title: Oregon teacher fought school attacker before armed dad shot suspect 'multiple times'
articles.summary: The 16-year-old suspect previously attended the primary school and had targeted a special educational needs classroom, police say.

blocks.text: Police say the suspect was armed with about 44 more rounds of shotgun ammunition when he was stopped. He fired as many as 15 rounds in the class.

"To the people who showed courage in the face of such violence, and intervened to prevent this tragedy from being any worse, we owe you a debt of gratitude," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said on Friday.

Police offered more information on the attack at at a news conference on Friday, where they identified two of the four victims. They include five-year-old Rhoam Summer and 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert.
The families of the two other students who were killed, an eight-year-old and 11-year-old, did not wish to have them publicly identified yet, police said.
Two others were injured in the attack. Another teacher, a 54-year-old, was still being treated at hospital, and a seven-year-old student, who was in serious but stable condition.
Krantz said the heroic actions of both the teacher and the father who ran inside the school saved lives.
He said the teacher who wrestled with the gunman was not hurt but "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed".
He identified the suspect as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, who previously attended the school and was a special educational needs student there.
A search warrant has been executed at the suspect's home and a search is ongoing, the police chief said.
Police believe the suspect travelled to the elementary school on foot, but police are still investigating his exact movements and how he acquired the gun. A motive is also not clear.
Officials did not confirm the name of the father who intervened and fatally shot the suspect.
But Kaylub Giamanco's family has identified him to US media as the person who sprang into action.

The 36-year-old carpenter had just finished lunch and was on his way home when he passed the school, his brother told NBC News. He saw the suspect open fire on a vehicle outside the school then shoot through a window and go inside.

Police said he had a legally concealed .40 caliber in his vehicle and his brother said he grabbed the pistol "and decided to go in after" the suspect. Police say he fired at the suspect "multiple times", killing him.
In a statement to the BBC's partner CBS News, Giamanco's family said he is a "lifelong resident of Bend" and that he "is not seeking recognition".

The family said Giamanco wants to express his "gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support". He and his family "respectfully ask for privacy".
US President Donald Trump praised the bystander's actions on Friday, calling him a "great hero".
Addressing reporters at the White House before departing for Georgia, Trump said the situation could have been "much worse" with no intervention.
"It's a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it," he said.

Without naming the bystander, Governor Kotek acknowledged the man's heroic actions stopping further loss of life, but noted they "carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well".
Kayla Epstein contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trial of German steakhouse heiress that sparked a huge spy scandal
articles.summary: For 15 months, a high-security courtroom in Hamburg has been hearing the case of Christina Block, accused of ordering the abduction of her children.

blocks.text: It is a trial that has gripped Germany, with a wealthy heiress in the dock for months and a case that triggered the country's biggest espionage scandal in recent history.

Christina Block, heir to a popular chain of steakhouses, is accused of ordering an Israeli security firm to carry out the violent abduction of her children from Denmark, following a bitter custody battle with her former husband.
There are allegedly connections with at least two former secret agents, from Germany and Israel.
In the latest twist, investigators in the case stumbled across evidence that has led to Germany's former intelligence chief, August Hanning, being arrested this month for treason and espionage.

Hanning's arrest stunned the intelligence community. Although his case has nothing to do with the Hamburg trial, he has denied allegations of involvement in an earlier attempted abduction of the children.
There was enormous media interest in Germany when Christina Block and six others went on trial in a high-security courtroom in Hamburg in July last year.

Block House restaurants, specialising in steak and baked potatoes, are a feature of many German towns. Their success over the past half century has helped make Christina Block's father Eugen a multimillionaire.

Prosecutors allege that she and a family lawyer, Andreas Costard, organised the forcible abduction of two of her children, who were staying with her former husband, Stephan Hensel, at his home in Denmark.
They say the operation was carried out by a 36-year-old Israeli citizen named only as Jonathan G and five others.
The abduction took place during the New Year celebrations of 2023-24, as the two children and their father were watching a firework display, according to the indictment.
Prosecutors say several men ambushed and beat up Stephan Hensel, and dragged the boy and the girl, then 10 and 13 years old, into a car.
On the approach to the border with Germany, they are alleged to have changed vehicles, taped up the children's mouths and tied the girl's hands.

The group are then said to have travelled on to Baden-Württemberg in a campervan. Prosecutors say the children were held there against their will until their mother arrived to pick them up on 2 January 2024 and took them to her home in Hamburg.
Christina Block, Andreas Costard and Jonathan G are charged with the abduction of minors, grievous bodily harm and unlawful detention.
Block's partner, a former TV sports presenter called Gerhard Delling, and three others are charged with aiding and abetting.
All of them deny wrongdoing, except for Jonathan G, who has admitted his involvement. However, he told the court he thought he was taking part in a rescue operation.
The trial comes after years of legal battles between Christina Block and her former husband, Stephan Hensel, over who had the right to look after the children.
Immediately after their separation, all four children lived with their mother in Hamburg. Hensel, who remarried, later moved to Denmark, where they regularly visited him.
In 2021, the two youngest children went to visit their father in Denmark, but then were not brought back to Hamburg as agreed.

A court in Hamburg ruled that Christina had custody and that the children should be returned. However, in February 2023, a Danish court ruled that, although the boy and the girl had been brought to Denmark unlawfully, they could not be taken back.
In May 2023, Hensel was charged with the abduction of minors, in a case which is still pending.
He has accused Christina of being violent with the children, charges she denies. She told the court Hensel wanted to take revenge on her.
She also denied knowing anything about plans for the abduction of the children from Denmark. Her defence argues that the Israeli security team had acted on its own initiative.
She told the court it was "a catastrophe" and that she had never wanted anything like that.

The head of the Israeli security team, David Barkay, who is not on trial but faces future legal proceedings, told the court that Christina Block and Costard had known about the planned repatriation operation.
Barkay, who was described by another witness as a former agent with Mossad, the Israeli secret service, said he had not shared all the details because he "didn't trust them."
The alleged connection with Germany's former spy chief, August Hanning, relates to accusations of an earlier attempt to abduct the children and bring them back from Denmark in 2022.

Prosecutors have said Hanning was responsible for arranging security staff sent to Denmark with Christina Block. His lawyer denies the accusations. Hanning has not been charged over the current Block court case.

However, while investigators were searching his home, they came across evidence to suggest Hanning was involved in buying some 2,000 documents from his former chief of staff and then passing on state secrets to foreign powers.
Which foreign power and who he is alleged to have given the secrets to is unspecified, but it has prompted widespread speculation.
Now 80, Hanning is in custody charged with treasonous espionage. His lawyer says he is being "unjustly persecuted" and that the charges are "unfounded".
Meanwhile the trial against Christina Block is currently on hold for two weeks - one of numerous delays and extensions over the course of the past 15 months.
The latest delay is because a witness, Stephan Hensel's new wife, failed to appear in court.

articles.title: Shooter in fatal Bend, Oregon, school shooting was former student there
articles.summary: One teacher and three children killed after Griffin J John II, 16, barged into elementary school and began shooting
articles.byline: Dani Anguiano in Bend, Oregon, Uwa Ede-Osifo, Anna Betts and Abené Clayton

blocks.text: The 16-year-old who barged into an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, and unleashed a barrage of gunfire that killed a teacher and three children was a former student at Silver Rail elementary, officials confirmed in a Friday press conference.
The heavily armed gunman, identified as Griffin J John II, climbed over a fence and onto the school’s property before shooting through a set of locked doors to enter the building.
The shooter, a former special needs learner, beelined toward a special education classroom left of the entrance doors, firing as many as 15 rounds.

All of the victims from Thursday’s shooting were in that room: five-year-old Rhoam Summer, two other students, ages eight and 11, whom authorities have not identified, and 25-year-old teacher Megan Lambert.
Lambert, a central Oregon native regarded Silver Rail as a “dream job”, her family said in a statement read by police. “She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs.”
The shooting also left a seven-year-old still in serious condition, police said, and a 54-year-old educator with serious, but non-life-threatening injuries.
A 36-year-old Silver Rail parent, identified by relatives as Kaylub Giamanco , heard the gunshots as he was driving by and entered the school.
He saw an educator in a scuffle with the gunman, at which point he intervened, shooting and killing the teen.
Police say the teacher threw her phone at the shooter before tackling him, as she fought to disarm him.
“She almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed,” Bend police chief Mike Krantz said.
Authorities recovered 44 more rounds of ammunition in the shooter’s backpack.
Police have not offered a motive, citing the continuing investigation.
Candlelight vigils and memorials have sprung up around Bend, as the city has been thrust into a gruesome, but tragically familiar American story.
Outside the school on Friday, a steady stream of people arrived to deliver flowers in front of the campus.

They left dozens of bouquets, teddy bears, Minnie Mouse stuffed animals and a pumpkin. Most people stopped by for just a moment to pay their respects. Some sat, and parents held their children and cried together.
It was eerily quiet at a time when the campus would normally be teeming with activity, said Joe Camarlinghi, father of a third grader at the school.

blocks.caption: Children draw with chalk during a candlelight vigil in Bend on Thursday. Photograph: Eli Imadali/Oregon Public Broadcasting/AP

blocks.text: Fabiola Caseres, who runs a local preschool and came by to deliver flowers, said the sadness was palpable all around the close-knit city.
“It just feels so heavy,” she said. “Everybody is looking like deer in the headlights. It’s so sad, and you can’t stop thinking about the kids. They’re supposed to come home.”
Thursday’s events mark the most deadly school shooting since the September 2024 mass killing at Apalachee high school in Georgia, where a 14-year-old shooter killed two teachers and two students.
Although a motive in this school shooting remains unclear, the age of the shooter points to a troubling pattern.

Some of the most recent high-profile shootings on and off school campuses have been carried out by teenagers and young adults, many of whom are a part of nihilistic online communities where posters praise, and seek to emulate, prior shooters like those who carried out attacks at Columbine high school, in Christchurch in New Zealand and at Virginia Tech.

In May, two teenagers who met and were radicalized online shot and killed three people at a mosque in San Diego before shooting themselves. In their manifesto, they explicitly named the Apalachee high school shooters as their inspiration.

blocks.caption: A woman cries during a vigil for the victims in Bend on Thursday evening. Photograph: Eli Imadali/Oregon Public Broadcasting/AP

blocks.text: The city of Bend, home to about 100,000 residents, held a candlelit vigil on Thursday night. Hundreds of people gathered in Bend’s Drake Park as the sun set. Oregon governor Tina Kotek and Bend mayor Melanie Kebler attended the vigil.

“There is power and love in this park tonight,” Kotek said. “On behalf of everyone who lives in Oregon, I am so sorry for what you are experiencing today. No parent, no family, no community should have to have this kind of day.”
All schools in Bend and La Pine, a neighboring city, were closed on Friday.

articles.title: Prosecution asks ICC to include prior testimonies of 5 witnesses in Rodrigo Duterte case
articles.summary: The Prosecution in the case of former president Rodrigo Duterte on Friday asked the International Criminal Court Trial Chamber III to allow the prior recorded testimonies of five witnesses as…

blocks.text: Published October 17, 2026 7:03am

The Prosecution in the case of former president Rodrigo Duterte on Friday asked the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III to allow the prior recorded testimonies of five witnesses as evidence.

In a 12-page document, a redacted version of which was posted on the ICC website, ICC Acting Prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang requested that they be allowed to submit the transcripts and associated material of witnesses P-1087, P-1151, P-1158, P-1161, and P-1204 (referred to as Five Witnesses).

"Granting the request will enhance the expeditiousness of the proceedings by reducing the length of the witnesses’ direct examination from [REDACTED] hours to [REDACTED] hours, thus saving at least [REDACTED] hours of court time," Niang said.
The Five Witnesses' prior recorded testimonies are relevant, reliable, and probative, he added.

"As [REDACTED], the Five Witnesses provide evidence on [REDACTED]. As such, their evidence is particularly relevant to the policy to ‘neutralise’ through violent crimes, including murder, alleged criminals in the Philippines and to [REDACTED] to implement this policy," Niang said.

"The introduction into evidence of the Prior Recorded Testimonies is not prejudicial to or inconsistent with the rights of the Accused, as the Five Witnesses will be available for cross examination by the Defence and any further questioning by the Chamber, the parties, and the Common Legal Representatives of Victims (the “CLRV”)," he added.

Duterte is facing charges of crimes against humanity in connection with the alleged extrajudicial killings in the war on drugs during his term as president, and during his term as mayor of Davao City.
He was arrested in March 2025 at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport Terminal 3 and is currently detained at the ICC Detention Centre in Scheveningen in The Hague, The Netherlands.
Duterte's trial will start on Nov. 30.
The ICC Trial Chamber III found fDuterte fit to stand trial, stating that he “is able to effectively exercise his fair trial rights in the proceedings.” —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Gone to the dogs: racing fans mourn closure of ‘Wenty’, Sydney’s historic greyhound track
articles.summary:
Thousands pack Wentworth Park for the final time before the stadium is demolished and returned to parkland

  • Get our

blocks.text: The end of an era has fallen upon an Australian sporting landmark as the greyhound races at an inner-city track kicked off for the very last time.
Thousands packed into Wentworth Park in central Sydney on Friday night, where greyhound races have been held since 1932, for the last race meeting before the track’s planned demolition.
The final race of the night was the richest in the world – the Million Dollar Chase – and was won by Magical Ang.

blocks.caption: Magical Ang, winner of the Million Dollar Chase at Wentworth Park, with her handler.   Photograph: Robbie Stephenson/AAP

blocks.text: For Geoff Rose, the closure was a sign of the times – the land in the inner-west suburb of Glebe is worth a fortune in a city where growth will not slow down.
But the NSW Greyhound Breeders, Owners and Trainers Association chair remained sad to see the park go.
“It is quite heartbreaking to a lot of people,” he said.
Another spectator mourning the closure was Jeff Collerson, a veteran greyhound writer who first set foot on the track at Wentworth Park in December 1962 as a 17-year-old cadet journalist.
Now 81, he was trackside as the dogs raced around the circuit, nestled against the Sydney city skyline, for the final time and reminisced about his career.

blocks.caption: Jeff Collerson not longer wants his ashes scattered at Wentworth Park. He is pictured at the track on Friday night. Photograph: Robbie Stephenson/AAP

blocks.text: He said the closure of what locals refer to affectionately as “Wenty” was tragic.
“I remember saying to my wife years ago, I want you to cast my ashes in front of the winning post at Wentworth Park, but I told her not to do that now,” Collerson said.
“Wentworth Park’s got a special aura about it that the other tracks won’t have … it’s got a special buzz to it.
“That will be lost forever because having a city track is just fantastic.”
All buildings are slated for demolition after October 2027, and the site is planned to be returned to parkland under the auspices of Sydney’s council.
Wentworth Park was created between 1876 and 1880 using silt dredged from Sydney’s harbour. Greyhound racing began in the park in 1932, and by the 1970s, the sport was attracting large crowds.

blocks.caption: Spectators at Wentworth Park on Friday. Photograph: Robbie Stephenson/AAP

blocks.text: Greyhound Racing NSW, the state’s regulator for the sport, announced this week it had chosen the existing Richmond race club, about an hour north-west of central Sydney, as the replacement site for the industry.
Rose said his association was also exploring another option, which could see it establishing race meetings at a site near Appin, south-west of Sydney.

Either way, the state’s racing minister, David Harris, has previously promised $10m in government funding to help the industry find a new home – a move criticised by those calling for the industry to be shut down altogether.

blocks.caption: Anti-greyhound racing protesters outside the stadium. Photograph: Robbie Stephenson/AAP

blocks.text: Some have welcomed the track’s closure as a move towards the whole industry’s end.
A crowd of protesters stood outside the park as punters filed in, chanting that the sport kills dogs, and calling for an end to taxpayer dollars propping up the industry.
Aleisha Kernan and Kirsten Lambros work for Greyhounds as Pets, which helps facilitate the adoption of retired racing dogs.
Kernan said the sport’s potential new facilities would “open new avenues”.
“I think people should look at the future as well,” she said.
But for one young punter, Harry Dunlop, nothing would replace what he described as a “prominent piece of Australia”.
“It’s very unlikely that we’ll be going out to Richmond,” he said.

articles.title: Mortgage repayments are now cheaper than rent in some Australian suburbs. Is yours among them?
articles.summary:
As house prices plateau, the gap between the cost of buying and renting is narrowing in dozens of suburbs

  • Get our

blocks.text: High rents and falling property prices have opened a rare window for Australian tenants to become homeowners, with mortgage repayments cheaper than rent in dozens of suburbs.
Guardian Australia’s analysis of Cotality data shows that median rents in inner-city Melbourne, suburban Canberra and Darwin are now nearly matching weekly home loan repayments.
In one in 10 suburbs and towns across the country, repayments are less than $200 a week higher than rent, for the typical property. In some suburbs, they are actually cheaper.

Australia’s median rent prices rose 5.5% over the year to September to reach $713 per week, Cotality data shows. The median property price across houses and units was flat over the year, after six months of steady falls.
The typical rent for a Melbourne apartment was $628 a week after rising 4.8% over the last year.
The typical repayments for a Melbourne flat were $211 more, or $839 a week, based on a median value of $624,740 in September, down nearly $25,000 from a year earlier.

The analysis assumes a new 30-year loan of 95% of the value, at a 6.2% interest rate. It does not account for any additional costs. Smaller loans made with bigger deposits would make repayments even more affordable compared with rents.
Owner-occupiers purchasing with a 5% deposit would typically do so through the government’s low deposit scheme, which is designed to help first home buyers.
Repayments were cheaper than rent for the typical property in Carlton, Melbourne CBD, Notting Hill, Travancore and Southbank.

Repayments on new loans had risen overall in the last year for most suburbs, as lower values were offset by interest rates rising 1 percentage point. Where values had fallen more than 10%, though, repayments were likely lower.
Clint Waters, a Melbourne mortgage broker, said home buying interest had dropped but renters were inquiring in strong numbers as they weighed lower house prices against higher rents.
“They’re certainly doing the maths … [and] the equation at the moment is starting to narrow,” Waters said.
Waters, director at Axton Finance, said a stable or growing number were looking to buy direct from their landlord, making the switch without moving.

“Landlords are getting slammed left, right and centre, and going ‘screw this, I’m going to offload,” Waters said. “Tenants will ring us up and say, ‘I need to work out if I’ve got the capacity to buy this thing.’”
New apartments pushing down prices
In Sydney, repayments were just $100 a week more than rents in inner-city Ultimo and western suburbs Warwick Farm, Rosehill, Liverpool and Granville.
In the Canberra suburbs of Belconnen and Phillip, repayments were less than $75 a week more than rents. If only apartments are included, Braddon, Lyons, Gungahlin and Harrison join the list.

Gerard Burg, Cotality researcher, said areas with significant apartment development tended to be cheaper to buy than rent, especially where flats were being sold direct to owner-occupiers and not rented out.
“That just [shows] this influx of supply pushing down the value of the purchase, while comparatively tight rental availability had led to this increase in rents,” Burg said.
But such areas were “anomalies”, he said. Houses remain generally more expensive to buy than rent.
“If it was a sustained thing that you could buy a property more cheaply than renting it, then everyone would buy and everyone would exit the rental market,” Burg said.

It was cheaper to buy in a quarter of suburbs in Darwin, where rents have risen 11.6% in the year. Most areas where buying was cheaper than renting were mining or resource project areas in which fly-in fly-out workers temporarily rent rather than buy, Burg said.
Burg said mortgage repayments would likely fall if the Reserve Bank held rates steady and values kept falling, as expected by financial markets, potentially narrowing the gap with rents.
“[With] rents continuing to increase or … go sideways, that could occur.”

articles.title: Trump in Georgia falsely claims election of Jon Ossoff was illegitimate
articles.summary:
President appears at rally for struggling Mike Collins, dismisses critics and touts ‘most successful’ two-year run

At a rally in north Georgia, Donald Trump again claimed that the 2020…

blocks.text: At a rally in north Georgia, Donald Trump again claimed that the 2020 election in Georgia was fraudulent, alleging that the election of US senator Jon Ossoff was illegitimate.
Ossoff, who faces US congressman Mike Collins in November, does not represent Georgia’s values, Trump said.
“And he was never elected,” Trump added.
Ossoff has maintained a consistent lead against Collins, with most recent polling showing him with a nine-point lead against his Republican rival.

Trump claimed he was about to complete the “most successful” two-year run of a president in history, touting stock market gains, low unemployment and poverty rates, and the establishment of “Trump accounts” for newborns. Trump again said that American voters would receive a $5,000 government check if Republicans hold the US House of Representatives, claiming that $21tn in foreign manufacturing investments pledged on his watch would offset the trillion-dollar cost.
Most of those pledges remain unfulfilled.
Trump also touted his immigration record and the overthrow of the Venezuelan government.
“Forty-eight hours, and that war was done,” Trump said.
He described the early days of the war on Iran from the perspective of Oval Office meetings and damage reports, particularly of strikes against Iranian leadership.
“They’ll blow up Israel, they’ll blow up the Middle East,” Trump said of Iran and the imperatives of launching attacks. “Iran is the only country where nobody wants to be president.”

The Iran war has caused a spike in gasoline and diesel prices. Trump was dismissive of critics citing the increased cost of living on his watch, describing the term “affordability” as Democratic propaganda.
“In the past 17 months, zero illegal aliens have been admitted into the United States,” he said.
An undocumented migrant is rarely “admitted” in any official way.

Trump returned to his regular themes at the rally, which began at about 2pm. About 1,200 people packed grandstands at Dalton municipal airport. Trump took the stage at about 4.20pm, 80 minutes after his scheduled start, with about 300 people standing unshaded in the Georgia afternoon sun. His supporters were undaunted.

“Donald Trump is the greatest president of all time,” said Tracy Spencer of Chattanooga, Tennessee, as she awaited the president’s arrival in Marine One. Asked how she addresses the increasing criticism of the president from disillusioned conservatives, she scoffed.

“Well, none of my friends and family are expressing that to me, because they know better,” she said. “But I have heard the rumors that there are some people that think that, and I would say to those people that growth doesn’t happen overnight and that there are growing pains.”
Trump obliquely discussed his administration’s attacks on anti-discrimination policies he terms “DEI” while describing the “handsomeness” of a US soldier he encountered at the White House.
“Everything is based on merit,” Trump said. “I really have my difficulties with the supreme court, but … our country now is based on merit.”

Two protesters briefly unfurled a banner with an anti-ICE slogan. They were hustled out of the grandstands by security quickly. The assault of a protester in Ohio by Trump supporters in the stands on Monday was not repeated.

articles.title: Family of US man who died on Six Flags ride question if death was preventable
articles.summary:
Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem died after reportedly ‘passing out’ and falling off Goliath rollercoaster in Georgia

The family of a man who was ejected from a rollercoaster at a Six Flags amusement…

blocks.text: The family of a man who was ejected from a rollercoaster at a Six Flags amusement park in Georgia and died has publicly questioned whether the death could have been prevented.

Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem was riding the Goliath rollercoaster at Six Flags Over Georgia near Atlanta alongside his niece during a family trip to celebrate her birthday when he was thrown from the ride. His niece witnessed her uncle’s death, a relative told the Atlanta ABC News affiliate WSB-TV.
“A large part of me does believe, you know, it was a freak accident, but the other part of me questions … could this have been prevented?” Joshua Nelson, Kariem’s brother-in-law, told the outlet.
Nelson, whose daughter was seated beside Kariem, shared her account of the terrifying moments leading up to her uncle’s death.

“She said he fainted, or passed – her words were ‘he passed out,’” Nelson said. “And then they went up and down, up and down, up and down – and she said it went up again and his latch, I guess, snapped or came loose and he fell,” Nelson remarked.
During the celebratory family outing, Kariem had expressed his excitement about riding the Goliath, which was one of his favorite attractions, according to Nelson.
Nelson said that he hoped Kariem did not experience pain during his final moments.

Kariem was an educator and a father to a 10-year-old daughter. According to Atlanta public schools, Kariem started his career at Wesley International Academy as a technology teacher before being promoted to an information technology manager.

Georgia authorities as of Friday were still investigating the circumstances of Kariem’s death at Six Flags Over Georgia, which opened its gates Friday evening for the first time since the incident. Cobb county police department’s major crimes unit has launched an investigation.
Since Kariem’s death, Six Flags temporarily closed nine rollercoasters across six amusement parks around the US.
Deaths such as Kariem’s are rare. But his death has prompted some to call for federal oversight of amusement parks, which in the US has been left to individual states, as the New York Times reported.

articles.title: Reform councillor resigns after being filmed making racist remarks
articles.summary:
Alan Feeney, who sat on Solihull and Birmingham councils, said there was ‘no excuse’ for his comments

Alan Feeney has resigned as a Reform councillor for Solihull and Birmingham after…

blocks.text: Alan Feeney has resigned as a Reform councillor for Solihull and Birmingham after backlash over racist comments that were captured in an undercover investigation.

In a Facebook post on Friday, Feeney wrote: “There is no excuse for my comments. With responsibility comes accountability, and it is for that reason that I have resigned every post I hold on both Solihull borough council and Birmingham city council.”

Earlier this week, an ITV investigation revealed secretly recorded footage of Feeney making racist comments about Asian homeowners, calling them “parasites”, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”, during a local election campaign.

Feeney has apologised for his comments. “My remarks were wrong, offensive and completely unacceptable. They do not reflect the standards that the public rightly expects from an elected representative, and I take full responsibility for what I said,” he wrote in a Facebook post.

“The comments do not reflect my true beliefs or opinions, particularly of the communities mentioned in the report. These are communities I have supported countless times in my personal and professional life over many years, many of whom I have been lucky enough to call friends.”

Earlier this year, Feeney won seats in the Shard End ward of Birmingham city council and the Castle Bromwich ward of Solihull metropolitan borough council, and was then appointed deputy mayor of Solihull.

Following the ITV investigation, which is part of a longer series on Reform UK, Feeney announced on Facebook that he was leaving Reform for “personal reasons”, but kept his seats as an independent councillor before resigning.

In a Facebook post, Feeney wrote: “Byelections will be held on a timescale laid out by those councils in the due course. I hope that in time these councils, and the communities they serve can heal and move on.”

Secretly filmed footage showed Feeney making racist remarks alongside two other Reform candidates who went on to become councillors, Jamie Campbell and Chris Whelan, while canvassing during May’s local elections. Both Campbell and Whelan have also resigned after the fallout from the investigation.
Nigel Farage has repeatedly pledged to rid Reform of “extremists” and “bigots”. The party says it carries out vetting checks on everyone who wants to stand for election.
The clips from ITV’s year-long undercover investigation showed Feeney calling Asian homeowners “parasites”, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”.

In a Facebook post Feeney wrote: “I understand that my words have caused hurt and anger, particularly among those from the communities I serve. For that, I am deeply sorry. I will be undertaking intensive personal analysis to understand how these sentiments could have taken root, and ensure they can never do so again.”
Alan Feeney and Reform UK have been approached for comment.

articles.title: Brazil: Amazon deforestation lowest in nearly 40 years
articles.summary: The latest figures show that 3,335 square kilometers of the Amazon rainforest were cleared in the year ending in July, the lowest level since 1988. The drop has been described as an "historic…

image.caption: Brazil's president said his goal is zero illegal deforestation by 2030Image: Rafael Guadeluppe/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Brazil has recorded the lowest level of deforestation in the Amazon rainforest in nearly 40 years.

According to data released by the Brazilian space research agency Inpe on Friday, between August 2025 and July 2026, 3,335 square kilometers (1,288 square miles) of forest were cleared, the lowest level witnessed since records began in 1988.
The numbers showed a nearly 42% decrease from last year's figure of 5,731 square kilometers.
The Amazon is the world's largest tropical rainforest and one of its most biodiverse ecosystems, most of which lies in Brazil.
It also extends into parts of Peru, Colombia and other South American countries. Deforestation and the illegal exploitation of resources have been pushing it closer to a climate tipping point.

blocks.caption: The Amazon is the world's largest tropical rainforestImage: Pablo Porciuncula/AFP

blocks.text: Drop hailed as 'historic achievement'
"It's an absolutely stratospheric drop...it's like a dream," said Environment Minister Joao Paulo Capobianco at a press conference in the capital, Brasilia.
"Our goal is to achieve zero illegal deforestation by 2030," said President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in a post on X.
"The figures released today are a historic achievement," said Marcio Astrini, executive secretary at climate advocacy group Observatorio do Clima.

"They put Brazil at the forefront of the forest protection agenda and show the world that, with political will, it is possible to stop the chainsaws and curb greenhouse gas emissions," Astrini said on his organization's website.

Observatorio do Clima said the figures were the result of a "sustained commitment" to protecting the environment by the government, which introduced greater monitoring and stiffer penalties for illegal logging.
The news comes ahead of the October 25 runoff election between Lula and conservative senator Flavio Bolsonaro with the two running neck and neck according to polls.
Brazil's $125 billion plan to save the world's rainforests

articles.title: ‘Crypto King’ spent $16.3M of investor funds on cars, credit cards, jets, security, accountant testifies
articles.summary: Self-described “Crypto King” Aiden Pleterski spent nearly half of the $36.3 million investors gave him on himself and paid out about the same amount to investors as returns between 2020 and 2022,…

image.caption: A forensic accountant testified in Toronto court Friday about the millions of dollars of investor funds self-described 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski spent on cars, flights on private jets, shopping and other expenses. (aiden.ptrs/Instagram)

blocks.text: Toronto·New

Self-described “Crypto King” Aiden Pleterski spent nearly half of the $36.3 million investors gave him on himself and paid out about the same amount to investors as returns between 2020 and 2022, according to a senior forensic accountant who testified at his trial in Toronto’s Superior Court on Friday.
Aiden Pleterski paid $16.1M to investors, but no funds went to trading platform named in contracts: accountant

Self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski spent nearly half of the $36.3 million investors gave him on himself and paid out about the same amount to investors as returns between 2020 and 2022, according to a senior forensic accountant who testified at his trial in Toronto’s Superior Court on Friday.

Albert Ciorma, who works for the Ontario Securities Commission (OSC), told the court that none of the funds Pleterski received from investors were ever sent to FXChoice — the trading platform their contracts said he’d use on their behalf. And only about $113,000 was ever sent to other foreign exchange and cryptocurrency platforms.

Instead, Ciorma said his forensic audit found Pleterski spent about $5.6 million on luxury vehicles, $4.9 million on credit card bills, $870,000 on travel and private jets, $598,000 on security, and Pleterski gave nearly $3.7 million to his parents. He also took $609,000 in cash advances from a credit card. Altogether, those expenses total more than $16.3 million.
Pleterski also paid out another $16.1 million to investors from the funds he received, according to Ciorma.

items: 'Crypto King' tells court he fears he might soon end up in jail cell with his kidnappers
Real estate developer testifies he gave 'Crypto King’ Aiden Pleterski $4.5M to invest

blocks.text: The 27-year-old has pleaded not guilty to fraud over $5,000 and money laundering. Pleterski was charged in May 2024 after a lengthy investigation by the OSC and Durham Regional Police.
Albert Ciorma, a senior forensic accountant, testified about self-described 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski's bank accounts at his fraud and money laundering trial on Friday. (Pam Davies/CBC)

Since the start of Pleterski’s jury trial last week, the Crown has alleged that he guaranteed the money his investors gave him for trading, but never actually invested the funds, instead spending the money on himself. Ciorma’s testimony on Friday was the first detailed evidence presented in court to support that aspect of the Crown’s case.

Previously, nearly a dozen investors testified to giving Pleterski more than $6 million collectively. They all shared similar stories of providing Pleterski funds to trade in foreign exchange, and in some cases cryptocurrency, with weekly gains of about two to 10 per cent. They received texts from Pleterski updating them on these returns.
Most of them said they never got any of their money back.
Millions flow in, and then out
Crown prosecutor Scott Patterson went through dozens of pages of records Ciorma compiled summarizing Pleterski’s bank accounts with the forensic accountant in court.
“We see the same pattern, money in and expenses to credit cards,” said Patterson, referencing transactions from the spring of 2021.
The records showed millions of dollars of investor money flowing in, and then flowing out of Pleterski’s bank accounts to pay for credit card bills, cars, hotels, designer clothing and jewelry.
Other expenses include more than $84,000 for a luxury property rental in Miami in October 2021 and $95,200 to the Toronto Blue Jays baseball team in April 2022.

The jury in Aiden Pleterski's trial was shown this photo last week of Mitchell Learning holding his own phone with a screenshot he testified Pleterski sent him of Pleterski's trading account with a balance of more than $311 million. (Ontario Superior Court of Justice)
Two investors who previously testified spoke about seeing a video of Pleterski’s FXChoice account showing a balance of $311 million in the spring of 2022.

items: 'Crypto King' investor recounts the moment he learned $311M investment fund didn’t exist
'Crypto King' investor who lost $890K recounts visit to Aiden Pleterski’s lakefront mansion

blocks.text: One of them, Mitchell Learning, later gained access to Pleterski’s email account and found an email showing the same FXChoice account had been closed. He then testified that Pleterski confessed to him that he’d lost investor funds and then started using new money from investors to make payouts to others.
“Did you see $311 million in either of those accounts?” Patterson asked the accountant about the FXChoice accounts he reviewed.
“No, just what we’ve seen today,” replied Ciorma.
Pleterski’s trial is expected to continue Monday with further testimony from the forensic accountant.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Nicole Brockbank is a reporter for CBC Toronto's Enterprise Unit. She digs up, researches and reports GTA-focused investigative and enterprise stories. nicole.brockbank@cbc.ca

articles.title: McNuggets, booze smuggled by drone into Canada's most secure prison: union
articles.summary: The union representing correctional officers is raising the alarm after it says an inmate had a drone drop off a McDonald's meal and alcohol to what's supposed to be Canada's most secure prison…

image.caption: A drone delivered McDonald's chicken nuggets (not the ones pictured) fries, sauce and some alcohol to an inmate's cell window at the Sainte-Anne-des-Plaines, Que., facility this week, according to the correctional officers' union. (Shannon Stapleton/Reuters)

blocks.text: Politics·New

The union representing correctional officers is raising the alarm after it says an inmate had a drone drop off a McDonald's meal and alcohol to what's supposed to be Canada's most secure prison earlier this week.
Union says it's at 'breaking point' for illegal goods entering Quebec facility

The union said the drone delivered McDonald's chicken nuggets and fries complete with sauce and some alcohol straight to the inmate's cell window in the special handling unit at the Sainte-Anne-des-Plaines, Que., facility at around 3 a.m. on Thursday.
"The inmate found that really funny in the morning when the guards did their rounds," said Mike Bolduc, regional president of the UCCO-SACC-CSN union, in an interview.
But he's not laughing. The union has been growing increasingly concerned about contraband, from cellphones to knives, getting into the maximum security facility via drone.
"We're at the breaking point where an inmate went and delivered himself McDonald's.… What's the next thing? Is that a loaded gun? You know, it's scaring us, it's really scaring us," he said.

The inmate's unit — known as the SHU — houses extremely violent and high-risk offenders. Some of Canada's most notorious killers, like Clifford Olson and Allan Legere, spent part of their incarceration at the Quebec prison along with convicted terrorists.

items: Drug trafficker tied to minor's overdose death used drones to bring contraband into prison

blocks.text: "It's supposed to be the most secure jail in Canada and he's eating McDonald's," said Bolduc.
The details of the story were first reported on by TVA Nouvelles.
Drones are an escalating problem for Canada's penitentiary system and those who run it.
'What in the heck?' Conservative MP
Correctional Service Canada (CSC) deploys unmanned aerial vehicle detection technology at its institutions, but Bolduc said it's concerning that the radar didn't appear to detect this drone.
He thinks inmates probably get multiple drones sent out to find blind spots.
"So what happened here is that they beat the technology," said Bolduc. "The drones are incredible [with] the damage that they're causing."
The union been pushing for a far more low-tech solution: physical netting
"It's not harder than that," Bolduc said. "This now has to be a cry for help saying that we need that netting as fast as possible."
The entrance of the Sainte-Anne-des-Plaines penitentiary is shown on July 3, 2005. (Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press)
Bolduc said the McDonald's delivery should be a "wake-up call" for federal Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree, whose government cut $132 million from CSC's operational budget.
"I'm scared for Canadians, for their security," he said.
In a social media video Conservative MP Frank Caputo, the party's public safety critic, said the minister has been too slow on the issue of drones delivering illegal goods to prisons.
"What in the heck are we doing in Canada?" he said.
In a statement, CSC said the incident is under review but wouldn't comment on the case further, citing security considerations.
"The introduction of contraband and unauthorized items into correctional institutions remains an important issue that CSC continues to actively address," said spokesperson Kevin Antonucci.

"CSC continues to implement a multi-layered approach that includes staff vigilance, security intelligence activities, searches, detection technologies and collaboration with police and other partners."
Anandasangaree's office referred CBC News to the CSC comment.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Catharine Tunney is a reporter with CBC's Parliament Hill bureau, where she covers national security and the RCMP. She worked previously for CBC in Nova Scotia. You can reach her at catharine.tunney@cbc.ca

articles.title: Healey backs pro-growth case for Heathrow third runway after Burnham ducks issue
articles.summary:
Chancellor says government will study responses to public consultation, with airports being ‘big part of jobs and growth’

John Healey has said there is a pro-growth case for going ahead with…

blocks.text: John Healey has said there is a pro-growth case for going ahead with a third runway at Heathrow despite the prime minister declining to back it.

Healey’s predecessor as chancellor, Rachel Reeves, put approval of the long-planned runway at the heart of her “growth speech” last year, saying it would “make Britain the world’s best-connected place to do business”.
However, since arriving in No 10 in July, Andy Burnham has ducked the issue of whether the runway should go ahead, suggesting it should be “a matter for London and Londoners”.
A recent Sunday Times report suggested the prime minister had told the transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, that he was “unconvinced” by arguments for the megaproject.

Asked for his views in Bangkok this week, Healey said the government would study responses to a public consultation, which recently closed. He appeared to strike a markedly more positive note than Burnham, however.

“I think in recent decades, and this is true in Heathrow and airports right across the UK, that they have been a big part of jobs and growth. And the case for a third runway at Heathrow has always been a case for growth,” he said.
Healey has insisted economic growth is his and Burnham’s “number one mission” in government.
Heathrow’s chief executive, Thomas Woldbye, has warned that investors could reassess their backing for the £33bn infrastructure project if it does not receive the prime minister’s support.

“Our shareholders would like to do this,” he said earlier this week. “They do think that things are taking a long time, and so far they have decided to be OK with that … But of course we cannot wait for ever.”

The airport’s owners include Qatar’s investment authority; the French private equity firm Ardian; Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund and Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund, GIC. They are expected to decide in the coming months whether to apply for formal planning permission.
Healey voted in favour of the third runway when the question was put to the House of Commons in 2018.
after newsletter promotion
The chancellor was in Bangkok to attend the International Monetary Fund annual meetings but has returned to London to put the finishing touches to his 28 October budget.

The UK was praised by the IMF this week for taking action to cut its deficit, while other large economies have opted not to do so. The IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, urged Healey to “stay the course” in his budget.
On Thursday, official figures showed the UK economy unexpectedly continued to grow in August.

articles.title: Selma Blair's team breaks silence after plane incident and arrest
articles.summary: Selma Blair's team is speaking out about the actor's recent arrest following an alleged mid-flight incident on Oct. 11. She was arrested after being accused of injuring two flight attendants on a…

image.caption: Selma Blair leaves court on Oct. 12 in New York after her arraignment on charges of injuring two flight attendants during a cross-country flight. (Ryan Murphy/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Selma Blair's team is speaking out about the actor's recent arrest following an alleged mid-flight incident on Oct. 11. She was arrested after being accused of injuring two flight attendants on a trip from Los Angeles to New York.
'Selma did not intend to harm anyone,' representative says in a statement
Selma Blair's team is speaking out about the actor's recent arrest following an alleged mid-flight incident on Oct. 11.

"Since Sunday night, the public account of what happened to Selma aboard a flight to New York has been built almost entirely on a police statement and a decade-old headline,” Blair’s representative said in a statement to CBC News.

The actor was arrested after being accused of injuring two flight attendants on a trip from Los Angeles to New York. She was also charged Monday with assaulting a police officer who was taking her to the hospital and a nurse after she arrived there.

“A handful of journalists have taken the time to report on Selma as a human being rather than a headline, and we are grateful to them," the statement says. "But fair reporting has been the exception, and in the space left by our silence, speculation has hardened into something being treated as fact.
"We can, however, correct the record on a few points already in public circulation."
'Selma did not intend to harm anyone': rep
Blair appeared in court on Oct. 12 and pleaded not guilty to two counts of second-degree assault. She was later released on bail.
"Selma Blair experienced a medical emergency on the flight. There was no attempt to open the door of the aircraft. Selma did not intend to harm anyone," her representative wrote.
Blair leaves court on Oct. 12. (Ryan Murphy/The Associated Press)

A police officer who took her to Jamaica Hospital Medical Center said in charging documents that while Blair was being secured to a stretcher, the actress pulled her leg from the straps and kicked the officer repeatedly around the face, neck and chest, causing serious pain and substantial swelling.
Later, a nurse moving Blair said the actress kicked her in the chest, causing substantial pain.

One of Blair's attorneys, Shawn Barnes, previously told a judge her actions were not intentional and that the actor, who has multiple sclerosis, missed several doses of "a powerful medication that controls severe neurological symptoms," according to the New York Daily News and New York Post.
Blair, was diagnosed with the autoimmune disease in 2018 and has been an advocate for disability rights.

He said she had gotten on the plane in Los Angeles after a heavy workload, and hit her head during the flight. Those factors, as well as the plane's altitude, led to "a state of severe confusion and disorientation," he said.

items: Selma Blair accused of assaulting and injuring flight attendants, police officer and nurse
Selma Blair says she's in remission from multiple sclerosis

blocks.text: Blair's representative in the statement also addressed apparent comments about her diagnosis.

"The suggestion by anyone that Selma does not have multiple sclerosis is outrageous. Her diagnosis has been public since 2018. What Selma has been able to do physically in the years since is nothing short of a miracle," they wrote.

"She still has bad days, and she lives with pain daily. Selma also has pseudobulbar affect, a neurological condition secondary to her MS, which bears directly on how a medical episode presents to people who do not know her.

"For the same reason, she travels with a service dog who doesn’t leave her side, and the authorities took her dog from her. It should be noted Selma has worked on seven film and television projects in 2026 alone, only a couple of which have been announced," they wrote.

items: Support pours in after Selma Blair shares MS diagnosis
Actress Selma Blair apologizes for airplane outburst

blocks.text: The statement also continues: "She has launched a skin care line, a clothing line, and a line of eye-glass readers, each built around the idea of beauty and utility for people whose bodies do not always cooperate.

This is not the first time the actress, known for roles in films like Cruel Intentions, Legally Blonde and Hellboy, has allegedly had issues while on a plane. In 2016, Blair apologized for making statements she regretted on a flight from Cancun to Los Angeles, saying that she mixed alcohol with medication, which made her black out.
Blair has been involved in advocacy, rep says
Her representative's statement also addressed the actor's recent advocacy work.

"She remains a visible and relentless advocate for disability rights, for the MS community, and this year for the Jewish community in the face of rising antisemitism, including from the stage of the ADL’s State of the Arts event at The Jewish Museum two weeks ago.
"Selma had never been arrested before Sunday night."
Blair attends the 35th Annual Environment Media Association Awards in Studio City, Calif., in October 2025. (Michael Tran/AFP/Getty Images)

Blair has kept a low Hollywood profile as of late, but competed on Dancing With the Stars in 2022 and is set to return to the big screen in the upcoming supernatural thriller Silent, whose release date has yet to be announced.

“There is much more to this story than has been reported," her spokesperson said, "and we ask to consider the entirety of the facts before rushing to judgment, whether in the courtroom or in the court of public opinion.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Griffin Jaeger is a reporter and producer with CBC's entertainment unit. He also formerly hosted and produced content for The National’s digital platforms. You can reach him at griffin.jaeger@cbc.ca
With files from The Associated Press

articles.title: Katie Zacharia leaving her White House role less than five days on the job
articles.summary: Her public debut as White House press secretary on Tuesday ended with a flurry of media criticism about her credentials and preparedness.

blocks.text: Katie Zacharia will be leaving her post as White House press secretary, the BBC has confirmed, as the fallout from her shaky public debut appears to have reached its climax.

Speaking to reporters moments before news of her exit dropped on Friday, President Donald Trump said he had told her "you don't have to do this if you don't want to" and "honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider".
Zacharia faced heavy criticism for her first press briefing in the role on Tuesday, which lasted less than 15 minutes and included only three questions from reporters.
She spent the days after playing defence, answering tough questions from news outlets about her credentials and preparedness for the job.
Trump hinted at her impending exit early on Friday afternoon, during a press gaggle outside Marine One.
"I said, 'Is this for you, Katie? Because honestly, you don't need this," Trump said.
"You don't have to be treated this badly," he continued, adding that he believed she had been treated "pretty nastily" by the media.
The BBC confirmed she was leaving the job a few hours later.

As the country draws closer to the November midterm elections, which will decide who controls the US Congress, Democrats are seizing on Zacharia's abrupt departure as a sign of failure in the Republican White House.
"The White House Press Secretary is gone. MAGA extremists continue to fall apart," the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries, posted on X.

Zacharia's tumultuous week began on Tuesday, after she appeared visibly nervous during her inaugural White House press briefing that lasted 14 minutes, where she read talking points from a notebook, answered only a few questions, and referred to her husband as the president.

During the briefing, a reporter asked Zacharia - who had been called an attorney by Trump and others and who graduated from Pepperdine University's law school - about where she passed the bar exam. To practice law in the US, an attorney must be admitted to a state's bar association by passing a rigorous exam.
She replied: "When I was in China."
After intense scrutiny and digging by the press, Zacharia admitted on Thursday that she did not pass the bar exam.
She did say in a statement that she had practised international transaction law in China with the "appropriate credentials".

Questions about her legal credentials became a major talking point throughout the week, with Sean Hannity from conservative-leaning Fox News lobbing particularly pointed questions at her during an interview on Thursday.
When she said she had not passed the bar, he replied: "Why didn't you just say, 'I never practiced law?'"

Zacharia also described for Hannity how quickly she had taken on the press secretary role - having been hired less than a week before her debut - prompting him to ask: "Am I hearing that you think the staff should have better prepped you?"
When she appeared on Fox & Friends, which Trump often watches, on Friday, Zacharia faced a similar line of questioning.
She told the show's hosts she did not disclose to Trump that she was not an attorney, because "those questions weren't asked", saying she was hired for a communications role, not a legal one.
Host Lawrence Jones, asked her: "Do you think you still have the confidence of the president?"
She avoided offering a direct answer but ended by saying: "I hope to be able to build the confidence and trust of everyone around me."
Zacharia's early exit is the quickest among Trump's White House press team.
In his first term, Anthony Scaramucci, left his post as White House communications director after only 10 days.
"Records are made to be broken," Scaramucci wrote on X on Friday. "But I take no pleasure in other people's pain."

articles.title: High-profile legionnaire apologizes following profanity-laced outburst at Carbonear, N.L., wedding reception
articles.summary: A wedding reception at the Royal Canadian Legion branch in Carbonear ended earlier this month in an angry outburst after high-profile legionnaire and veteran Berkley Lawrence confronted the bride as…

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador

A wedding reception at the Royal Canadian Legion branch in Carbonear ended earlier this month in an angry outburst after high-profile legionnaire and veteran Berkley Lawrence confronted the bride as she prepared to throw her wedding bouquet.
Bride was about to throw her wedding bouquet when Berkley Lawrence erupted
N.L. bride says her Legion wedding reception was ruined — by a legionnaire’s outburst

A high-profile legionnaire is apologizing and pondering his future with this century-old veteran support and community service organization following an angry outburst at a wedding reception in Carbonear, N.L., earlier this month.

The Oct. 3 wedding reception at Legion Branch 23 for newlyweds Justin and Janell Clarke came to an abrupt end after Berkley Lawrence, who was the top legionnaire in Canada until this summer, lost his temper and angrily confronted the bride and other members of the wedding party.
The bride said she was afraid and humiliated, and described Lawrence's behaviour as "aggressive, erratic, unprofessional and very, very disrespectful.”
When contacted Friday by CBC News, Lawrence admitted he crossed the line.

“I handled it completely wrong. I lost control of my emotions. I swore at her, I swore at a few other people that tried to calm me down. I was loud, and it was not a good scene," Lawrence said by telephone.
Not a happy day
Clarke said Lawrence ruined her wedding day, and the days that followed the incident.

“We cannot look back on that day now and say that was a great day. That it was the best day of our lives. When we look back on that day now, we don't look back on a happy day. The only thing I look back on when I think of that night was an unfamiliar man charging [at me] and verbally assaulting me."
Lawrence is no ordinary legionnaire. Up until August, he was the dominion president of the Royal Canadian Legion, which is the Legion's top post in the country.

Justin and Janell Clarke pose with their dog after exchanging wedding vows on Oct. 3. Their dream wedding day ended on a sour note, however, following an angry outburst by a high-profile member of the Carbonear Legion during the couple's wedding reception. (Facebook/Justin Clarke)

He served in the army for 33 years, has played leading roles at Branch 23 for more than two decades, and two years ago he was a key figure in the establishment of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at the war memorial in St. John's.

On the night of the wedding reception, Lawrence was attending a separate event at the Legion, and said he drank about five beer. As he left, he witnessed people outside the building holding alcoholic beverages, which is not permitted.

Lawrence was worried that liquor corporation inspectors or police officers might witness the behaviour, and that the Legion might lose its licence to sell beer and alcohol. He said the branch has long struggled to stay within the rules of its licence.
"People treat us … like a private club and [believe] they can do whatever they want," said Lawrence.
'He just kept screaming'
He admitted he lost his cool, stormed back into the Legion, and came face-to-face with the bride, just as she was about to perform the traditional newlywed ritual: the throwing of the bouquet.
"He never did say what it was about. He just kept screaming," said Clarke, adding she was unaware that guests were drinking alcohol outside the building.
For about a minute, Lawrence shouted profanities, angrily pointed his finger at the bride and others, and threatened to shut down the party.
Lawrence left after another legionnaire intervened.
Clarke said she was too shaken to carry on, and never tossed the bouquet. The party, she said, fizzled out.
“I was, as you can imagine, crying and humiliated in front of all my wedding guests," she said.
Oct. 3 started out as expected for the couple. They exchanged vows at a church in nearby Salmon Cove, and then hosted about 100 people at the Legion.
'Ruined my life'
The decorations were elaborate, the meals were tasty, and the dance floor was hopping for most of the evening. But the fun ended abruptly with Lawrence's outburst just before midnight.
On Thursday night, Clarke told her story on Facebook, with her post shared nearly 600 times as of Friday afternoon.

The wedding reception at the Carbonear Legion on Oct. 3 for Justin and Janell Clarke ended early following an outburst by Legion member Berkley Lawrence. As a result, Janell Clarke did not get to throw her wedding bouquet. (Janell Clarke)
On Friday morning, she received a letter of apology from Lawrence.

“All I can do is apologize to everybody involved in the situation, to the bride, to the groom, to the people upstairs, to my Legion, to my wife. It's not the way I behave normally. This incident has absolutely ruined my life," said Lawrence.
Five people, including Clarke, who witnessed the incident, wrote letters to the Legion executive.
Clarke had asked for Lawrence to be suspended from the Legion, and she also wanted to be compensated for having her reception cut short by Lawrence's outburst.
The branch executive met on Wednesday night and decided an apology was sufficient, and that's when Clarke decided to go public.
Branch president defends Lawrence
Branch president Mike Butt chaired Wednesday's special meeting, but said he was not able to vote on the decision to have Lawrence apologize.
Butt admitted, without offering any specifics, that he was not entirely happy with the executive's decision to limit their response to an apology.
"I may have went a little bit different," Butt said, adding "we are deeply sorry this happened."
But the president also defended Lawrence, saying "I don't think he should be made to suffer for 45 seconds or 60 seconds of a lapse."
Butt described Lawrence as "number one in the Legion and he will always be number one."
Clarke, meanwhile, said her perfect wedding day ended on a sour note, and now she gets emotional every time she glances at her wedding dress in the closet.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Terry Roberts is a reporter with CBC Newfoundland and Labrador, based in St. John’s. He previously worked for the Telegram, the Compass and the Northern Pen newspapers during a career that began in 1991. He can be reached by email at Terry.Roberts@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Measles outbreak declared over in Manitoba
articles.summary: ​A measles outbreak first declared in Manitoba more than a year and a half ago is now over, the province says.

image.caption: A measles outbreak that resulted in 1,038 reported cases in Manitoba is now over, the province said Friday. (Povorozniuk Liudmyla/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Manitoba·Updated
​A measles outbreak first declared in Manitoba more than a year and a half ago is now over, the province says.
Last lab-confirmed case of highly contagious disease in Manitoba was detected in August, province says
Public health officials declared the outbreak over on Friday, with the province saying the last case of the highly contagious disease confirmed in a laboratory was identified in August.
The outbreak, which began in February 2025, led to a total of 1,038 reported measles cases — 931 confirmed and 107 probable cases, according to provincial data.
The province has led the country in measles cases in 2026, with 680 reported this year — more than half of the 1,121 cases reported in all of Canada as of Oct. 3, according to federal monitoring.
Manitoba saw a monthly peak of 177 confirmed cases and 34 probable in February 2026, but case numbers dropped each month following, with two confirmed cases reported in August and none in September.

items: Manitoba measles cases hit lowest point in over a year, but experts warn infections could spike again

blocks.text: There were 52 measles-related hospitalizations, including six intensive care unit admissions, in Manitoba during the outbreak, the provincial government said.

Eighty-seven per cent of Manitoba's measles cases during the outbreak involved people who were either not vaccinated against the disease or had an unknown immunization status, according to the province.

Expanded eligibility criteria for measles vaccination, which allowed babies in some hot spot regions of the province to get vaccinated, is no longer in effect now that the outbreak has been declared over, the province said in Friday's bulletin.
The province said children should now follow Manitoba's immunization schedule, which recommends a first vaccine dose at 12 months old or older.
There were 5,462 measles cases reported in Canada in 2025, the vast majority in Ontario and Alberta. Manitoba had 358 cases last year.
Ontario and Alberta each reported one death from measles last year, both involving pre-term babies who contracted the disease congenitally.

Measles outbreaks in Alberta, British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Nova Scotia were all declared over earlier this year, according to federal data. New Brunswick and Ontario declared their outbreaks over in September and October last year, respectively.

Manitoba's Friday bulletin said while there are now no measles outbreaks in Canada, transmission remains high in some parts of the world and outbreaks continue in the U.S. The province encouraged people to ensure their measles immunizations are up to date.

articles.title: Crown to seek dangerous offender status for Daniel Senecal, convicted of sexually assaulting toddler
articles.summary: The Crown Attorney's Office will seek a dangerous offender status for a registered sex offender who pleaded guilty in June to sexually assaulting a toddler in Welland, Ont., causing what were…

image.caption: Daniel Senecal was arrested on Aug. 31, 2025, as pictured here, and charged with sexual assault of a person under the age of 16. (Submitted by Koreen Perry)

blocks.text: Hamilton

The Crown Attorney's Office will seek a dangerous offender status for a registered sex offender who pleaded guilty in June to sexually assaulting a toddler in Welland, Ont., causing what were described as potentially life-threatening injuries.
Crown proved beyond reasonable doubt that weapon used in violent sexual assault of 3-year-old: judge
WARNING: This story contains details of child sexual assault.

Daniel Senecal used a weapon to sexually assault the girl, Ontario Justice David Andrew Thomas ruled at a Friday hearing at the St. Catharines courthouse, where the courtroom was filled to capacity and a second courtroom broadcast the proceedings to an overflow crowd.
The victim was three at the time of the assault. Her identity is protected under a publication ban.

Senecal was 26 when he pleaded guilty to breaking and entering, aggravated sexual assault on a person under 16, sexual interference, assault by choking, failing to comply with probation and possessing child sexual abuse exploitation material.
Senecal's lawyer and the Crown Attorney's Office had disagreed on whether the assault involved a weapon.
That factor could impact the length of his sentence and whether the court applies a dangerous offender status, which can result in the offender being kept in indefinite detention.
Severe injuries inflicted on a child
Court heard earlier that on the evening of Aug. 30, 2025, Senecal had several drinks and, sometime between 3 a.m. and 3:30 a.m. ET the next day, broke into the girl's home and sexually assaulted her.
Senecal was arrested on Aug. 31 in the backyard of his residence after police were sent to a home in Welland for a "medical assistance call involving a child."
In late June, court was told about the severe injuries inflicted on the child, which her mom discovered the morning of Aug. 31.

Assistant Crown Attorney Todd Morris said that after the assault, the victim was taken to McMaster Children’s Hospital in Hamilton, where medical staff identified the injuries as consistent with use of force and strangulation.
Thomas said on Friday that expert testimony noted the toddler's injuries were "potentially life-threatening."

Senecal's roommate, Brittany Duclos-Robins, told the court in July that the morning after he broke into the home, he admitted to her that he used the weapon, something she told police 11 days after the crimes were committed.

The St. Catharines courthouse is shown on Friday after a judge ruled that registered sex offender Daniel Senecal used a weapon in a sexual assault of a three-year-old Welland, Ont., girl. (Paul Forsyth/CBC)
Thomas said he found Duclos-Robins — who has been friends with Senecal since childhood — to be "a very credible and reliable" witness.
"She was steadfast in what he said to her," he said.
Thomas also noted surveillance camera photos showed the weapon in Senecal's pocket as he broke into the girl's home and then him carrying it out after the assault.

Combined with the earlier testimony of Dr. Valerie Bloomfield, a pediatric and adolescent gynecologist who treated the toddler for her injuries at McMaster Children's Hospital, the Crown proved "beyond a reasonable doubt" that a weapon was used in the assault, Thomas ruled.
Dangerous offender application coming
Morris said the Crown Attorney's Office can now proceed with its application for dangerous offender status for Senecal. The next proceedings in the case are scheduled for Dec. 10.
The dangerous offender designation is reserved for Canada's most violent criminals and sexual predators.

Senecal was on probation at the time of his crimes for what the judge described as a "violent" sexual assault of a 12-year-old boy in 2021. He was released from prison early in March 2025 after serving a partial sentence.
Senecal is also in the National Sex Offender Registry.

items: Registered sex offender pleads guilty to new charges, including assault of toddler in Welland, Ont.
Accused in sex assault of girl, 3, in Welland, Ont., was let out of jail early after 'violent' attack of boy

blocks.text: The case garnered widespread community outrage across the Niagara Region, with calls for criminal justice reforms and harsher sentencing for sex offenders.

Since then, reforms to Canada's bail and sentencing system have become law, receiving royal assent earlier this month. Bill C-14, the Bail and Sentencing Reform Act, amends the Criminal Code, the Youth Criminal Justice Act and the National Defence Act to tighten the bail and sentencing framework across all three.
Bikers and supporters of a far-right extremist group have also held rallies demanding justice for the girl, prompting police to warn against "vigilante actions."

If you're in immediate danger or fear for your safety or that of others around you, please call 911. For support in your area, you can look for crisis lines and local services via the Ending Sexual Violence Association of Canada database. ​​
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Paul Forsyth is a St. Catharines-based CBC reporter covering communities in the Niagara Region. He has decades of reporting experience in Niagara, having worked for Niagara This Week, the St. Catharines Standard and the Welland Tribune before joining CBC. You can reach him at paul.forsyth@cbc.ca.
- with files by Aura Carreño Rosas
