articles.title: Winnipeg zoo's newest orphaned polar bear cub now has a name: Mantayo
articles.summary: The first polar bear cub to arrive at Winnipeg's Assiniboine Park Zoo in nearly a decade now has a name.

image.caption: Mantayo's name was chosen from four that related to places in or near Churchill. The names were shortlisted by the town and students from Duke of Marlborough School. (Submitted by Assiniboine Park Conservancy)

blocks.text: Manitoba
The first polar bear cub to arrive at Winnipeg's Assiniboine Park Zoo in nearly a decade now has a name.
Name is derived from Mantay-sîpî, the Cree name for the Churchill River
The bear, believed to be about 10 or 11 months old, is now called Mantayo, zoo officials announced via social media posts on Thursday.
It's derived from Mantay-sîpî, the Cree name for the Churchill River, which literally translates to "river of strangers."
"It feels like the [name] most connected to the north in a lot of ways. So I think it's a really good choice," Lindsay Hughes, a spokesperson for the Assiniboine Park Conservancy, said Friday.
Mantayo arrived in late August, shortly after being found near his dead mother just outside Churchill. (Submitted by Assiniboine Park Conservancy)

Mantayo's name was chosen in a public poll from a list that also included Duke, Marly, and Fletcher — all names related to places in or near Churchill. They were shortlisted by students from Churchill's Duke of Marlborough School and other town residents.
"Duke" and "Marly" honoured the school, while "Fletcher" was a nod to Fletcher Lake in Wapusk National Park.

Over 12,000 votes were cast in an online poll to name the bear — "the highest number that we've really ever seen in one of our naming polls," said Hughes, noting such polls typically get about 5,000 votes.
"There was a lot of attention and a lot of love for the little cub."

The public can see Mantayo in the zoo's old bear enclosures, at the Leatherdale International Polar Bear Conservation Centre. Staff will decide if he can move into the zoo's Journey to Churchill exhibit. (Submitted by Assiniboine Park Conservancy)
Mantayo arrived in late August, shortly after being found near his dead mother just outside Churchill. The province is still investigating how she died.

He underwent a quarantine period at the zoo's Leatherdale International Polar Bear Conservation Centre, where his care team has been building his trust, helping him adjust to his new home and being around people, Hughes said.

items: Orphaned polar bear cub arrives at Winnipeg's Assiniboine Park Zoo

blocks.text: Mantayo made his public debut last week but remains at the Leatherdale's cub care centre, on view in the zoo's old bear enclosures.
"He is going to stay there for a little while. He's still at a point where he has growing to do before he can meet big, grown bears," Hughes said.
Since the zoo underwent a massive renovation, replacing those old enclosures with the Journey to Churchill exhibit and the Leatherdale centre, it has welcomed 12 bears.
The majority were found orphaned in northern Manitoba, although brothers Hudson and Humphrey were born in captivity in Toronto, and later returned to that zoo.

The only others that were not orphans were Storm — who was shipped out of Churchill after attacking a man and arrived in 2013 as a three-year-old adult — and Agee, who came to the zoo from British Columbia in 2022 as a 26-year-old retired film star. She died in 2025.

items: Play-fighting led to death of Calgary Zoo polar bear Baffin, say officials

blocks.text: Two other orphaned bears from Manitoba, Baffin and Siku, were transferred to the Calgary Zoo in 2023 after being in Winnipeg for six years.
Baffin died in 2024 after some roughhousing with Siku crushed his trachea.
Transition needs to be 'carefully managed'
Journey to Churchill is currently home to five bears: Storm, Nanuq, York, Kaska and Willow.
"The hope is that one day [Mantayo] will be able to move in, but there's a lot of decisions to be made about which bears he might meet first and who's the best fit for him," Hughes said.
"That transition process is super, super carefully managed, so we're just taking it one day at a time at this point."
The conservation team has researched polar bear personalities, which helps identify which might be the best for Mantayo's initial greeting, she said.
Polar bears are also naturally solitary animals that come together only for breeding and when the mothers are raising cubs, so "introducing polar bears is not an easy process," Hughes said.
Another bear, Star — who arrived with her brother Blizzard in 2014 — never took to group life and now lives at the Leatherdale centre, where visitors can see her in one of the old bear enclosures.

items: Winnipeg zoo's newest polar bear cubs named Blizzard, Star

blocks.text: "She really showed a bit more of an independent lifestyle … and demonstrated she was not necessarily comfortable in that space with the big bears," Hughes said.
"So the decision was made back in 2018 that she would be better off on her own with an independent home."
Blizzard lived with the large group of bears until his death in 2019.
Hudson, who was born at the Toronto Zoo in 2011 but was rejected by his mother, was the first bear to call the Journey to Churchill exhibit home. He arrived in 2013, before it was open to the public.
Humphrey followed in 2015.
Aurora was the first orphaned polar bear cub to live there. She arrived shortly after Hudson and died in 2022 following a dental procedure.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Bernhardt has been with CBC Manitoba since 2009 and specializes in offbeat and local history stories. He is the author of two bestselling books: The Lesser Known: A History of Oddities from the Heart of the Continent, and Prairie Oddities: Punkinhead, Peculiar Gravity and More Lesser Known Histories.

articles.title: Brazil’s Lula says he now backs lowering age of criminal responsibility to 16
articles.summary:
Lula reverses position on age of responsibility for ‘heinous’ crimes in what many see as a desperate electoral gambit

Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has announced that he now…
articles.byline: Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has announced that he now supports lowering the age of criminal responsibility for “heinous” crimes from 18 to 16, reversing a longstanding policy in what is widely seen as a desperate electoral gambit.

The U-turn, which Lula announced during a Thursday night interview with TV Globo, comes with the presidential runoff in just over a week. The incumbent faces an uphill battle to overturn the first-round victory of his opponent, the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who remains slightly ahead at the polls.

Both the senator and his father, the former president, Jair Bolsonaro, have long supported lowering the age of criminal responsibility – they want it reduced to 14 rather than 16 – but Lula and his party have always opposed the change.

After repeated opinion polls, the latest of them this week, showed that 80% of the population supports lowering the age, Lula said: “My view, as a Brazilian citizen, is that for any and every heinous crime, I am in favour of lowering the age.”
He answered “yes” when the reporter asked whether he meant lowering it to 16.

The list of crimes classified as “heinous” under Brazilian law is extensive, ranging from murder and rape to the falsification of medicines and drug trafficking – the offence for which about a quarter of the 816,000 people serving prison sentences in Brazil were incarcerated.

Human rights organisations and security experts have long criticised proposals to lower the age of criminal responsibility, arguing that they do little to tackle violence while increasing recruitment into organised crime in Brazil’s overcrowded prisons.

On Thursday, before Lula’s interview, the proposal had been discussed in the senate. The Episcopal Conference of Brazil, a Catholic bishops’ organisation, had criticised it for “not addressing the causes of violence”, adding that placing young people “prematurely in the prison system tends to deepen cycles of violence and exclusion, undermining their rehabilitation”.

The columnist Josias de Souza wrote in his UOL column that, by reversing his longstanding position, Lula “decided to change himself. It was no ordinary transformation. On public security, Lula turned himself inside out. He began defending what he had always rejected.”

The incumbent has doubled down in recent days in an effort to overturn Bolsonaro’s 2.2 million-vote first-round lead by appealing to independents and undecided voters. He has secured congressional approval for a shorter working week – a proposal on which Bolsonaro himself U-turned and decided to support at the last minute, when it appeared ready to pass – and debt relief for microentrepreneurs, as well as promising free public transport on weekends.

articles.title: Philippines 5th most targeted by Chinese cyber operations -- Microsoft
articles.summary: The Philippines is the fifth-most targeted country by Chinese state-sponsored cyber operations, according to a report by tech giant Microsoft.

blocks.text: Published October 17, 2026 12:30am
The Philippines is the fifth-most targeted country by Chinese state-sponsored cyber operations, according to a report by tech giant Microsoft.
In its Microsoft Digital Defense Report 2026, the company detailed its findings on state-sponsored hacking and digital operations involving China, Iran, North Korea, and Russia.
The Philippines also ranked 10th among the countries most targeted by North Korea and 12th among those most frequently targeted by cyber threats overall, according to the report.
Microsoft said Chinese state actors focused on large-scale information gathering from a wide range of targets.

“This supports their government’s international objectives and whole-of-state intelligence fusion, an approach that combines political oversight, military apparatus, and commercial industries into a single party-led apparatus,” the report said.
“The goals of Chinese state actors remain largely consistent over time and center on long-term access to facilitate espionage,” it added.

The United States was the most targeted country by Chinese state actors, accounting for 27% of the reported activity, followed by Taiwan at 24% and Japan at 20%. Hong Kong, at 3%, and the Philippines, at 2%, rounded out the top five.
Other targets included Malaysia, Italy, and the United Kingdom, each accounting for 2%, while Germany and Belgium each accounted for 1%.

Chinese state actors have reportedly employed various cyber techniques, including exploiting vulnerabilities in publicly accessible applications, uploading web shells or malicious scripts, and deploying remote access trojans.
However, Microsoft noted that some Chinese state actors were shifting toward identity-based attacks, cloud-native persistence, and data theft.

Their cyber operations prioritized data collection from information technology and government organizations. Other targeted sectors included research and academia, think tanks and non-governmental organizations, critical manufacturing, transportation, consumer retail, finance, defense, and public health.
Artificial intelligence has further enhanced the capabilities of these threat actors, Microsoft said.

“Chinese state actors experiment with new technologies as they gain adoption, fitting them into existing workflows. Some actors now use AI tools to search for vulnerabilities or tips on exploiting them,” the report said.

The Armed Forces of the Philippines has previously warned of escalating Chinese cyber threats in 2026, as geopolitical tensions between Manila and Beijing intensified over the West Philippine Sea. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: India’s Cockroach Janta party leader detained amid crackdown on protests
articles.summary:
Abhijeet Dipke was arrested ahead of planned anti-government demonstrations in Delhi

The leader of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) youth movement, Abhijeet Dipke, was detained by police from…

blocks.text: The leader of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) youth movement, Abhijeet Dipke, was detained by police from his home on Friday as authorities cracked down on fresh anti-government protests in the Indian capital.
It came ahead of a planned Friday evening demonstration called by Dipke in central Delhi, urging supporters of the movement to come out and hold up the Indian flag.
The Cockroach movement – which initially emerged back in May as online satire – has since grown into one of the most substantial challenges to the powerful Modi government over its 12-year rule.

Alongside student groups and opposition parties, its supporters have in the past month been out on the streets across India’s biggest cities calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing a revision of India’s electoral rolls that allegedly favours the ruling Narendra Modi government with the deletion of 130m names. The election commission and Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) deny the claims.

The authorities, particularly in Delhi, have met the recent protests with a draconian crackdown, including bans on public gatherings, the deployment of tens of thousands of police, and detentions of thousands last weekend.

Friday’s protest was called by Dipke after the arrest and jailing of two of his fellow CJP leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka. They were sentenced to five days in jail this week for jumping police barricades and holding a brief protest – including waving the Indian flag – at a site recently restricted by police for demonstrations in Delhi.

At a press conference on Thursday, Dipke condemned the “repressive” attempts to silence the CJP movement and called on supporters to come out and show Narendra Modi “that we are not afraid”. He added: “If waving the Indian national flag lands you in jail, we are ready.”

Delhi police had once again taken extreme measures to try to prevent Friday’s demonstration, due to be held at a park in a busy commercial centre in the heart of Delhi, from going ahead. Police were deployed en masse to the area and a police notice was sent to Dipke instructing him to call off the protest. The Delhi local authority also shut down the park where the protest was due to take place.

When Dipke refused to call it off, police detained him en route, just as people began to assemble for the protest. In videos captured of his arrest, the CJP leader was seen holding an Indian flag aloft and saying, “I have not broken any law right now … how can you detain me?” as he was bustled away by dozens of police officers.
In a post after his detention, the CJP posted on social media: “This government is so scared of the youth waving national flag.”
Neha Bora, the student leader who has become a figurehead of the protests, was also detained on Friday as she began a march in the centre of the capital.

Despite Dipke’s detention, about 2,000 protesters still gathered and unfurled flags at the protest around Delhi’s Connaught Place. Among them was 23-year-old Sanna who said the brutal police crackdown on peaceful protests over recent weeks demonstrated that India “was on a pathway to dictatorship under the Modi government”.

“We are only out here to peacefully hold up the Indian flag and they treat us as if we are criminals, not citizens exercising our democratic rights,” she said. “Gyanesh Kumar must resign, and no matter what the police do, detaining us or crushing our skulls, we still won’t stop protesting until he is gone.”
Smaller protests also took place in Mumbai, Bengaluru and Patna on Friday.

The BJP has claimed that the Cockroach movement and the political opposition alliance have been holding protests to cause “anarchy” in the country. “Their sole intention is to stage a coup in the country,” said BJP national spokesperson Sambit Patra.
The authorities have also gone to unusual lengths to punish figures who have been seen at the recent protests calling for Kumar’s resignation.

In Mumbai, Bollywood actor Imran Khan was given a notice to leave the country after he was detained by police while attending a demonstration last weekend. Khan, who holds a US passport, was told to leave the country by the end of the month, an order he is now challenging in the courts.

articles.title: Ethiopia's Abiy Ahmed appoints interim Tigray government
articles.summary: Abiy Ahmed's office said there would be elections held in Tigray within 6 months. The move comes after an escalation in fighting between federal forces and a rebel alliance.

image.caption: Abiy Ahmed has served as Ethiopia's prime minister since 2018Image: Ethiopian Parliament

blocks.text: Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed on Friday announced an interim government in the northern Tigray region.
The move follows an outbreak of fighting in recent weeks involving a rebel alliance and the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF).

"To attain the peace that has long eluded them, to secure their right to self-administration, ​and to finally enjoy the fruits of development — which have been out of reach for many years — the people of Tigray must break free from this cycle ⁠of conflict," ​Abiy said in a statement posted on X.
The new rebel alliance transforming the Tigray conflict
What the PM's office has said
Ahmed's office said on social media that "repeated efforts" to resolve the conflict in the region have ultimately failed.
The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) leadership "did not desire peace," it said, and instead initiated the latest "devastating war."
The prime minister's office said that in order to secure peace, an interim administration was being appointed in the region and would administer Tigray for the next 6 months.
Ahmed's office listed 10 primary tasks, among them, "free and fair elections" within a 6-month period.
Returning displaced communities, the restoring of government services and protection of basic infrastructure were also among the tasks listed.
Recent return to hostilities
In September, the TPLF and six other armed groups launched an offensive against Abiy's administration.
Federal forces have managed to push the rebel alliance back, resulting in the loss of strongholds, including the regional capital Mekelle.

Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of backing the TPLF, while Asmara denies the allegation and says Addis Ababa is using the conflict as a means of justifying military action with the aim of seizing control of the Red Sea Port of Assab.
More than 600,000 people were killed in a civil war from 2020 to 2022, and the region is still battling with large numbers of internally displaced people.

articles.title: DPWH cites failed biddings for slow classroom construction
articles.summary: The Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) said Friday that failed biddings are among the reasons for the slow progress in classroom construction under the education sector's 2026…

blocks.text: Published October 17, 2026 12:14am

The Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) said Friday that failed biddings are among the reasons for the slow progress in classroom construction under the education sector's 2026 infrastructure budget.

During the Senate Finance Committee hearing on the Department of Education’s (DepEd) proposed 2027 budget, the report of Secretary Sonny Angara showed that the targeted 6,000 DPWH-led new classrooms, allocated P21.45 billion, are still under procurement.

“We’ve been encountering failure of biddings… We’ve been encountering quite a few failures in bidding; they've been concerned with the costing of classrooms with fuel price increases,” DPWH Undersecretary Lara Esquibil said.
She added that prospective project bidders found the allocated costs too low, but noted that the agency is now actively exploring strategies to minimize logistical expenses.
“But we are repackaging it to be more attractive to prospective bidders. Repackage it in order to minimize mobilization…. More strategic location,” Esquibil said.
According to the DPWH, out of the target new DPWH-led classrooms under the 2026 funds, it has advertised P7 billion, equivalent to around 2,000 classrooms.
At present, around P1.87 billion worth of projects are already in the advanced stages of procurement.
“We’re at post-qualification, finishing post-qualification and short of award, or awarded for P1.87 billion, which is 533 classrooms,” Esquibil said.
Senator Bam Aquino raised concern over the slow progress of procurement for the school building projects managed by the DPWH.

He inquired with the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) whether the remaining untransferred funds could instead be allocated to other implementing entities, to which the DBM confirmed is still possible.

“Considering na October na… 8% pa lang yung napapa-bid out ninyo, 92% pa ‘yan, doon natin siya ilagay sa kabayong tumatakbo, ‘wag na doon sa kabayong hindi gumagalaw. That's my take,” Aquino proposed.
(Considering that it's already October… and you've only put 8% out for bidding while 92% remains, let's give the funds to the running horse rather than the horse that isn't moving. That's my take.)
Aquino noted that the remaining P13 billion that DPWH has yet to bid out could potentially fund the construction of around 4,000 additional classrooms.
The DPWH is only one of several implementing entities leading the construction of the targeted 18,950 new classrooms in 2026, which have a total allocated budget of P65.4 billion.
Other programs tasked with new infrastructure construction for 2026 include:

items: LGU-led Implementation - 10,671 classrooms target; P37.02 billion budget
DepEd Learning Continuity Spaces - 1,622 classrooms; P3.50 billion budget (352 completed)
DepEd Last Mile Schools - 515 classrooms; P3.01 billion budget
DepEd Acquisition - 142 classrooms; P500 million budget

blocks.text: The budget for new construction comprises 73.6% of DepEd’s total infrastructure budget for 2026. The remaining 26.4% was allocated for repairs and “others.” —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back on front line where Starlink plays a key role
articles.summary: The BBC joins Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi as it regains crucial territory in the Donbas, but optimism has been dampened by souring relations with President Trump.

blocks.text: Watch: BBC follows Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi pushing Russia back on frontline
ByDan Johnson
Ukraine correspondent Reporting fromnear Lyman, eastern Ukraine
A Russian drone zips across the computer screen, startling the commanders keeping watch over the battlefield via a live stream in their bunker.

Cigarette in one hand, radio in the other, one of them calls in their own drone to bring it down and warns the soldiers below of the threat. The men are dangerously exposed, on the long walk across open ground from their front line positions. They are being replaced after three months forcing the Russians back.
This is part of Operation Vivaldi, a Ukrainian counter-offensive which they say has liberated 277 sq km (106 square miles) in the eastern Donbas region in recent months.

The name reflects the offensive's four stages, or seasons - like the Italian composer's violin concerto. The successful assault blunted an attempted Russian pincer movement that threatened to encircle the key Fortress Belt cities still under Ukrainian control.

While Russia this month pummels Ukraine from the air, crippling its energy infrastructure and killing scores of civilians across the country, at the front, it is Ukraine that has made recent gains. Kyiv says it has inflicted heavy losses - 8,000 Russian casualties in Vivaldi alone, and close to 50,000 along the front in the month of September – and suffered few casualties in return.
Image source, Reuters
The Starlink system was integrated into Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi, but this week Kyiv said restrictions had been imposed on it without warning

The Institute for the Study of War reported that pro-Russian military bloggers had acknowledged the Ukrainian advances, and expressed fears this could lead to more losses for Russia in the future. No Russian official has publicly acknowledged the Ukrainian gains. Russian ministry of defence briefings say only that they were "repelling attacks" in the Lyman region, or "improving the tactical position at the front".
Despite Ukraine's forward moves, Russian drones are still ever-present. Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, tells me his men face 10 on an average day.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ukraine's military says it has liberated 277 sq km in the eastern Donbas region

blocks.text: Ukraine's military says it has liberated 277 sq km in the eastern Donbas region

He is fixed on the live stream as a Ukrainian snare swoops in, hovers for a few seconds and drops a net on to the drone, dragging it from the sky. This Russian drone was for reconnaissance, but if it had locked on to the soldiers, another drone carrying explosives would have followed.

This moment of peril illustrates the layers making up the modern battlefield. The command bunker receives live pictures from a hovering camera, while below a Ukrainian attack drone attacks another enemy spotter which would have called in more flying firepower.
Integrated in all of this is Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications network, providing broadband connectivity across the battlefield.
Ukraine said this week, as Operation Vivaldi concluded, that the system had restrictions imposed without warning, limiting their capability.

Musk and media reports suggest the order may have come from the White House. While Ukraine is not wholly reliant on Starshield, it is a key tool in their arsenal, vital for interceptor and mid-range strike drones. And knowing this tool can be restricted without any warning or consultation has sparked major concern in Ukraine.
Beneath the battle for aerial superiority, unmanned ground vehicles scurry back and forth delivering supplies, evacuating the wounded or, increasingly, leading the charge against the enemy.
Everything here relies on digital connectivity - to see, to move, to fly, to communicate, to fire. But at the bottom of this stack, it is still human beings in trenches who are holding the ground.
The weary soldiers have made it safely to the command post. After 95 days pushing forward on the front line there is an emotional reunion.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Dealer, a soldier in the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, just came off the front line

blocks.text: Image source, Matthew Goddard/BBC
Dealer, a soldier in the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, just came off the front line
An infantryman with the call-sign Dealer tells me he feels strong, but it is good to be finally heading home: "It's an impressive operation. Over three months, we moved positions four times."
He tells me the most frightening threat was Russian drones, piloted remotely and determined to hunt down their target.
Commandant Phoenix said the preparation for the offensive was "enormous".
"The men trained for months. We had to completely restructure our approach because previously we had been defending, and now we had to go on the offensive."

Robots and drones led the assault on Russian positions and, for the first time, remote-controlled explosive vehicles were dropped behind Russian lines - 250 Russians surrendered. According to Ukrainian commanders, their year-long campaign has freed 16 settlements from Russian occupation.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit

blocks.text: Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit

In Karpivka, a village occupied since April, the Ukrainians found one local resident remaining - 61 year old Volodymyr Zamota, the last man standing when his neighbours fled the Russian advance in 2025. He says he survived for eight months in total isolation.
"As they say, hope dies last," he told me. "I'm the only person left in the whole village, and the village has been almost completely destroyed."
"I thought I would live to old age without experiencing anything like this, but then it happened. It's a terrible tragedy".

That devastation defines the region Ukraine has just recaptured. It's still too risky for residents to return, if they even have a home intact. But Ukraine's soldiers are celebrating this regained ground, the halted Russian advance and the future potential this operation may present.
"The real value of this is securing advantageous positions, favourable lines, and a bridgehead that grants us a superior position," Andriy Hitt, Revenge Bridge chief of staff, explained.

"This allows us to create the necessary conditions for subsequent successful operations, seize the initiative in battle, and plan future successful manoeuvres… each of these actions is a building block towards victory."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Nets now span roads in eastern Ukraine to protect from drones

blocks.text: Nets now span roads in eastern Ukraine to protect from drones
All this could be threatened by the limitations on US technology, and American intelligence. Relations between Kyiv and Washington are at an all-time low.

This week President Zelensky said he felt "betrayed" by Donald Trump, while the US leader declared he was "not a fan" of his Ukrainian counterpart, saying he was harder to deal with than Vladimir Putin.
Trump says Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries have hiked oil prices. Ukraine says the US and Israeli war against Iran is the cause.
But despite the diplomatic divisions, among the soldiers we met, morale is high. Dealer says Operation Vivaldi has renewed his belief Ukraine can win the war.
The unit is ensuring Volodymyr, Grandpa as they call him, has enough to eat - drones drop off food parcels on their way to feed soldiers at the front.
I asked Volodymyr if he believed Ukraine could win. "Yes, of course I do. I would just like to know when it will happen, when all of this will finally end."
Additional reporting by Kostas Kallergis and Anastasiia Levchenko

pagasa.dost.gov.ph

MANILA, Philippines — A potential super typhoon is expected to enter the Philippine area of responsibility (PAR) next week, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration said yesterday.
Champi is moving at 100 kilometers per hour, with gustiness of 125 kph while moving westward at 20 kph.
PAGASA weather specialist Daniel James Villamil said Champi is expected to enter PAR by Tuesday.

articles.title: Philippine removes 250,000 fake overseas job posts
articles.summary: The Philippines has worked with social media platforms Meta and TikTok to remove about 250,000 online posts advertising fraudulent overseas jobs, the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) said.

blocks.text: October 17, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines has worked with social media platforms Meta and TikTok to remove about 250,000 online posts advertising fraudulent overseas jobs, the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) said.
The department disclosed the figure during the 19th ASEAN Forum on Migrant Labor (AFML), held on Oct. 14 and 15 at the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay.

During a session on emerging trends and challenges in online recruitment, DMW Undersecretary Darlene Pajarito stressed the need for governments, digital platforms and other stakeholders to work together to protect Filipinos seeking employment abroad.

“We cannot work in silos. That’s why we also forged many memoranda of agreement with concerned agencies, published materials for public awareness and took down fraudulent job posts through our partnership with Meta and TikTok Philippines,” Pajarito said.
Participants called for stronger laws on online recruitment, verification of employers and job advertisements and faster removal of fraudulent posts and accounts.
They also recommended closer coordination among governments, digital platforms, law enforcement agencies and financial service providers to disrupt illegal recruitment networks.

articles.title: Zaldy Co’s bagmen, Baligod arrested for unjust vexation
articles.summary: Fourteen alleged bagmen of ex-lawmaker Zaldy Co and their lawyer Levi Baligod have been ordered arrested yet again, this time by a Zambales court for unjust vexation.

blocks.text: October 17, 2026 | 12:00am
MANILA, Philippines — Fourteen alleged bagmen of ex-lawmaker Zaldy Co and their lawyer Levi Baligod have been ordered arrested yet again, this time by a Zambales court for unjust vexation.
The group was arrested at the San Juan Hall of Justice on Friday around 9:30 a.m. after attending a hearing there.

Presiding Judge Santiago Beltran Jr. of Iba, Zambales Regional Trial Court Branch 69 issued the arrest warrant on Sept. 23 against Baligod, Bernard Tube, Rosebert Waupan, Johny Buduan, Rodante Orbillo, Reyneboy Julian, Christopher Esquivel, George Villalon Jr., Romeo Rommel Bobares, Gil Navidad Jr., Anselmo Taberdo, Joely Cadiao, Rommel Galapon, Cecilio Larroder Jr., Bernard Gumban, Crisanie Dado, Fidel Corpuz, Walter Manalansan and Benny Bulontate.
They all face charges of unjust vexation in relation to the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012. It is unclear who filed the case against them in Zambales.

Tube, Waupan, Bulontate and Larroder Jr. had already turned their backs on the group, executing new affidavits in July that accusations of flood-control kickbacks delivered to over 30 government officials were untrue.
The remaining bagmen – who call themselves the “Brave 14” – were at the San Juan court to attend a hearing in one of their cyber libel cases.
The Zambales court fixed the bail at P10,000 each.
Baligod and four bagmen were released in the afternoon, but 10 others remain in custody after they failed to complete their release documents during office hours.

articles.title: Ombudsman: Plunder cases vs Legarda, Leviste filed soon
articles.summary: A plunder case against Sen. Loren Legarda and her son, Batangas Rep. Leandro Leviste, will be filed before the Sandiganbayan soon as the complaint undergoes preliminary investigation, Ombudsman Jesus…

blocks.text: October 17, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — A plunder case against Sen. Loren Legarda and her son, Batangas Rep. Leandro Leviste, will be filed before the Sandiganbayan soon as the complaint undergoes preliminary investigation, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said.
“It’s coming soon,” Remulla said in a press briefing.

Ombudsman investigators have accused the mother and son of allegedly conspiring to secure exclusive government rights over the country’s solar energy resources through legislative and regulatory actions, resulting in about P10.4 billion in unpaid financial obligations to the government.
Remulla said the complaint against Legarda and Leviste is undergoing preliminary investigation before the Office of the Ombudsman.
Legarda’s camp earlier said it had filed a counter-affidavit in response to the complaint.
Remulla rejected the camp’s claim that the complaint was a case of political persecution, saying it was “far from that.”
“You can probably see the conflict-of-interest angle. We did not invent that. Everything will be recorded. The facts will be presented to the courts,” he said.
Both Legarda and Leviste are currently out of the country. The senator has been on medical leave since Aug. 3, while Leviste’s two-month travel authority expired on Sept. 24.

articles.title: VP: Tackle SALN issues in court, before ombudsman
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte on Thursday said the Senate impeachment court and the Office of the Ombudsman are the proper forums to answer allegations that she failed to declare properties linked to…

blocks.text: October 17, 2026 | 12:00am
Vice President Sara Duterte
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte on Thursday said the Senate impeachment court and the Office of the Ombudsman are the proper forums to answer allegations that she failed to declare properties linked to her family.

“Regarding my statement of assets and liabilities, it is already a subject of the impeachment. And it has also been submitted to the ombudsman. So, these are the proper forums where it would be better for us to give our answers and explanations. Rather than having to answer to (National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin) Attorney Matibag,” Duterte said in Zamboanga City on Thursday night.
Matibag said the investigation had moved beyond the affidavit of dismissed police officer Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. and is now focused on properties declared in Duterte’s SALN.
Duterte maintained the claims of Matibag that she owns properties were inaccurate. “I’m not interested in him. No one is interested in Attorney Matibag. He’s a nobody,” Duterte added.
Mr. Nobody

In response, Matibag affirmed what the Vice President had said. “Well, that’s true – if the basis is mansions, businesses and companies receiving funds from Chinese state-owned companies,” the NBI director said. “I’m really a nobody.”

Matibag has challenged Duterte to file a case if she believes that the NBI is biased in its investigation on properties linked to her family, adding that the NBI inquiry is backed by official records and evidence.

He noted that the NBI obtained copies of the titles from the Land Registration Authority, visited the properties based on their descriptions, conducted geotagging and interviewed residents to verify ownership.

Matibag also cited an agricultural land in Catigan, Davao City, which he said was declared in Duterte’s SALN at a combined assessed value of about P890,000. He questioned the valuation after investigators documented the property.
In response, Duterte’s camp described the NBI’s probe as “the latest example of the Marcos administration’s weaponization of government institutions for political persecution.”

“That is not the work of a fair and impartial investigative body. That is a shameless smear campaign against the Vice President using public funds, headlined by a man with a documented conflict of interest against her,” Duterte’s spokesman Paolo Panelo said.

Meanwhile, Duterte thanked the public following the recent surveys showing continued majority trust and approval ratings despite the ongoing Senate impeachment hearings on corruption and unexplained wealth allegations.
She continues to enjoy much higher trust and approval ratings than President Marcos, a Pulse Asia survey from Sept. 17 to 24 showed.

Duterte retained a majority of trust and approval ratings, despite dropping from 58 percent to 55 percent, while those who distrust her remained at 27 percent. Undecided respondents increased from 16 percent to 19 percent.

Meanwhile, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said his office will look into the alleged misuse of P612.5 million worth of confidential funds by Duterte for possible filing of cases before the Sandiganbayan. — Roel Pareño, EJ Macabbabad, Daphne Galvez

articles.title: 60 percent think some senators won’t be fair in impeachment trial
articles.summary: While there will be some senators who will be impartial, a majority of Filipinos believed that there will be some who would not be fair in their decision in the impeachment trial of Vice President…

blocks.text: October 17, 2026 | 12:00am

Office of the Vice President Assistant Secretary and Assistant Chief of Staff Lemuel Ortonio, the second hostile witness, responds to questions from counsel to prosecution Mae Divinagracia during direct examination on the 18th day of the impeachment trial at the Senate in Pasay on August 25, 2026.
The Philippine STAR / Ryan Baldemor

MANILA, Philippines — While there will be some senators who will be impartial, a majority of Filipinos believed that there will be some who would not be fair in their decision in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, a survey conducted by Pulse Asia showed.

The survey, conducted from Sept. 17 to 24, found that 60 percent of the respondents have views aligned with the statement, “there will be some senators who will be fair and others who will not be fair in judging the impeachment case.”
Only 20 percent believed that all senators will be fair and will not favor any one in judging the case, while 17 percent said the senators will not be fair in their decision.
The remaining four percent did not provide an answer.
The poll results were part of Pulse Asia’s survey on the ongoing impeachment trial of the Vice President.
It did not ask the respondents to identify who among the senator-judges they think would not be fair in their decision.
The survey also asked respondents what they think of the impact of the trial on democracy. Thirty percent said it will have a positive impact, while 31 percent said it will be negative.
The remaining 39 percent said they cannot say if the impeachment trial would have a positive or negative impact on the country’s democracy.
It was previously reported that only 41 percent of the respondents had sufficient or great deal of knowledge about the case against Duterte. Fifty-nine percent said they had little to no knowledge.
Most respondents also want Duterte to personally appear before the Senate impeachment court.
The survey had 2,400 respondents and a margin of error of plus/minus two percent.
Palace: No talks on possible VP replacement
There are no talks about possible scenarios in case Vice President Duterte is convicted in her impeachment trial, Malacañang said yesterday.

“There is no conviction yet. We cannot anticipate. We cannot speculate because the defense will present its evidence. There is no decision yet from the impeachment court so it is not being discussed,” Palace press officer Claire Castro said.
“So in fairness to and out of respect to the position of vice president, it is not being discussed. Let us allow the process to move forward,” she added. — Alexis Romero

articles.title: Self-rated poverty highest so far this year – SWS
articles.summary: More than half of Filipino families considered themselves poor in the third quarter of the year, the highest so far in 2026, based on a survey conducted by Social Weather Stations (SWS).

blocks.text: October 17, 2026 | 12:00am
Residents of Barangay San Nicolas in Binondo, Manila go about their daily routine.
STAR / Edd Gumban

MANILA, Philippines — More than half of Filipino families considered themselves poor in the third quarter of the year, the highest so far in 2026, based on a survey conducted by Social Weather Stations (SWS).
Results of the Sept. 21 to 27 survey found that 55 percent of respondents considered their families as poor, up six percentage points from 49 percent in June.
The latest self-rated poverty rate also surpassed the 52 percent in March and the average 51 percent last year.
Based on the latest results, 36 percent of the respondents considered their families as “not poor,” hardly moving from 37 percent in June.
Those who considered their families as neither poor nor not poor – considered by SWS as “borderline” – decreased from 14 percent to nine percent.

Self-rated poverty increased across all areas. It was highest among those in Mindanao at 64 percent (from 61 percent), followed by those in the Visayas at 63 percent (from 59 percent), balance Luzon at 51 percent (from 41 percent) and Metro Manila at 44 percent (from 40 percent).
Food poverty
The latest survey also found that 44 percent identified their families as “food poor” or poor based on the food they eat, up from 36 percent in June.

Those who rated their families as “not food poor” slightly decreased from 49 percent to 47 percent, while those who considered their families as “borderline food poor” dropped from 15 percent to nine percent.

Self-rated food poverty was highest among respondents in Mindanao at 52 percent (from 45 percent), closely followed by those in the Visayas at 51 percent (from 45 percent), balance Luzon at 40 percent (from 31 percent) and Metro Manila at 31 percent (from 27 percent).
The SWS survey had 1,500 respondents and a margin of error of plus/minus three percent.

articles.title: Gas prices tipped for P4.20/liter rollback
articles.summary: After two consecutive rounds of hikes, gasoline prices may finally drop by at least P4 per liter next week amid easing supply concerns in Asia.

blocks.text: October 17, 2026 | 12:00am
Based on the four-day average of the regional benchmark Mean of Platts Singapore, industry estimates suggest a potential gasoline price rollback of P4 to P4.20 per liter.
The STAR / Miguel de Guzman
MANILA, Philippines — After two consecutive rounds of hikes, gasoline prices may finally drop by at least P4 per liter next week amid easing supply concerns in Asia.
Diesel prices, however, are seen to increase by P0.20 to P0.40 per liter, potentially ending three consecutive weeks of price cuts.
Jetti Petroleum president Leo Bellas said gasoline supply improved across the region as refineries resumed operations after maintenance.
For diesel, prices rose amid persistently low global inventories.
Expectations of additional supply from Russia and the release of diesel stocks by Group of Seven (G7) countries tempered the increase.
The G7 – comprising Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States – agreed to release 100 million barrels of petroleum supplies.
Bellas stressed, however, that doubts remain over whether the diesel deal between the United States and Russia would deliver a meaningful increase in global supply.
Strategic reserve too costly
Meanwhile, Shell Pilipinas independent director Edgar Chua said establishing a government-managed strategic petroleum reserve would be too costly for the country.
“It is a good concept, but can we afford it?” Chua said when asked whether Shell was interested in taking part in setting up the planned emergency reserves.
A strategic petroleum reserve is an emergency stockpile of crude oil and refined products held by the government, private entities or both.
It is released during supply disruptions caused by geopolitical conflicts, natural disasters or global shocks to stabilize supply, moderate prices and ensure fuel availability.
Industry estimates pegged the cost of establishing oil reserves sufficient to provide an additional 30 days of fuel supply at around P30 billion.
“The strategic reserves are for rich countries. Sorry to say, we think we’re rich (because) we have a sovereign wealth fund,” Chua said.

articles.title: Nova Scotia to host massive data centre to power artificial intelligence

image.caption: Nova Scotia announced on Friday morning that a data centre to power artificial intelligence is under construction in Cape Breton. (Taryn Grant/CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia
A massive data centre to provide computing power for artificial intelligence is under pre-construction just outside a town on Cape Breton Island, Nova Scotia.
EverWind Fuels will own it, AI giant Anthropic will lease it
A massive data centre to provide computing power for artificial intelligence giant Anthropic is under pre-construction just outside Port Hawkesbury in Cape Breton.

EverWind Fuels will handle construction of the facility, while Anthropic will lease the first phase for a term of at least 20 years. Anthropic said in a news release the data centre "will power Claude models and serve growing demand from Canadian and global customers."
EverWind, headed by Australian-American private equity veteran Trent Vichie, had previously confirmed it has data centre ambitions, but said little else.
On Friday, EverWind released more information about its plans.
EverWind Fuels said it will build the facility in two stages, with the first phase to come online by the end of 2027 and the second in 2028.
The first phase would have a capacity of 95 megawatts and the second, 325 megawatts, for a total of 420 megawatts. Nova Scotia’s current electrical generating capacity is close to 3,000 megawatts.
EverWind said it will pay for any required upgrades to Nova Scotia’s electricity system.
EverWind raising $8 billion for project
EverWind said it is raising $8 billion in private capital to fund the project and an additional $2 billion for four of the onshore wind farms it is planning to build.

"This is investment that is in the ground here, supporting Nova Scotians, not only its energy economy but its knowledge economy as well," Vichie said at an announcement in Point Tupper, the industrial park where the facility is to be built.
Land clearing is underway and officials said they hope to have foundations poured before winter.
Trent Vichie, CEO of Everwind, spoke at the event. (Tom Ayers/CBC)
EverWind's four wind farms would eventually support the data centre’s electricity needs, but existing generation on the provincial grid would be the primary supply to begin.

The Independent Energy System Operator, which manages the provincial grid, told CBC News it studies all new projects to ensure the grid can handle them, before allowing them to connect. It did not answer specifically whether there is capacity to connect this data centre, although EverWind officials said they've been assured there is capacity, at least for phase 1.
Vichie was joined at Friday's announcement by politicians from every level of government, who are enthused about the idea.
Premier Tim Houston thanked Vichie for bringing such a large sum of money to Nova Scotia, and said it demonstrates "what is possible in our province."
"Please don't stop, keep moving, we'll be here to support you in that," he said, directing his remarks to the EverWind CEO.
EverWind's data centre will be in Point Tupper, just outside Port Hawkesbury. (Tom Ayers/CBC)
Kings-Hants MP Kody Blois, who is parliamentary secretary to the prime minister, said the data centre aligns with the Liberal government's priorities.
"Today is an example of how we're building a stronger Canada," he said.

Richmond County Warden Lois Landry noted there has been some skepticism in the community in recent weeks as people have been speculating about the project's specifics, but she said she feels optimistic after learning more information.
"We're hearing about potential construction and long-term employment, opportunities for local businesses and infrastructure investment that could support future growth," she said.
EverWind has been trying to develop renewable energy projects in Nova Scotia for several years. It says those plans remain unchanged.
The data centre is to be built at the same site as one of EverWind’s other proposed projects — a green hydrogen and ammonia facility.
Data centre controversies

Data centres have become a flashpoint across Canada, especially those that power AI, because they can have huge footprints and require vast amounts of energy and water for cooling. Concerns about AI’s potential impacts on jobs and dire warnings about risks to human existence also have some people pushing back.

There are some proposed data centres that would dwarf this one in size, including the Wonder Valley data centre in Alberta — the first phase of which is meant to be more than a gigawatt — but this project is still on the larger end of facilities that have been recently announced in Canada.
EverWind said it has signed on to Ottawa’s responsible data centre development principles — a set of non-binding guidelines the federal government released last month.

Houston recently laid out similar guidelines. Both levels of government say they expect any data centre to have local benefits, minimal environmental impact and minimal water use, and for there to be no resulting power rate spikes.

“We applaud the federal and provincial governments for setting high standards for responsible development,” Vichie said in a news release. “And we will continue to work with communities to ensure that our work meets their expectations.”
$10 billion private investments in Nova Scotia to include AI data centre

EverWind said it will use a closed-loop water-glycol system. The company’s preliminary estimate for water usage is an average of 100,000 litres per day for the first phase and 500,000 litres of water per day including both phases.

Water would be drawn from nearby Landrie Lake. The provincial regulator has approved the Landrie Lake Water Utility to withdraw 34 million litres from the lake each day, which would make EverWind’s daily requirements about one per cent of the total safe withdrawal volume.

The company promised the data centre would come with a community benefit program worth tens of millions of dollars. A specific dollar figure was not provided. Local communities and Anthropic would consult on how to spend the money.
A consortium of Mi’kmaw communities, fronted by Membertou First Nation, is negotiating a nine per cent equity stake in the project.
But not everyone is ready to endorse the project.
Nova Scotia's Ecology Action Centre (EAC) said it poses more questions than it answers.
Thomas Arnason McNeil, policy advocate on grid decarbonization at the EAC, raised concerns about the project's scale.
"There will need to be analysis and work that is done in terms of quantifying ... the impact on ratepayers and understanding what the environmental impacts of the project will be," he said.
McNeil added that while the group is reserving judgment for now, thorough impact assessments are essential before moving forward.

articles.title: ‘Tough to watch, impossible to ignore’: what the reviewers say about NAZA documentary
articles.summary:
Film interviewing military insiders about mass killing of civilians in Gaza receives widespread praise around the world

Critics around the world have hailed the award-winning documentary…

blocks.text: Critics around the world have hailed the award-winning documentary NAZA as a “brilliant and harrowing” film that is “impossible to ignore”.

NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian and details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, was released in UK cinemas this week and will be shown in more than 50 countries. As well as its global cinema releases, NAZA will be available free on the Guardian’s website from late November.
The investigative documentary, which contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders speaking anonymously on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night, has received widespread praise.

In a five-star review, the Financial Times’s Danny Leigh says that as a piece of cinema, “journalism and film-making brilliantly entwine”. The Times calls the film “hugely provocative and a disturbing account” of Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, and the Irish Times brands NAZA an “essential record of engineered nightmare”. In a four-star review, the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw says the “anguish of Gaza is brought into pin-sharp focus”.

British Vogue calls NAZA a “brilliant and harrowing film” that outlines the “restrained, meticulous, bone-chilling depiction of the progressive erasure of Gaza”. The magazine says the film “feels destined to become an enduring historical document, one which will and should be seen by generations to come”.

Time Out magazine says NAZA “puts together a restrained, intelligent, articulate, precise and utterly damning case against Israel’s actions in Gaza and their ongoing actions through the region. As a work of cinema, it is exemplary. As a work of journalism, it is inarguable. As a document, it is an indictment.”

The New York Times makes the film a “critic’s choice” and calls NAZA a “haunting” documentary that is “tough to watch, and impossible to ignore”. The Los Angeles Times says NAZA is a “stone-cold frightening” film that “burns the conscience”. And in New York magazine, it is described as “one of the most important films of our time”.

The Hollywood Reporter praises NAZA as a “sober and thoroughly documented bombshell of an expose” that “leaves one with a deadening feeling, as if humanity may have lost all hope”. The Toronto Star says “NAZA is heartbreaking but essential viewing, questioning the systems that cause and quantify civilian death in modern warfare”.

The Spanish outlet El Mundo hailed NAZA as “the film of our time, a superb, electrifying, and devastating documentary about the systematic model of annihilation of the Palestinian people” that ultimately “points the finger at us. At night, in silence.”

The French newspaper Le Monde says the film “has the effect of an uppercut that leaves the viewer stunned”, while the Danish culture magazine Soundvenue calls NAZA a “soul-crushing testimony to the genocide in Gaza” that is an “example of how the world increasingly seems like a dystopia”.

The United Arab Emirates’ state-owned newspaper the National calls NAZA a “sickeningly tough film to watch”, and an editorial in the Israeli-outlet Haaretz says the film is “trying to force Israelis to confront what they already know: that Israel’s conduct of the war in Gaza has left a black stain”.

When the film opened in Italy last month, it topped the charts. The Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera says NAZA lasts “only 80 minutes, but no more is needed: the ‘scientific’ coldness with which the interviewees reconstruct how they are destroying Gaza is something unforgettable”.

The film contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders who detail how an AI-assisted apparatus of mass surveillance was activated during the Gaza war, revealing the systems that were used to target Hamas operatives in the knowledge that large numbers of Palestinian civilians would also die.

Various bodies, including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based, have said Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
The film premiered at the Venice film festival, where it was received a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. The documentary went on to win the special jury prize.

articles.title: Starlink access still not fully restored for Ukraine’s military, says Zelenskyy
articles.summary: Ukrainian president says US limiting access was a ‘dangerous and unpleasant surprise’, amid reports the order came from inside White House
articles.byline: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels and Andrew Rothin Kyiv

blocks.text: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink satellite internet service has not yet been fully restored, as media reports suggested the order to throttle the service had come from within the White House.
Zelenskyy met European leaders on Friday in Brussels, where he asked the EU for another €70bn next year to fund Ukraine’s defence against Russia.

The meeting offered an important opportunity for Zelenskyy and Europe to align their strategies, as Zelenskyy once again found himself embroiled in a major quarrel with the US president, Donald Trump.

Hours earlier, Trump had called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace” and criticised ⁠Zelenskyy, after an purported “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold.
“All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher,” Trump told the Newsmax television channel. “Well, I think that’s a disgrace.”
Energy analysts told the BBC that the US-Israeli war on Iran was having the biggest impact on diesel export volumes, although the Ukraine war was also significant.

Trump’s administration is suspected of withholding intelligence from Ukraine on incoming Russian ballistic missile strikes, and of throttling Starshield, the military version of the Starlink satellite internet network, to prevent it from being used on drones flying above 100mph. Neither has officially been confirmed.

blocks.caption: Firefighters working at the scene of a Russian drone strike in a residential area in Kyiv on Thursday. Photograph: Vincenzo Circosta/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Speaking after meeting EU leaders on Friday, Zelenskyy said that Starshield had not yet returned to normal.

“Our defence ministry is in touch and my partners, they told me that there were signals from the White House that they would return these capabilities,” Zelenskyy said. “Have they returned to the previous speed limits? No. But is it coming back now? Yes.”

Reuters on Friday reported that the order to throttle Starshield had come from inside the White House, according to two US officials and a western official briefed on the matter. They did not identify the White House official who had made the decision, but said the Pentagon had been informed that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military had to be slowed.

Zelenskyy called it a “very dangerous and unpleasant surprise” that speeds had been reduced on Starlink, which Ukraine uses to support its most effective air defence systems against Russian jet-powered drones.
Starlink is produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, but controlled by the US government.

When Zelenskyy arrived for talks with EU leaders, he was applauded by the heads of state and government of the bloc’s 27 countries. Zelenskyy later said he had heard “only support”, when asked about reports that European leaders had asked him to dial down his criticism of Trump.

blocks.caption: Zelenskyy with the presidents of the European Council, Antonio Costa (left) and the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen (right) on Friday. Photograph: Pier Marco Tacca/Getty Images

blocks.text: According to a transcript of his remarks, he told EU leaders that the war would cost €155bn in 2027. “And we need at least €70 bn more from you – for defence, for weapons, and for our resilience,” he said. “This is a realistic amount.”

The EU is currently giving Ukraine regular payments from a €90bn funding plan agreed last December that was intended to cover two-thirds of Kyiv’s civilian and military needs for 2026-27. The remaining third was to be filled by other “international partners”, such as the UK, Canada, Norway and Japan.

The realisation that Kyiv again risks a financial crunch has put Russia’s €210bn assets frozen inside the EU back on the table. The EU takes the profits from those assets to support Ukraine, but last year decided against using the funds themselves, instead opting for an EU-backed €90bn loan.

Belgium, which hosts the vast majority of the Russian funds, remains strongly opposed to using the frozen assets, fearing it will be left to carry the financial burden if the plan goes wrong. But Zelenskyy said there could be an alternative.

“We need something like a special EU-controlled custodian to reduce the risk of them being unfrozen and divided up among those who clearly do not want what is best for Europe or an end to this war,” he said.

The European Commission, a strong backer of last year’s rejected frozen assets plan, has been reluctant to propose new variants – such as an EU-controlled custodian – because it fears running into same opposition from Belgium and other sceptical member states.

Before the summit, Belgium’s prime minister, Bart De Wever, said Zelenskyy would “probably look everybody straight in the eye and say: thank you for the €90bn, but that money is going to run out because a war is a very costly thing”.

The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said the EU had supported Trump’s energy ceasefire, “but we have seen that Russia did not respect it, not a single minute” and instead had escalated its attacks. She said the EU intended to increase pressure on Russia, promising a 22nd round of sanctions and adding: “We will not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops the war.”

articles.title: Attacks on Ukraine’s power plants show Russia has given up on military victory
articles.summary: Strikes increasingly resemble an intercepted Russian blueprint to make life unliveable in major Ukrainian cities

blocks.text: As Russian missiles and drones have systematically slammed into power plants in Kyiv and Kharkiv this week, the rolling blackouts and water outages have increasingly resembled a supposed Russian blueprint to destroy life in major Ukrainian cities seen by the Guardian.

Even as Donald Trump unilaterally declared an “energy ceasefire” last week between Moscow and Kyiv, Russia continued with its methodical and devastating strikes on Ukraine’s power grid, in particular in Kyiv, in a strategy meant to punish Ukraine’s population and drive the country to capitulation.

The potential goals of the Russian campaign, according to an assessment seen by the Guardian that Ukrainian intelligence said it intercepted from Russia last month, range from “degrading the quality of life” of Ukrainians through power outages to fully shutting off the water supply, which the document cooly predicts would cause the “deterioration of sanitary conditions and the forced outflow of residents from cities.”

The document does not specify which Russian agency developed the assessment, which is titled Analysis of Ukraine’s Energy, Housing and Utilities Sectors, includes vulnerable Ukrainian energy grid targets and even contemplates strikes against high-risk sites, including the switchyards at several nuclear power plants. But several European officials familiar with the document have said it is likely to have been produced by analytical departments linked to the Russian military or intelligence agencies, and that copies have circulated in Ukraine in previous years.

This year, however, Russia appears to be putting those plans into practice. On Tuesday night, Russian strikes hit three major power plants in the Kyiv region – Combined Heat and Power Plants 4 and 5, and the Trypillya Thermal Power Plant in the Kyiv region – as well as a major electrical substation that transfers electricity from two of the country’s main nuclear power plants to the capital. Those, along with other substations that make up the “Kyiv energy ring” that helps bring electricity from across the country to the capital, have all been targets of a Russian barrage that, if it succeeds, could threaten a humanitarian catastrophe in a city of 3 million people.

Ukraine’s energy minister first briefed European allies last month about the plan, a copy of which was first reported on by the New York Times. Russia has stepped up its attacks on the Ukrainian power grid precisely as Washington and Kyiv are embroiled in a major political quarrel. The Guardian is withholding some specifics of the military assessment at the request of Ukraine’s energy ministry, which said it could aid in further strikes against the country.

“There are two large documents, written very coldly and very clearly, with tables showing the number of weapons needed for each facility to destroy it,” Ukrainian energy minister Denys Shmyhal said last month. “The types of weapons range from ballistic missiles to jet-powered and conventional drones. We understand how they are going to act.”

The leaked documents identify bottlenecks and prescribe the number of ballistic and hypersonic cruise missiles and jet-powered drones needed to knock out power plants and substations with brutal efficiency. If that was done, it could destroy more than 90% of the power that Kyiv is budgeted for each winter, the document predicts, plunging the city into the dark and cold. A worst-case scenario could lead to blackouts lasting up to 20 hours a day until damaged equipment is repaired, according to expert projections.

The strikes on Ukraine’s energy system have become the country’s new frontlines – and the country is badly outgunned, as its stocks of US-provided PAC-3 missiles have dwindled. Zelenskyy this week castigated city authorities for poor planning for the winter and for failing to protect the city’s energy infrastructure. Protests over heat and electricity blackouts are also planned for Saturday, highlighting how the difficult conditions in winter could provoke a political crisis for the wartime government.

Economic Pravda, a leading Ukrainian news site that covers business, reported on Thursday that the three major power plants in Kyiv no longer have the ability to generate electricity, leaving the city more reliant on electricity brought from elsewhere in the country (the government generally does not confirm specific damage to critical infrastructure). The outlets’ experts predicted that, given a moderate winter and quick repairs of damaged substations, Kyiv residents could face up to eight hours of blackouts a day. Its worst case scenario of frigid temperatures and frequent attacks would leave Kyiv in the dark for up to 20 hours a day.

This is no accident for the Kremlin, which has increasingly turned to punishing Ukraine’s population in major cities as the frontlines of the conflict have frozen. “Last year, we were really on the brink,” said Volodymyr Fesenko, a Ukrainian political analyst. “But the risk this year will be even worse, so the plan [to attack Ukrainian infrastructure] does seem realistic. There’s a very high chance that Russia tries to break us this winter.” If the Kremlin believed in the chance of a clean military victory before now, he added, it may now believe that not to be possible, and focus on destroying Ukraine’s remaining infrastructure rather than trying to capture it.
after newsletter promotion

The secret plan, which officials here say was intercepted by Ukrainian intelligence and then briefed to senior European diplomats by Shmyhal last month, sets itself several goals: to destroy electricity generation, heating, water and sewage systems in such a way as to to make life in Ukrainian cities unliveable. Destroying electrical generation alone, it says, would lead to a “significant decrease in the quality of life of the population.”

To do so, it specifies the number of weapons that should be allocated – Geran 4/5 jet-powered drones and hypersonic or cruise missiles – in order to destroy key infrastructure such as thermal power plants, substations, water pumping stations and more.
Considering strikes against the basis of Ukraine’s water, sewage and heating systems, the document says it would create a “large-scale municipal infrastructure crisis.”

When contacted by the Guardian, the Ukrainian Energy Ministry said that the document contained information that could aid in attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. It did not reply to questions on how the current Russian bombing strategy matched with the proposals made in the document, or which Russian agency had developed the plans.

articles.title: Prosecutors end evidence presentation vs. Marcoleta on first day of trial, says Remulla
articles.summary: Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said that prosecutors have finished presenting their evidence against Senator Rodante Marcoleta in the plunder case lodged against him --on the first day of trial.

blocks.text: Published October 16, 2026 11:27pm
Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said that prosecutors have finished presenting their evidence against Senator Rodante Marcoleta in the plunder case lodged against him —on the first day of trial.

In a "24 Oras" report from Raffy Tima on Friday, the prosecution was quickly able to present before the Sandiganbayan all of its evidence on the first day of Marcoleta’s trial for plunder and the violation of Presidential Decree 46.

This came only three months and three days after the case against Marcoleta was lodged on July 3. Marcoleta’s co-accused in the case are former House lawmaker Mike Defensor and businessmen Joseph Espiritu and Aristotle Viray.
Remulla said that this was the fastest that a case has been resolved in the history of the Office of the Ombudsman.

“We rested our case; we presented our evidence. Ang ibig sabihin niyan, is that, if it took us three months, two or months or three months to present our case, he would have to do the same,” Remulla said.
(We rested our case; we presented our evidence. This means that, if it took us three months, two to three months, to present our case, he would have to do the same.)

The case stemmed from Marcoleta’s own admission that he accepted P75 million from his co-accused as a campaign donation while he was still sitting as a House lawmaker. However, this was not declared in his Statement of Contributions and Expenditures.

“Ang lumalabas kasi sa case ni Senator Marcoleta is actually purely a legal question. Yung nangyari, everything is admitted, so there is only one question, whether or not he committed plunder. And that’s what we presented before the court,” Remulla said.

(What is apparent from the case of Senator Marcoleta is actually purely a legal question. What happened was, everything is admitted, so there is only one question: whether or not he committed plunder. And that’s what we presented before the court.)
Remulla explained that it was Marcoleta’s own request for bail that quickened the process, as the prosecution had to lay out all the evidence already, with most of the facts being uncontested.
The Ombudsman said that Marcoleta “brought it upon himself to make us do it also if you think about it.”
The Office of the Ombudsman is hoping that the defense will also be able to present its case fast. The prosecution did not present witnesses for Marcoleta’s co-accused.

“We might be breaking records here, especially if the Sandiganbayan will really do its job, in less than one year pwedeng matapos ang isang kaso (the case could be done),” Remulla said. —Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News
