articles.title: School staff wrestled with 'anxiety and dread' before emaciated teen's rescue
articles.summary: Court records show an Ottawa school asked police to do a wellness check on a student who was found to be severely malnourished. The school had previously reached out to the Children's Aid Society of…

image.caption: The Ottawa Courthouse on Elgin Street in September 2022. Earlier this week, an Ottawa mother was sentenced to nine years in prison after pleading guilty to criminal negligence causing bodily harm. Police found her emaciated 18-year-old son forcibly confined to a bed earlier this year. (Matthew Kupfe

blocks.text: Warning: This story contains graphic details about child abuse and animal abuse.

Staff at an Ottawa school who called on police to do the wellness check that led to the rescue of a severely malnourished 18-year-old earlier this year did so after months of "suffocating anxiety and dread" about the growing absence of the complex-needs student.

They also contacted police because when they had previously reached out to the Children's Aid Society of Ottawa (CASO), when the teen was a minor, the school was "dissatisfied" with CASO's response, a courtroom heard this week.
"I knew something wasn't right," one school employee said in court about the days, weeks and months that passed without the teen coming to school.
Another recalled that after a distressing update from the teen's mother, she lay awake at night "haunted by thoughts of what he was enduring."
"Something in our system needs to change so that there are checks and balances so that [vulnerable students] cannot just disappear," she added.
CASO said it doesn't comment on specific cases or actions taken, citing confidentiality.

"However, we can assure you that every report concerning the safety and well-being of a child is carefully assessed through a child protection and safety lens," the organization said in an email to CBC News on Friday.

"The Society's priority is always the evaluation of potential risk to a child, and all concerns are reviewed and responded to in accordance with applicable child protection standards, legislation and professional practices."
'Difficult to imagine a more vulnerable human'

On Tuesday, the teen's mother pleaded guilty to criminal negligence causing bodily harm, failing to provide the necessaries of life, and failing to care for a family cat that was found dead by the teen's bedside.
The judge sentenced her to nine years in prison for the first conviction and shorter concurrent sentences for the other two.

According to an agreed statement of facts read out in court, police discovered the teen, who is now 19, in January 2026. He was found in what court heard described as a boarded-up "cage bed" in a decrepit basement bedroom.

Though he was 18 and therefore an adult at the time of his rescue, "it's difficult to imagine a more vulnerable human being," assistant Crown attorney Louise Tansey said. The teen was born with a rare genetic disorder affecting his speech, movement and cognitive development. He is also prone to seizures.
"He will forever remain childlike, forever in that vulnerable state," Tansey said.

items: Teen was 'near death' when his school asked police for a wellness check, court hears

blocks.text: In the fall of 2025, the teen remained absent from school amid a series of red flags about his family situation. But as detailed in the victim impact statements read out by three school staff members on Tuesday, the concerns about his well-being stretched over years.

And even after the vice-principal shared the good news about the teen being removed from the home, the relief school staff felt was coupled with shock over the teen's condition — and guilt over not having sounded the alarm sooner.
"How I wish I never sent him home the last day of school the previous June, " the first staff member said.
Out of sight
Neither the teen nor his mother can be identified under a publication ban.
The first staff member said she worked with the teen one-on-one for years. He needed help to walk around but loved crawling on the floor during gym time.
"[He] isn’t a complicated guy. He has needs and wants like every other human, but if he’s fed, clean, well-dressed and loved, he is beyond happy," she said.
According to the second staff member, "the decline in the care that [he] was receiving from home," plus the amount of time he was being kept at home, compelled staff to push for a wellness check.

It was an agonizing dilemma that tortured all of us who cared for him, always suspecting the worst but not having any factual evidence. We needed to tread lightly for fear that we would not ever see him again.School staff member

The growing boy who'd been "a smiley, chubby-cheeked [and] active" student began showing up to school with bruises and a "ravenous" appetite, "desperately eating as if every meal might be his last," the third staff member said.
Staff were once told he'd fallen down the stairs at home after his chair locks were disengaged, but there was no damage to the chair, she said.
"A suffocating anxiety and dread took hold of every staff member watching this sweet boy wither away before our eyes," she said.
The school spoke to the mother often, provided the family gift cards and, when the funding for that ran out, staff bought food and other supplies with their own money.

"We would drop them off at his home hoping to catch a glimpse of our smiley friend," the third staff member continued. "Unfortunately, each time we would go to drop off things at home, we were not allowed to see [him]. [She] would always meet us outside the house."
Children's Aid Society contacted
According to the agreed statement of facts, the school contacted the Children's Aid Society of Ottawa in 2024 because the teen had appeared gaunt and pale.

He missed a lot of school that fall, and when a staff member ran into the mother at a store and went to see the teen who was waiting in the family's car, she was horrified by his "shockingly emaciated" appearance, the third staff member said.
It's unclear how CASO responded when contacted in 2024. The school reached out to CASO again at a later point when the teen was now 18, the third staff member said.
"[CASO] stated they could not act because he was [an adult] and suggested a police wellness check," she said.

items: Children's Aid Society of Ottawa at breaking point, organization says
Children's aid workers in Ottawa ratify deal, end strike

blocks.text: According to the agreed statement of facts, "the school was dissatisfied with [CASO's] response to their concerns and so on Jan. 21, 2026, they contacted the Ottawa Police for assistance."

In a statement emailed to CBC News on Thursday, the Children's Aid Society of Ottawa said it can't comment on, confirm or deny any involvement with specific people or families, adding that child welfare records are confidential.
The organization confirmed that once a young person reaches their 18th birthday, they are no longer subject to the child protection provisions of the Child, Youth and Family Services Act.
Not much was shared in court Tuesday about the mother's background.
Oliver Abergel, the lawyer representing her that day, said she was abandoned by her mother and grew up with a father who was not particularly present.

"I can only imagine that the background did not help, and it's not being offered as an excuse," Abergel said, adding that the mother "was not particularly interested in having a violin brought out for her" and has accepted responsibility for her crimes.
Abergel did not say whether the mother struggled as a result of any systemic gaps to getting her son the care he needed.
But in a letter of support filed with the court and which was provided to CBC News on Friday afternoon, the mother's aunt wrote that the mother needed help and still needs help, "not jail time."
The death of the mother's own grandmother hit her hard, according to the aunt.
"Our entire family kept saying ... [she] would not be able to handle it but she kept saying she would never abandon her children like her mother did and honestly she did her best."

"I know she could have reached out to an organization for help but honestly I think she just wanted to prove everyone wrong who doubted her and unfortunately went about it the wrong way," the aunt added. "What she did wasn't malicious. It was a cry for help. I'm not saying it was right but it definitely wasn't intentional."
The mother's guilty pleas spared the court a potentially lengthy trial and witnesses being re-traumatized, the lawyer who represented her Tuesday said. (Guy Quenneville/CBC)

In response to a request to talk about what supports are available for caregivers of complex-needs teens who turn adult, CASO wrote that that transition "can create challenges in situations where vulnerable young adults continue to require significant care, supervision or support but no longer fall within the child welfare system's protection mandate."

"In such circumstances, concerns about an adult's safety or wellbeing may fall under the responsibility of other community systems, including health care providers, developmental services, community agencies, adult protective supports where available or police services when there are immediate safety concerns," CASO added in its written statement.

There is ongoing discussion across Ontario and Canada about the need for strong transition planning and "enhanced services" for youth with complex needs as they age out of the children's systems, the organization added.
Stopped coming to school
For staff at the teen's school, the decision to contact CASO was not easy, according to the third staff member.

"[Some] staff were so worried that we would strain the relationship with the mom and that she would pull him from school," she said, adding that the school later learned the mother was "furious" CASO had checked in on the family.
"[She] had told his support workers that once [her son] turned 18, she wasn’t required to send him back [to school]. This threw my colleagues and I into a panic," she added.
By the fall of 2025, the teen had stopped showing up to school altogether and CHEO had lost contact with the mother, court heard.

The school called and emailed the mother weekly. "In one response, she claimed [her son] refused to come upstairs to eat and that she refused to bring food down to his basement room," the third staff member said.

In October 2025, one of the teen's teachers offered to send a personal support worker to the family's home to help get him ready for school. "There was no response," according to the agreed statement of facts.
Two months later, when hospital staff went to deliver a new stroller, the mother would not let them inside their home. She also refused the school's delivery of a new wheelchair in January 2026.

In arguing for the nine-year sentence on the criminal negligence charge — which was a joint submission with the defence — Tansey, the Crown attorney, described the mother's behaviour as "deprivation being paired with preventing others from rendering life-saving assistance."
'An indelible scar on my soul'
The night before school resumed in January 2026, the teen's mother told staff that he would not be returning to class and that she was placing him in a home.
"Our fears had come true," the third staff member said.
She was no longer on staff at the school, but she and others encouraged the school's vice-principal to call police and ask for a wellness check, she said.

"I wrestled with making that call, terrified of losing the relationship that kept a link to him," she said. "It was an agonizing dilemma that tortured all of us who cared for him, always suspecting the worst but not having any factual evidence. We needed to tread lightly for fear that we would not ever see him again."
The horror of knowing he endured extended starvation, solitary confinement, and severe cruelty in that basement leaves an indelible scar on my soul.School staff member

Police went to the home on Jan. 21 and found the teen in dire condition. The agreed statement of facts lists a host of medical issues, including severe respiratory failure, infestation by bugs and renal failure.
"Police, when they attended, thought they had discovered a body," Tansey said.
The teen is now back at school but can't crawl on the gym floor anymore because his legs suffered substantial atrophy and contractures from his time in confinement, the second staff member said.
When she visited him in the hospital, "I apologized to him for taking so long," she told the courtroom, her voice racked with emotion.
The third staff member said the entire school community is grateful he survived.
But she added, "The horror of knowing he endured extended starvation, solitary confinement and severe cruelty in that basement leaves an indelible scar on my soul."

If you’re affected by this report, you can look for mental health support through resources in your province or territory . If you’re in immediate danger or fear for your safety or that of others around you, please call 911.

articles.title: Pope Leo recovering from surgery, will deliver Sunday prayer
articles.summary: The Vatican has said that Pope Leo XIV is recovering from lung surgery. Photos released on Friday showed the pontiff celebrating Mass at Rome's Gemelli Hospital unaided.

image.caption: Pope Leo XIV thanked staff at Gemelli Hospital in Rome for the care they provide for the frail and those suffering diseaseImage: Vatican Media/AFP

blocks.text: The Vatican on Friday announced that Pope Leo XIV is swiftly recovering from lung surgery and will make his first public appearance on Sunday, when he will deliver the traditional noontime Angelus Prayer.
Vatican representatives did not specify whether he would deliver the prayer at St. Peter's Square or from the hospital.
Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Pietro Parolin said Friday that a recitation from the hospital was a possibility but would depend on Leo's post-operation recovery.

Leo, who is 71, shocked the world and its 1.4 billion Catholics last Sunday by announcing that he would be undergoing surgery within days. Two day's later, on October 13, doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung after the pontiff was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.

Doctors are awaiting the results of Leo's biopsy, which will tell them about the make-up of the tumor and give insight into whether his cancer has spread, allowing them to determine whether he may need to undergo further treatment, such as radiation or chemotherapy.

On Friday, the Vatican said Leo was going about normal activities on his own and released photos of the pontiff saying Mass at Rome's Gemelli Hospital. He was seen wearing vestments and standing next to his personal secretary, Edgard Rimaycuna, a Peruvian priest.

blocks.caption: Pope Leo XIV celebrated Mass alongside his personal secretary, Peruvian priest Edgard RimaycunaImage: Vatican Media/AFP

blocks.text: "His post-operative recovery allows him to carry out his normal daily activities completely on his own," said a medical update signed by Dr. Luigi Carbone, Leo's personal physician, and Dr. Stefano Margaritora, head of thoracic surgery at Gemelli Hospital.
The doctors said blood tests and chest x-rays had confirmed Leo's steady improvement.

"At the moment, we have not received any communication from the doctors ⁠regarding ​his discharge, other than what we ​were told from the beginning about a one-week timeframe," a Vatican spokesman ​said.

"The question now is when he will return, under what circumstances he will return, and what the doctors say. And based on all these factors, the pope will then adjust his pontificate, if it needs to be adjusted," said Cardinal Parolin, who added, "We can't make any predictions."
One of the first questions raised by Leo's hospitalization and surgery was whether he would be able to go through with a planned papal trip to South America in just a few weeks' time.

Though this remains an open question, the Vatican on Friday said planning was "going forward" regardless, releasing the names of those journalists accredited to travel with Leo to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17.

articles.title: Is Leamington still Canada's 'tomato capital' with Chatham-Kent producing more?
articles.summary: Leamington has long dubbed itself the "Tomato Capital of Canada." But did you know that neighbouring Chatham-Kent actually produces the most outdoor-grown tomatoes, anywhere in the country?

image.caption: The Big Tomato is a landmark in uptown Leamington, Ont. (Mike Evans/CBC)

blocks.text: Windsor·Audio
Leamington has long dubbed itself the "Tomato Capital of Canada." But did you know that neighbouring Chatham-Kent actually produces the most outdoor-grown tomatoes, anywhere in the country?
Leamington has long dubbed itself the 'Tomato Capital of Canada'
Windsor Morning8:31Leamington is dubbed the tomato capital of Canada, but does it still deserve that title?
As we're in the middle of October, the tomato harvest is winding down across southwestern Ontario.
Leamington has long dubbed itself the "Tomato Capital of Canada."
But did you know that neighbouring Chatham-Kent actually produces the most outdoor-grown tomatoes, anywhere in the country?
A handful of companies in Essex County and Chatham-Kent process them, while the vast majority of Ontario's output is from area fields, according to agricultural specialist Kim Cooper in the region.
A southwestern Ontario tomato farmer makes their way across a field in this file photo. (CBC)
He says the tomato pendulum swung east of Leamington over the past 12 years or so.
"The grower base has shrunk, and a lot of that was because when Leamington closed up their Heinz plant in 2014, that really threw the tomato sector into a spin," Cooper said.
Vehicles drive past the former Heinz plant in Leamington, Ont., in 2014. (Geoff Robins/The Canadian Press)

"It affected 50 growers back then … so some of those growers kind of packed it in and some of those growers were absorbed by other companies. Then, Highbury Canco came into the picture in Leamington. So they got a lot of those acreages back. That's why Leamington was always referred to as the 'Tomato Capital of Canada' — just basically because of Heinz."
Cooper says the climate in southwestern Ontario makes it the perfect place to grow outdoor tomatoes.
"People don't realize if you look at a map of North America, southern Ontario … Windsor-Essex, Chatham-Kent is the same latitude as northern California. Heat units is the key … and the soil."
Tomatoes grown in southwestern Ontario are shown in a large pile after being shipped to a processing facility in this file photo. (CBC)
According to Cooper, he’s not debunking Leamington as Canada’s tomato capital. Instead, he says, he's stating the fact that Chatham-Kent grows more now than in Essex County.
"Not because we [Chatham-Kent] tried to, but I think it was really because of the Heinz situation."

items: How Leamington got caught up in one of Canada's greatest food fights
Inside the ketchup war: what happened after Heinz closed in Leamington

blocks.text: Agricultural economist Philip Shaw says tomatoes are one of the most important crops grown in Chatham-Kent and Essex County.
But historically, he adds, it hasn’t proven to be overly lucrative.

"I wouldn't call it a cash cow because tomato production is incredibly and capital intensive," said Shaw, who’s based out of Dresden in Chatham-Kent and primarily farms corn, wheat and soybeans himself.
"In other words, it takes an awful lot of money to grow tomatoes and to be able to farm tomatoes in terms of land and equipment and dedication."
A worker tends to tomatoes being processed at the Highbury Canco processing plant in Leamington in this file photo. (Dale Molnar/CBC)
Whether the tomatoes are processed into things such as juice, soups, paste or cocktail mixes, a lot goes into growing them.

"You could put all the tomato farmers in a school bus and drive down the road because over a period of time the industry has changed and there's less producers. It takes an awful lot of money and an awful lot of risk to get into tomato production."

items: It took nearly a decade. But this man thinks he's perfected Ontario tomatoes
Tomatoes cost how much now? Why inflation has come for Canada's produce section

blocks.text: Shaw referred to farming tomatoes as "more of a closed shop" to those who’ve been in the business for many years with existing relationships with processors.
"Then there's negotiations between Ontario vegetable growers and these processors, and the processors also constantly change over a period of time. But also you just can't grow tomatoes every year."
A tomato harvesting machine picks and deposits tomatoes into a trailer being pulled by a tractor in southwestern Ontario. (Brent Hodge)
Trucking is another huge cost, says Shaw, which limits the geography of where they’re grown and processed.
"It's just not an economic panacea. There's a whole bunch of moving parts that have to fit together to have profitable tomato production in southwestern Ontario."
Capital of what then?

Just because Chatham-Kent produces more outdoor-grown tomatoes, doesn’t mean Leamington can’t continue to stake claim as the "Tomato Capital of Canada" — a slogan more than anything else — based on its history with the red fruit-vegetable.

items: Leamington's Big Tomato to be restored

blocks.text: But let’s just say it did lose the moniker. What else should the southwestern Ontario coastal municipality along Lake Erie be known for?
Leamington’s Cherise Charron was quick to respond when asked.
"I think it is the greenhouse capital for sure," she said. "I was looking at a map on Google, and you can see at night how lit up it is from all of the greenhouses we do have."
Greenhouse lights from the area of Leamington and Kingsville, Ont., are seen in a photo taken from the International Space Station on March 13, 2026. (NASA/International Space Station)
Nick Klym, also from Leamington, agreed with Charron.
"The greenhouse capital of Canada," he echoed.

items: The hot pink glow seen from space: Why these Ontario greenhouse lights still shine at night

blocks.text: Others told CBC News the municipality’s “beautiful waterfront” should be in the running.
Whereas Dave Brown from Leamington focused his attention elsewhere.

“It's the [retirement] capital of Canada, which serves diversity in labour and retirement … because of our climate. I've lived here all my life. It's a great place to live. I've seen a lot of people retiring here now and … from Toronto and bigger cities.”
Mayoral candidates have their say
The two people running for mayor in Leamington have also weighed in on what Leamington should be known — aside from tomatoes.
Incumbent Hilda MacDonald, who’s seeking a third term in the chair, says it would "100 per cent" be her community’s waterfront.
"With the with the amphitheater and now the stage, it's a wonderful place," she told CBC Radio’s Windsor Morning on Friday.
Hilda MacDonald, left, and Cris Biron are running for mayor in Leamington in 2026. (Peter Duck/CBC)
"It's not just for tourism, it's for our residents as well. And to me that's [the] quality of life that makes people come, work, play and stay … I'm very proud of that," MacDonald added.
Cris Biron is challenging MacDonald for a second straight election.

“Thanks to Ms. MacDonald, we have a beautiful waterfront – it’s fantastic,” he told CBC Radio’s Windsor Morning on Friday. "[But] what we did was to paint the vehicle before the fixing the engine. I mean we should have taken care of the downtown first … solidify our tourism … that is not really happening right now."
Windsor Morning18:16Candidates for mayor of Leamington introduce themselves and debate issues
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Bob Becken is with CBC's digital team. Previously, he was an executive producer with CBC Windsor, and held broadcast and digital news director duties with Bell Media and Blackburn Media. You can reach him at bob.becken@cbc.ca.

articles.title: German colonialism on agenda in Bundestag debate on Namibia genocide
articles.summary: Germany's opposition parties have forced a debate in the Bundestag on the early-20th-century genocide it carried out in Namibia. Will this finally spur progress in addressing colonial crimes?

image.caption: Gaob David Timotheus Frederick (left) and Mutjinde Katjiua visited Germany this week to demand recognition and restitutionImage: Christian Ditsch/epd

blocks.text: Gaob Daniel Timotheus Frederick was sitting in the front row of the visitors' gallery in the Bundestag this week. Wearing a suit and hat, he had traveled all the way from Namibia to see this parliamentary debate unfold. For almost 120 years, his family had been waiting for the return of human remains of their ancestor, Cornelius Frederick (sometimes spelled Fredericks), who had led the Nama resistance against German colonial rule and died on Shark Island in Germany's first concentration camp.
In the name of his great-grandfather and as a member of the Nama Traditional Leaders Association (NTLA), Frederick was there to demand an "unconditioned apology" from Germany.

Sitting next to him, in uniform and white gloves, with a carved lion on the handle of his walking stick, was the head of the Ovaherero Traditional Authority, Paramount Chief Mutjinde Katjiua. Speaking before the Bundestag debate, the chief said, "We call upon the Bundestag to recognize unequivocally the genocides committed against the Ovaherero and Nama peoples."

Many people wonder why the German parliament hasn't already done this — and why the government is yet to issue an official apology. There is a draft joint declaration with Namibia in which the German government acknowledges that "from today's perspective, [it] would be called genocide." But there is no German-Namibian reconciliation agreement.

The evidence is overwhelming: From 1904 to 1908, the German Empire waged a war of extermination against the indigenous people of southwestern Africa, including the Ovaherero (also known as the Herero), the Nama, the Damara and the San. At least 100,000 people were killed, and just as many displaced. Many were subjected to forced labor and forced prostitution. The land seizures and expropriation carried out at the time continue to affect their descendants today.

Jürgen Zimmerer, a professor of history at the University of Hamburg whose research focuses on Africa, said the Bundestag and government lacked the will to confront this era in German history. "There are Bundestag resolutions on the Armenian genocide, one on the Holodomor [in Ukraine], and one on the genocide against the Yazidis [by the "Islamic State" in Iraq]. But there is no recognition of the genocide against the Herero and Nama by the German Bundestag." If there were any political will to do so, it could happen very quickly, Zimmerer told DW.

blocks.caption: Descendants of the Ovaherero and Nama visited the BundestagImage: Tina Gerhäusser/DW

blocks.text: Reconstruction or reparations?

The socialist Left Party initiated the Bundestag debate by drafting a resolution calling for full recognition and compensation in collaboration with representatives of the descendants. The goal: "Restorative justice." Paramount Chief Katjiua has rejected the existing agreement between the Namibian and German governments. "Development aid cannot substitute for comprehensive reparations," he said.

Since 2021, the governments have been negotiating a joint declaration that pledges €1.1 billion ($1.24 billion) in reconstruction aid to Namibia over 30 years. Once the agreement is signed, Germany's president is set to issue a formal apology.

But the Foreign Ministry warned: "Legal claims to compensation cannot be derived from the recognition of genocide. With these negotiations — which are unique worldwide — Namibia and Germany have broken new ground and are pioneers in confronting their colonial past."
Political scientist Andreas Mehler, director of the Anton Bergstraesser Institute, sees it differently. He says the government's plan sounds like "checkbook diplomacy."

Zimmerer also said there was a financial calculation: "If we were to recognize an obligation to provide reparations to the families of those killed — given the millions of victims of World War II, the victims of the Germans — it would ruin us."
German MPs rebuke far-right AfD during Namibia genocide debate
Promise in the government's coalition agreement

Four lines in the 144 pages of the coalition agreement of the current German government — between the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU)/Christian Social Union (CSU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) — summarize the extent of the government's commitment to reconciliation with Namibia.

"We will intensify our efforts to come to terms with colonialism," the text reads. "This includes transnational research into artifacts and the restitution of cultural property in dialogue with the countries of origin. Particular attention will be paid to establishing a dignified memorial site and the repatriation of human remains."

Compared with the efforts to address colonialism led by the SPD-led government from 2021 to 2025, "the issue has lost visibility," said Alexander Stroh-Steckelberg, a professor of political scientist at the University of Bayreuth who specializes in Africa.

Zimmerer has an even more critical take: "I wouldn't even call it a stalemate anymore. I believe this government is rolling back the progress that has been made in terms of raising awareness of colonial injustices."

blocks.caption: Historians say Germany hasn't done enough to address colonial crimesImage: KHARBINE-TAPABOR/IMAGO

blocks.text: Restitution of culture goods and human remains

Much remains to be done, as far the descendants of the Ovaherero are concerned: Tens of thousands of human remains are believed to still be in Germany. Direct descendants of the victims — such as Gaob D. Timotheus Frederick — have been fighting to heal these wounds for generations.

In March, the government established a coordination council, headed by the Foreign Ministry, which stated that the government did not wish to "dictate to the countries and societies of origin which cultural artifacts and human remains they should reclaim, what priorities they should set, or how restitutions should be handled."

Foreign Ministry official Serap Güler, chair of this coordination council, defends the government's actions so far. Recounting her own official trips — she has already been to Togo, and next week she plans to travel to Rwanda and Burundi — she claimed, "Everywhere I go, I receive recognition for our sincere and trusting approach to the past — as well as for our determined commitment to a future of freedom, security, and prosperity."
A dignified place of remembrance?

Zimmerer argues that Germany "has earned a reputation as a country that takes a critical view of its own history and learns from its mistakes," which, he says, represents "enormous cultural capital" on the world stage. But he is concerned that this capital is currently being squandered.

Colonialism does not appear to be included in the government's memorial policy. Even in the recent proposal by Minister of State for Culture Wolfram Weimer to create a dignified memorial site in Bremen, Zimmerer detects an attempt to "marginalize German colonial crimes." He notes that victim groups have not been included and that the colonial capitals of the German Empire — Berlin and Hamburg — must also become sites of remembrance.

Ninety-five percent of the colonial troops set sail from Hamburg's Baakenhafen, including Commander Lothar von Trotha, who issued the orders to exterminate the Ovaherero and Nama. According to Zimmerer, the fact that a new opera house — rather than a memorial site — is being built at Baakenhafen constitutes a staggering case of "art-washing of history." Mehler also hopes that a productive debate on memorial sites will still take place and that, overall, "many more places will come to terms with colonial history."

Meanwhile, Gaob D. Timotheus Frederick continues to call for a collective effort to come to terms with the past: "Let us give opportunity to the affected communities that are being represented by us to have a seat on the table to discuss with them the rest of the way."
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: Pope pictured for first time since surgery and cancer diagnosis
articles.summary: The pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer after having surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Pope Leo thanked medical staff as he was pictured for the first time since his lung surgery
Pope Leo XIV has been pictured celebrating Mass from hospital, in the first images of him released by the Vatican since he underwent lung surgery.

The 71-year-old pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer after the surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications.
The images shared on Friday showed the Chicago-born Pope wearing a green robe while standing behind a makeshift altar on the tenth floor of the hospital.
Pope Leo "celebrated with the medical and nursing staff" and thanked workers for their service, the Vatican press office said.
On Friday, the Pope's doctors said tests had shown "a steady improvement in his general condition" since his procedure.
His doctors said that a chest X-ray indicated "good recovery of the operated lung".
The whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical", the Vatican said following the surgery.
"After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it said earlier, before he spent a "peaceful night" at the hospital.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The pontiff is expected to remain at the hospital for about a week as he recovers

blocks.text: The pontiff is expected to remain at the hospital for about a week as he recovers

Pope Leo first announced that he would be having the operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a "well-contained" nodule on his lung "at an early stage" and advised him to have it removed.

Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said. He was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma.
The Vatican has stressed that the Pope had shown no symptoms of infection or illness prior to the procedure.

articles.title: Montreal police suspend 2 officers following report officer urinated on unhoused person
articles.summary: Montreal police have confirmed the suspension of two officers assigned to a downtown station following a report that an officer urinated on a person experiencing homelessness during working hours.…

image.caption: The SPVM confirmed that it has launched an internal investigation into two officers from Station 21, which covers downtown Montreal. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Montreal·Updated

Montreal police have confirmed the suspension of two officers assigned to a downtown station following a report that an officer urinated on a person experiencing homelessness during working hours. One advocate said it's "hard to imagine a more degrading or violent act."
Allegations 'undermine the dignity every person deserves,' says Montreal mayor
Montreal police have confirmed the suspension of two officers assigned to a downtown station following a report that an officer urinated on a person experiencing homelessness during working hours.

In a statement to CBC News, the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) confirmed that it has launched an internal investigation into two officers from Station 21, which covers downtown Montreal.
The police response comes after a report published Friday by La Presse detailing the alleged incident, which reportedly disgusted colleagues who then reported the behaviour to superiors.
The SPVM declined to provide further details on the investigation, citing privacy obligations under provincial law.

"Be assured that the SPVM takes any allegation against one of its members seriously," police said in its statement. "Regardless of the nature of an internal investigation, we are determined to get to the bottom of things and take the required actions."

items: Montreal opening 9 warming centres for unhoused people ahead of winter
Woman dies following fire at homeless encampment in Montréal-Nord

blocks.text: Another officer from the same station was also suspended in recent weeks in connection with a separate case. According to La Presse, the officer allegegedly appeared to be posing and mocking a suspect placed in a humiliating position during an arrest.
The officers have not yet formally presented a defence.
SPVM should not treat incident as isolated: advocate

Annie Savage, executive director of the advocacy group RAPSIM (Réseau d'aide aux personnes seules et itinérantes de Montréal), said she was "extremely shocked" but not surprised by the allegations, citing what she regularly hears from people living on the streets.
"It's hard to imagine a more degrading or violent act," Savage told Radio-Canada's Tout un matin.

Savage added that relations between police and unhoused residents have deteriorated as the city's homelessness crisis has deepened. She warned that police should not treat the incident as an isolated case.

Last June, RAPSIM released a joint report with legal aid organization Clinique Droits Devant that outlined tension between unhoused Montrealers and law enforcement, including Montreal police officers and special constables patrolling the city's transit network.

The study found that 40 per cent of unhoused individuals surveyed felt heavily ticketed or targeted, while 66 per cent reported rarely or never being treated like other members of the public. None of the respondents expressed high confidence in police during an emergency, with many saying they avoid calling 911 out of fear of being treated as suspects.
The report documented cases of physical and verbal abuse, unjustified searches, an increased reliance on private security guards in public spaces, and heightened surveillance across the Metro system.
The allegations come as Montreal prepares for La Nuit des sans-abri, an annual event held across Quebec to raise awareness about homelessness.
In a statement to CBC, Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada said the allegations are "extremely serious and undermine the dignity every person deserves."
She added: "I applaud the police officers who spoke up to report this situation. The investigation must now run its course so the full truth can come to light."
The Montreal police brotherhood, the union representing SPVM officers, said in a statement it "firmly condemns" any behaviour that violates human dignity or breaches professional standards.

items: Internal police documents describe 'radicalized' subculture at Montréal-Nord station
Montreal police allegedly cut locs from people's hair. Here's the anti-Black history behind that

blocks.text: While declining to comment on the specific allegations, the brotherhood called the reported conduct contrary to the values of Montreal police officers.
The SPVM is in the midst of another scandal involving its officers. A patrol unit at Station 39 in Montréal-Nord was disbanded last June after officers allegedly racially profiled residents.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Benjamin Shingler is an investigative reporter based in Montreal. He previously worked at The Canadian Press, CTV and the New Brunswick Telegraph-Journal. He can be reached at benjamin.shingler@cbc.ca or on Signal at @bshingler.67

articles.title: Palestinians and US journalist injured by Israeli settlers in West Bank harvest attack
articles.summary: The BBC sees masked settlers attack Palestinians trying to harvest olives, amid a surge in similar incidents.

blocks.text: Watch: Israeli settlers attack Palestinians in West Bank during olive harvest
ByLucy Williamson
Middle East correspondentReporting fromAbu Falah
Dozens of masked settlers have attacked Palestinians and set fire to cars and olive trees during the annual olive harvest in the occupied West Bank.

A BBC team witnessed one of several attacks in farmland near the Palestinian village of Abu Falah. A local official said the attacks had injured 12 Palestinians, including four dual Palestinian American citizens. A foreign journalist was also among those hurt.

Driving into the area early in the morning, we came across the first signs of the violence: a stream of cars carrying wounded Palestinian olive farmers racing out along the narrow stony track, piled high with olive picking equipment, as smoke rose from several fires nearby.
The bloodied face of Majdi Fheed peered out from the backseat of one car.
"We were getting our olive trees and almost 15 Jewish guys … started attacking us with guns, with rocks, with special weapons. They hit me on my head [and] my neck – look, I am bleeding!"

Yaser AlKam, a council member from the neighbouring village of Turmus Aya told me Majdi - an American citizen - was attacked by settlers with nail-studded sticks, and needed treatment for deep wounds on his head. His elderly mother was also injured.
Another man ferrying the injured to hospital told us that settlers had attacked them with sticks while they harvested their olives, and had burned three cars – including one of his own.
"As soon as we got to the land and put our things on the ground, they started to come, so we ran away" said a woman next to him.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Several Palestinian-American citizens and a foreign journalist were left injured following the attack

blocks.text: Several Palestinian-American citizens and a foreign journalist were left injured following the attack
Asked about the violence, a US State Department spokesperson said they were aware of the reports.
"We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and call for investigations, arrests, and convictions, of those responsible," the spokesperson said.

Watching the vehicles stream past her, 73-year-old Imm Khaldoun told me emphatically that, no matter what happened, she would always return to her land. "This is my land. It's my right [to be here]" she told me.
The UN says the past two weeks have already seen more attacks by violent Israeli settlers than during the entire harvest season last year.
Olive picking in the West Bank is now a test of speed, with trees rapidly stripped of fruit as soon as the sun rises, before violent Israeli settlers attack.

In another olive orchard nearby, we watched as dozens of farmers used power-tools to strip the trees as fast as they could – one eye on the ridge above us, where a group of settlers at a new illegal outpost had already gathered, and were watching the olive harvest below.

Standing on ladders, the Palestinian farmers worked quickly, sending streams of olives onto the plastic sheets laid out under the trees. Three villages had come together to harvest these olives, the landowner Amin Khalil, told me, as a form of protection against attack. He said his land was now surrounded by seven Jewish settlements and outposts.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Yaser AlKam was left bloodied from the attack

blocks.text: Yaser AlKam was left bloodied from the attack
All Israeli settlements are illegal under international law. Outposts – small encampments on hilltops – are illegal under Israeli law as well, but many still receive state support.

"This is a hotspot – there are seven settlements around here," Amin Khalil told me. "This year, all the people came together because when there are just a few people working alone at the edge of the village, the settlers attack. So all the families are working together today."
But the tactic doesn't work today. As we watch, dozens of settlers, all dressed in black, begin moving down the hill towards us, setting fire to several groups of olive trees.
There are shouts of panic from the Palestinian farmers, yelling for children to get out of the field. Some begin swiftly wrapping up the olives to leave.

But with large numbers of people on both sides, the confrontation stalls into an uneasy stalemate. We see settlers with slingshots hurl stones towards us, and young Palestinian men running to throw stones in return.

As Israeli forces arrive, the standoff explodes into action. Settlers begin running down towards us as the farmers swiftly retreat. Some Palestinians set off fireworks to try and push the settlers back.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The UN says settler attacks this year have so far killed one Palestinian and injured more than 120 others

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
The UN says settler attacks this year have so far killed one Palestinian and injured more than 120 others
American journalist Heidi Levine of the Washington Post was injured in the attack. She described how dozens of settlers ambushed her as she was reporting at the scene.

"I got jumped," she said. "I was on the ground and they were kicking me and I was trying to hold onto my camera and my bag. I had my helmet and flak jacket on which protected me. They made me stand up and they kicked me again, and this went on for at least 10 minutes."
In a statement, Washington Post executive editor Matt Murray said Levine had been clearly identifiable as a journalist.
"We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities," he said.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said personnel had been despatched to the area "following a report of a violent confrontation". It said a female journalist had been injured during the confrontation. And that "all circumstances" surrounding the incident would be examined.
As the farmers retreated, the sound of live ammunition cracked across the fields. It was unclear if settlers or Israeli forces were firing.
Minutes later, Israeli forces began firing tear gas into the Palestinian fields to end the confrontation – a well-worn Israeli pattern of managing these conflicts.
The UN says settler attacks on the olive harvest this year have so far killed one Palestinian and injured more than 120 others across the West Bank.
Illegal Jewish outposts have mushroomed here over the past few years, clustering in closer around Palestinian olive groves.
What we witnessed was part of a pattern being repeated day after day, as settler outposts here increase.

The yearly olive harvest has become a litmus test of how the policies of Israel's fiercely pro-settlement government are affecting Palestinians here, by presiding over growing violence by extremist settlers, and fuelling Jewish claims to the land.

articles.title: Iran: When 'honor' becomes a death sentence for women
articles.summary: The brutal murder of a young mother has once again sparked debate in Iran over so-called honor killings, the social acceptance of violence against women, and the lack of protection for those at risk.

image.caption: According to a 2020 study by Iran's Police Academy, so-called honor killings accounted for up to 45% of all murders in some traditionally conservative provincesImage: DW

blocks.text: In the early hours of Monday, October 5, 2026, the life of Maryam Yarmohammadi came to a violent end. The 28-year-old mother of two was attacked with knives by her brother and husband on Qeshm Island in southern Iran. Her genitalia were mutilated. She died shortly afterward in hospital. Both her husband and brother were arrested.

According to media reports, around 50 relatives gathered outside the hospital to protest the arrests. They reportedly believed that death had been the "least severe punishment" Maryam Yarmohammadi deserved.

What exactly the young woman had done, and why her relatives considered her guilty, remains unknown. Yet both the circumstances of the case and the extreme violence involved follow a familiar pattern seen in so-called honor killings.

In such cases, the underlying belief is often that a man must erase a perceived "dishonor" brought upon the family by a sister, daughter, or wife. Failure to do so may expose him to rejection, humiliation or social exclusion within his community.
All the Ayatollah's men — ensuring the regime's survival
No opportunity to defend themselves

What constitutes "honor" or "proper conduct" is often defined by family expectations or local social and cultural norms. In some traditionally conservative regions, even laughing loudly or engaging in a friendly conversation with an unrelated man may be viewed as a violation of these norms.
Women accused of such transgressions are frequently denied any meaningful opportunity to defend themselves against the allegations.

For years, women's rights activists in Iran have sought to establish nationwide support networks offering counseling and protection to women at risk. One such initiative is the Campaign to End Honor Killings.
Rezvan Moghaddam, a spokesperson for the campaign, told DW that there appeared to be no activist or local group in the region capable of supporting Maryam Yarmohammadi.
Through civil society networks, the campaign has in some cases succeeded in relocating threatened women to safe locations and securing shelter for them.

Moghaddam stressed that Maryam Yarmohammadi's death should not be interpreted as criticism of women's rights activists in those regions: "I myself come from Khuzestan in southern Iran and am fully aware of the restrictions that exist there."
Failure of the justice system

Iran's laws, based on the interpretations of Shariah, or Islamic law, do not treat women as equal citizens in many areas of life. Their ability to make decisions about education, employment or travel may depend on the consent of their fathers or, later, their husbands.
Even after a woman's death, male relatives can, under certain legal provisions, influence the course of criminal proceedings.

Iranian criminal law applies the principle of retribution in certain offenses, including murder. In homicide cases, the victim's relatives may choose either to demand retribution, which can result in the death penalty, or to pardon the perpetrator.

These provisions raise particular concerns in cases of honor killings. When an alleged perpetrator is also among the relatives empowered to influence decisions on punishment or forgiveness, a serious conflict of interest emerges.
Such situations expose the protection gaps critics say exist within Iran's justice system regarding violence against women.
Iranian Revolution: From Shah to Mullahs

According to a 2020 study by Iran's Police Academy, honor killings — defined as the murder of a woman by male relatives such as her father, brother or uncle for allegedly violating social norms of modesty and family honor — accounted for up to 45% of all murders in some traditionally conservative provinces in western and southern Iran.
In March 2025, the UN Special Rapporteur on human rights in Iran reported that at least 179 women were murdered by men within their family circles in 2024. These cases were recorded as femicides.
When violence is socially legitimized

In Maryam Yarmohammadi's case, it was above all the extraordinary brutality of the crime that shocked the public. The murder triggered a wave of grief and outrage on social media. Many women reacted strongly to what they saw as a femicide driven by hatred in the name of "honor" and "shame."

At the same time, numerous comments focused on victim-blaming, holding the victim responsible for her own death. Others described the killing as the "punishment of an unfaithful woman" or attempted to justify it by "understanding the men's anger."

Psychoanalyst Saba Alaleh argues that, for years, men have been socialized to believe they are responsible for controlling women and monitoring their behavior and decisions. Male identity, she said, is simultaneously tied to a woman's "obedience."
Violence becomes normalized when beliefs, social approval and silence reinforce one another within this structure, Alaleh explained.

"When cultural, social, political, economic, legal and educational factors are closely intertwined, they acquire enormous power. Under such conditions, women are also highly economically dependent and lack sufficient social support. Preventive mechanisms are absent as well. All of this increases the risk of violence."
Iranian women unveiled: A shift in hijab enforcement?
Women's struggle for self-determination

Atefeh Rangriz, a sociologist and women's rights activist, told DW: "Femicides have always existed, and their political manifestations can be traced throughout history, from forced unveiling [under Reza Shah Pahlavi in the 1930s] to the slogan 'Either the headscarf or blows to the head' in the Islamic Republic."
Rangriz believes that women understand the path toward liberation and, despite tremendous obstacles, have achieved significant progress over the past decades.

Women in Iran have been driving since 1940. They have been allowed to vote and run for political office since 1963. Women account for half of all university graduates in the country. The number of women filing for divorce or mutually ending unhappy marriages has also continued to rise.

The "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement, which emerged from the nationwide protests following the death of Jina Mahsa Amini in police custody in 2022, has further transformed public perceptions of women in Iran.

"Women have learned to focus on the present rather than postponing justice to the future. They demand it now," said Rangriz. "They want to exercise autonomy over their own bodies, live as they choose, and free themselves from the structures of domination, oppression and exploitation. It is a kind of radical revolution."
Many Iranian women no longer wear the mandatory hijab in public, openly defying the Islamic Republic's dress regulations.
Yet hardly anyone asks what the young mother Maryam Yarmohammadi wanted, or how she wished to live. She was brutally killed.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Albania: Students demand political change and resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama
articles.summary: Empty lecture halls, burning buildings and demands for change: Albanian students are spearheading a protest movement that has become the biggest challenge to Prime Minister Edi Rama in years.

image.caption: Student protests in the Albanian capital, Tirana, turned violent on TuesdayImage: Hameraldi Agolli/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The luxury high-rises transforming Tirana's skyline are meant to project the image of a modern European capital. But at the foot of one of these buildings, Samanta, a 22-year-old master's student in economics, is in tears.
She removes the mask she had been wearing to protect herself from tear gas.

"How could I ever afford an apartment in one of these towers on a salary of €540 [$608]?" she shouts, as she stands facing a line of police officers. "I share the rent with people I don't even know because my family has emigrated. We're exhausted."
University lecture halls in Tirana stand empty as students boycott classes and take to the streets, demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama, who has been in power since 2013.
Escalation after months of protests

Albanians have been protesting since late May as part of a broader anti-government movement known as the "Flamingo Revolution," which began in response to a multimillion-euro tourism development linked to Jared Kushner, son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, in the protected coastal area of Zvernec.

blocks.caption: Protesters destroyed an ATM during clashes with police during an anti-government protest by students on ThursdayImage: Florion Goga/REUTERS

blocks.text: The movement has, however, since grown into a broader challenge to Rama's government.

Over the past three days, the student demonstrations have erupted into violent clashes. Bins, businesses, buildings and banks have been set ablaze, with some completely burning out. Tear gas has filled the air.

A total of 152 people have been arrested and 324 are under investigation over the three days of protests. Injuries have been reported among both protesters and police officers, with the police saying 71 officers have been injured in the clashes.

The students are angry about conditions at universities, the cost of higher education and poor employment prospects after graduation. But above all, they want the government to step down and say they are not willing to negotiate any of their other demands with the prime minister.
"You didn't listen to us for four months while we protested peacefully. Now you'll listen as the city burns," said Samanta.
Rama breaks his silence
During the first two days of the student protests, the prime minister remained silent.

Then, at 8:03 a.m. on Thursday, Rama appeared in a video message recorded inside the fire-damaged College of Europe building, just meters from his office on Tirana's main street, the Boulevard of the Martyrs of the Nation.

blocks.caption: A total of 152 people have been arrested over the past three days, with injuries reported among both protesters and police officersImage: Florion Goga/REUTERS

blocks.text: "These are the hands of an opposition that, hiding behind masked people, wants to drag Albania back to a place it will never return to," he declared.
Later that day, Rama addressed the protesters' central demand — his resignation. In comments to Reuters, he ruled out stepping down, saying governments are changed in elections.
The following day, he also accused "foreign hands" of seeking to prevent Albania from joining the European Union.
The unrest comes at a critical moment for Albania's bid to join the European Union. Brussels has called for calm and restraint, urging all sides to avoid further escalation and engage in dialogue.
Sali Berisha, the 82-year-old leader of the opposition Democratic Party and a former prime minister, rejected Rama's accusations that the opposition was behind the violence.

"We have no idea whether it's Greece, Iran, Serbia or someone else," he told a press conference, mocking Rama's claims of foreign interference. "The Democratic Party fully supports this protest and will stand by it until the end. Resign and leave immediately!"
Students against the political establishment
For Rigels Xhemollari of the Albanian civil society organization Qendresa Qytetare (Civic Resistance), the student revolt is the culmination of months of peaceful protests.

"The main reason is the prime minister's failure to respond during four months of protests and his mockery of the demonstrators. Other reasons include the economic situation, corruption cases and successive scandals," he told DW, referring to a number of corruption investigations involving senior government officials.
But the anger is not directed at Rama alone. Protesters have also voiced their frustration with Albania's political opposition.

blocks.caption: The students are demanding that the government step down and say they are not willing to negotiate with the prime minister, Edi RamaImage: Brunilda Kazani/DW

blocks.text: "We want the political class of the past 35 years to go. We want a new Albania with new leaders," Skerdi Topalli, a 20-year-old journalism student, told DW.
What could come after the protests?
For political analyst Mark Marku, dean of the Faculty of History and Philology at the University of Tirana, the protests mark a turning point.
"This is the reaction of a generation. In a society that was not responding, they woke people up and made us think about change," he told DW.
But Marku warns that even Rama's resignation and fresh elections would not necessarily bring new political leadership.
"Challenging the government is not an end in itself. A protest must produce a result," he said. "There must be a platform, a political alternative. You cannot vote for a protest."
Xhemollari, meanwhile, sees Rama's resignation as the only way to end the revolt.
"The protest has just one political demand, and it requires a political solution: the prime minister's resignation," he told DW.

Xhemollari says that Albania's president should bring political parties together to form a caretaker government led by a non-partisan prime minister, paving the way for local and parliamentary elections in May 2027.

articles.title: Israeli settlers attack olive farmers and Washington Post journalist in West Bank
articles.summary:
Settlers hurl rocks at Palestinians and beat photographer Heidi Levine as part of yearly attacks to disrupt harvest

Israeli settlers have attacked Palestinians across the occupied West Bank…

blocks.text: Israeli settlers have attacked Palestinians across the occupied West Bank in a coordinated movement to disrupt the annual olive harvest, burning cars and trees and injuring Palestinians and a Washington Post photographer.

Masked settlers wielding clubs and other weapons attacked people attempting to harvest their olives in towns across the West Bank on Friday. At least six people were injured in the town of Abu Falah near Ramallah, the Palestinian Red Crescent Society said.

At least 80 settlers, some of whom were carrying firearms or clubs, gathered to stop Palestinians from harvesting their olives in Abu Falah, using slingshots to hurl rocks at the farmers in view of Israeli military vehicles. When some of the Palestinians then picked up rocks to defend themselves, the Israeli military fired teargas in their direction.

blocks.caption: Teargas fired by Israeli forces. Photograph: Léo Corrêa/AP

blocks.text: The Israeli Foreign Press Association said in a statement: “This is the latest in a long line of violent attacks by Israeli settlers against journalists and other civilians in the occupied West Bank. Yet our repeated calls for action to confront this lawlessness have been ignored by Israeli authorities.”

Among those injured was the Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine, who was beaten by settlers in an attack that lasted more than 10 minutes, according to witnesses. Settlers stole her passport, phone, wallet and equipment.

“I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily, I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn’t even be here, because they just kept kicking and kicking me,” Levine said from a hospital bed in Ramallah. She said the attack ended when her Palestinian colleagues intervened to save her.
In a statement, the Washington Post said Levine had been wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist.

blocks.caption: Levine speaking to journalists in hospital after the attack. Photograph: Ali Sawafta/Reuters

blocks.text: There has been a surge of settler violence against Palestinians over the past month. Settlers have carried out at least 170 attacks since 27 September, around the start of the annual olive harvest, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli rights group.
Every year, settlers attack Palestinians trying to harvest their olives, but this year’s harvest has seen an uptick in violence as Israel’s elections approach at the end of October.
At least four Palestinians have been killed and more than 100 others have been injured over the past month, Palestinian authorities said. Thousands of trees have been damaged.

Israel imposed new rules on the olive harvest this year, barring Palestinians from harvesting their trees located in Area C – an area under the Israeli military’s control, which comprises most of the West Bank’s agricultural land.

blocks.caption: Palestinians and activists collecting olives after the attack on Friday. Photograph: Léo Corrêa/AP

blocks.text: The new orders prohibit Palestinians from entering about 8,800 hectares (21,800 acres) of agricultural land – a 30% increase from the year prior – without approval of the Israeli military. By contrast, the military gave Israeli citizens access to more land this year.

The rights group Peace Now says the military decreased the amount of land Israeli citizens were prohibited from entering from about 1,070 hectares in 2025 to 680 hectares in 2026, for the purpose of preventing settler violence.

The olive harvest is an economic lifeline for Palestinians and has grown in importance since Israel revoked work permits for many Palestinians in the West Bank after the Hamas-led attack on 7 October 2023.
Photos and videos showed large swathes of agricultural land with uprooted olive trees in Kufur Malek, outside Ramallah, where Israeli bulldozers had razed trees.

Settlers rarely face accountability for their violence, even when well documented. Rights groups say settlers enjoy the protection of the Israeli military, which intervenes only if Palestinians try to defend themselves.

blocks.caption: Israeli soldiers move towards a Palestinian man lying wounded on the road after they shot him during the settler attack. Photograph: Léo Corrêa/AP

blocks.text: The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has on occasion condemned the violence, which he says is due to just about 100 settlers, but he has taken few steps to stop settler violence.

Settlements have rapidly expanded across the West Bank under his rightwing government, leading to international condemnation. The UN and most countries judge settlements to be in violation of international law.
Friday’s attack in Abu Falah followed a similar attack hours earlier near the West Bank village of Turmus Ayya, where settlers burned three cars after attacking Palestinians harvesting olives.
Videos shared by the Israeli rights group B’tselem showed hundreds of bags of olives “violently” stolen by Israeli settlers from Palestinians and taken to Israeli olive presses.
Sarit Michaeli, an independent activist, said settlers were stealing Palestinians’ olive crop on a scale “never seen before in my 22-year history of working on this issue”.
A spokesperson for the US embassy in Jerusalem said it was aware of reports of the attack and declined to comment further due to privacy laws.

articles.title: Houthi attacks on strategic Saudi assets threaten Riyadh's regional leadership and economic ambitions
articles.summary: As Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis continue to target Saudi Arabia, Riyadh's vulnerability threatens its claim on regional and religious leadership — as well as its standing as an economic powerhouse.

image.caption: Ongoing Houthi attacks threaten Saudi Arabia's claim to be a regional powerhouse. Is Riyadh's economic overhaul Vision 2030 in danger? Image: Rafiq Maqbool/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: As the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen continues to escalate, Saudi Arabia's most important national priorities are increasingly at risk. On Tuesday, the Houthis hit the headquarters of Aramco, the Saudi state-owned oil company in Dhahran. On Wednesday, the Houthis vowed to continue attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities, and on Thursday a cruise missile was intercepted over the Medina region. While it remains unclear who launched it, the mere attempt raises questions about Saudi Arabia's role as guardian of Islam's holiest places, the Saudi cities of Mecca and Medina.

Following last weekend's Houthi attacks that killed more than a dozen people and injured more than 300 at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, tourists and potential investors are keenly aware of the growing uncertainty over travel and security in the kingdom.

Several airlines suspended flights to Riyadh and the airport was expected to remain closed through at least October 17, according to media reports published earlier this week. Saudi Arabia's Future Investment Initiative, an economic summit that usually draws foreign leaders and key players in business to the country, plans to offer remote participation instead of hosting attendees on site.

"The hostilities between the Houthis and the Saudi government challenge Riyadh's image of stability and security amid the wider US-Iran war," said Timothy E. Kaldas, deputy director of the Washington-based think tank Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy.

"The attacks on Saudi Arabia also threaten Riyadh's efforts to diversify the economy," Kaldas told DW, noting that these ambitions depend on potential tourists viewing the kingdom as a safe destination.

Since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran in February, Tehran, and later the Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen, have been targeting Saudi Arabia, a close ally of the United States. Saudi Arabia also supports the Yemeni government in its fight against the Houthis with airstrikes in Houthi-held areas of Yemen.

blocks.caption: The Houthis targeted the headquarters of the Saudi Arabian oil company Aramco in Dhahran, after also successfully attacking the international airport in Riyadh this weekImage: AFP

blocks.text: Houthi attacks are a blow to Saudi Arabia's ambitions
A decade ago, Saudi Arabia launched Vision 2030, a sweeping economic and social reform plan, to reduce the kingdom's reliance on oil and transform its economy and society.

"Saudi Arabia is pursuing a highly nationalist 'Saudi-First' policy, aimed at propelling the nation to the global forefront as an aviation power, a hub for artificial intelligence and a major tourism destination," Simon Wolfgang Fuchs, a professor at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, told DW.
Fuchs views the Houthi attacks as a significant blow to these ambitions and the financial resources available to pursue them.

Pauline Raabe, a senior analyst at the Berlin-based Middle East Minds think tank, points out that Saudi Arabia urgently needs to find a solution that shields its population from the conflict while limiting the economic damage and reputational costs.

"It is a race against time," she told DW, even though the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis is no new occurence. Saudi Arabia supported the Yemeni government in its war against the Houthis between 2015 and 2022.
"The conflict has been flaring up again with renewed intensity due to the general situation in the Gulf and is as such actually a tightening of the status quo," Raabe said.
However, she views Saudi Arabia's loss of authority as a threat on the horizon. "In the short term, Saudi Arabia is a belligerent [player] in a region ravaged by conflict," she said.

blocks.caption: Saudi Arabia failed to secure US assistance in the fight against the Houthis, but regional states voiced firm supportImage: Osamah Abdulrahman/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Symbolic support from partners like Turkey, Pakistan, Egypt
Fuchs agrees.

"Riyadh remains a key player through its investments, its position as the world's largest oil exporter and its role as custodian of Islam's holy sites in Mecca and Medina," he said, adding that "by virtue of this role, Saudi Arabia can count on allies and call for the formation of alliances."

In August, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement. While the latter two have since offered intelligence and defense support for Saudi Arabia, they also made clear that they will not put boots on the ground in Yemen. France and the United Kingdom also offered limited defense support for Riyadh. Egypt, the most populous Arab country with a Sunni majority like Saudi Arabia, voiced verbal support.
"Riyadh is prioritizing the symbolic value of these countries, projecting an image of strong ties with regional powers," Kaldas said.

However, much attention has focused on Saudi Arabia's failure to secure defense support from the United States, he added. While Saudi Arabia's closest ally — the US signaled willingness to support Riyadh with intelligence sharing and targeting assistance against the Houthis — Washington has so far stopped short of committing US forces to direct strikes. For Saudi Arabia, the understanding is therefore that the US prioritzes avoiding opening another front in the regional conflict against Iran.
Saudi Arabia on the backfoot in the war against the Houthis

articles.title: House leader pushes investigation into Cale88 linked to VP Sara's spouse
articles.summary: House Deputy Speaker Jefferson Khonghun is pushing for a motu proprio investigation by the House of Representatives into the alleged remittance of hundreds of millions of pesos into Cale88, a company…

blocks.text: Published October 16, 2026 9:41pm

House Deputy Speaker Jefferson Khonghun is pushing for a motu proprio investigation by the House of Representatives into the alleged remittance of hundreds of millions of pesos into Cale88, a company linked to Vice President Sara Duterte's husband, lawyer Manases Carpio.

"Definitely kailangan ’yang imbestigahan, kailangan ’yang tingnan dahil importante na makita iyong involvement ng China, lalong-lalo na doon sa mga kumpanya na pag-aari ng ating bise presidente. Dahil katulad nga ng sinabi ng Department of (National) Defense, it is a national security risk na kailangan tignan," Khonghun said in an online interview today.
"Gusto nga naming i-motu proprio investigation na lang yan. Para kahit na walang resolusyon na ifa-file, makakapag-investigate ang House," he added.
When asked when the investigation will be conducted, Khonghun replied, "Sana magsimula na during recess para at least nalalaman na natin kung ano yung totoo."
Congress is currently on recess until November 8.
Among the House committees that may be involved in the investigation are the Committee on National Defense and the Committee on Good Government and Public Accountability.

When asked if Vice President Duterte will be invited to the hearings, Khonghun replied, "Well, it's up to the committee handling the investigation if they will invite the Vice President. Ang problema kasi, kahit imbitahan mo naman ang bise presidente, hindi naman nagpupunta. Hindi nagpunta sa impeachment, hindi nagpunta sa committee hearing. Napakagaling umiwas ng ating bise presidente. So if ever na magkaroon ng hearing, hindi natin ine-expect na pupunta siya."
Khonghun also said it is up to the committees if Carpio and former senator Antonio Trillanes IV will also be invited.
House Impeachment Prosecutor and Manila 3rd District Rep. Joel Chua, who chairs the House Committee on Good Government and Public Accountability, supports the investigation.

"Yes, dahil siyempre, gusto rin natin malaman kung bakit pumasok yung ganoong kalaki galing sa mga offshore accounts. Hindi lang naman ito tungkol sa isang bansa. Dahil kung nakikita po natin yung account, maraming bansa ang pinanggalingan ng mga account," Chua said in a separate online interview today.
In case the investigation is covered by the sub judice rule of the Senate impeachment court, Chua said he will assign one of his vice chairs to conduct the hearings. —LDF, GMA News
