articles.title: From Duterte to Big Tech: Maria Ressa’s blueprint on fighting back
articles.summary: From challenging Big Tech to protecting independent journalism, Maria Ressa offers a roadmap for fighting authoritarianism in the digital age

items: Maria Ressa warns of the threats to democracy posed by authoritarian governments, technology companies, and artificial intelligence, emphasizing the need for citizens to resist authoritarianism.

Ressa identifies a dangerous alliance between political leaders and tech companies, which she describes as an 'authoritarian stack,' and highlights the lack of accountability for technology executives compared to political leaders.
She urges individuals to be proactive in defending democracy through independent journalism, conscious technology use, and community organization, stating that hope comes from collective action.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – In a wide-ranging discussion with WNYC’s Brian Lehrer for the second edition of Democracy Dialogues on October 16, Nobel Peace Prize laureate and Rappler CEO Maria Ressa warned again of the growing, still unaddressed threats to democracy posed by authoritarian governments, powerful technology companies, and now, artificial intelligence.

blocks.caption: From Duterte to Big Tech: Maria Ressa’s blueprint on fighting back

blocks.text: The conversation, held at The Greene Space in New York, centered on Ressa’s new book, The Fight Back: A Citizen’s Guide to Standing Up to Dictators, which lays out practical strategies for citizens to resist authoritarianism, and reclaim control over the technologies shaping their lives.

Drawing from Rappler’s experience under former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte, Ressa argued that the Philippines offers important lessons for the United States and other democracies now confronting similar threats, emphasizing how the fight can start at the individual level, and that it will take a global effort to reverse the current course of the world.

Ressa identifies two forms of authoritarian power threatening democracy: traditional political dictators and technology companies that have long wielded enormous influence over information, public opinion, and society.

She argued that Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg represents an even greater concentration of power than Duterte because, unlike political leaders who can face prosecution, technology executives operate with limited mechanisms for accountability.
“The bigger dictator, and you’ll see this in both How to Stand Up to a Dictator and The Fight Back, is actually Mark Zuckerberg,” Ressa said.
“While Duterte is now detained at The Hague… We have systems of accountability for that, but for the technology that rules our lives, we have none.”
She added: “My dictators: One is on trial and the other one has gained more power.”

Ressa also warned of an emerging alliance between political leaders and technology billionaires, which she describes as an “authoritarian stack.” Through political funding, government contracts, and control over critical technology infrastructure, powerful companies can gain influence over government functions and democratic institutions.
“This is power and money. Look at the power and money,” she said, arguing that the concentration of political and technological power amounts to a “tech coup” unfolding in plain sight.
Ressa also described the Philippines as an early example of how social media could be weaponized to undermine democracy.

She recalled how during the Duterte administration, Rappler faced coordinated online attacks followed by legal cases and government investigations, and how the hashtag #ArrestMariaRessa began circulating in 2017, two years before her actual arrest.
She realized later that that had been “fertilizer” for a narrative that allowed the government to shape public opinion in order to make the arrest.
“When you repeat a lie a million times, it becomes a fact,” Ressa reiterated.
Beyond social media, Ressa warned that artificial intelligence presents a new and potentially more dangerous challenge to democratic accountability.

She described three stages in the evolution of technology’s influence over individuals: social media capturing attention, chatbots creating a sense of intimacy, and autonomous AI agents acquiring the capacity to perform actions independently.

Speaking about her work as co-chair of the United Nations’ Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence, Ressa argued that increasingly powerful AI systems are being deployed without sufficient safeguards or accountability.
“As early as July, we had actually already said, and these are from the scientists, that the frontier models cannot be controlled by the people who are making it,” she said.
“And if you really feel that, then you should not be releasing these. You should not be treating the public around the world as Pavlov’s dogs.”

Ressa criticized the argument that rapid AI deployment is necessary to compete with China, saying geopolitical competition should not become an excuse for exposing the public to potentially harmful technologies.
“The question here is, if we go back to impunity, right? Who is accountable for this?” she asked, saying the problem is the lack of legislation.

She emphasized that AI governance cannot be left to the United States and China alone. Developing countries and other governments must have a meaningful role in shaping global rules, particularly because they may bear significant consequences of decisions made by the world’s largest technology companies.
“The world needs to have a place at the table,” Ressa said.

She also discussed how AI has undermined journalism, noting that Google Search’s use of AI summaries has caused a drop that is “catastrophic for news organizations. This is part of the tech-fueled crisis that journalism faces now, along with how 85% of digital advertising in the Philippines now goes to these tech companies owning the platforms.

blocks.caption: Maria Ressa: Journalists must build, own technology to protect information integrity

blocks.text: That fuels the “market failure” for journalism right now she said.
Without journalism, authoritarian power wins.
“Why do you need journalists? Because the journalists are the ones that do the investigative report that hold power to account,” she said.

Ressa urged audiences to support independent news organizations through subscriptions and donations. She also argued that societies must consider building alternative, public-interest technology infrastructure rather than remaining dependent on platforms controlled by a handful of corporations.

Aside from supporting independent journalism, she also outlined other strategies for fighting authoritarianism, which includes identifying authoritarian forces in one’s country, protecting elections from manipulation, and organizing communities to resist abuses of power.

blocks.caption: Limit AI now or humanity will lose its agency, says Nobel laureate Maria Ressa

blocks.text: She also urged people to become more conscious of how technology influences their behavior.
“Track your screen time. Track how much time you spend on screens,” she advised. “And then the second step in chapter one is delete the social media app that makes you angriest.”
Ressa cautioned against becoming overly dependent on AI chatbots, warning that outsourcing thinking and writing to these systems could weaken people’s ability to reason independently.

“Don’t stop thinking, especially if you’re young. Like, write. Don’t stop writing because using a chatbot is like trying to run a marathon and outsourcing going to the gym,” she said. Avoid “cognitive surrender,” she said.
Again drawing from Rappler’s experience under Duterte, Ressa emphasized that organizations and individuals must prepare for authoritarian threats before they become crises.
“What we learned in Rappler, and this is like practical advice, whatever it is you’re most afraid of, imagine it. Take it, own it, embrace it, and then workflow a response to it,” she said.

She recalled how Rappler developed contingency plans for a possible government shutdown, dividing responsibilities among teams and regularly conducting drills to ensure the newsroom could continue operating.

Ressa also urged journalists to avoid amplifying authoritarian propaganda merely to criticize it. Rather than becoming distracted by inflammatory statements, she said journalists should identify lies, provide context, investigate underlying systems of power, and help audiences understand why events matter.
“If it’s a distraction, don’t amplify. If it’s a lie, just call it a lie and then find the deeper meaning,” she said.
Ressa closed the discussion by emphasizing that defending democracy is ultimately a matter of individual and collective action.

Her central message was that hope is not something citizens should passively wait for. It must emerge from their willingness to defend democratic institutions, support one another, and confront abuses of power.
“Hope comes from action,” Ressa said. “Act! That’s what I’m saying. Act, right? That’s what the moment demands. If we act, we can do something about it.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Museum releases historical photos of island where Amelia Earhart may have crashed
articles.summary:
Images from New Zealand aerial survey of Nikumaroro in 1938 offer new clues over aviator’s disappearance

A New Zealand museum has released nearly 50 photos from a 1938 aerial survey of the…

blocks.text: A New Zealand museum has released nearly 50 photos from a 1938 aerial survey of the island where Amelia Earhart is believed to have crash-landed, offering amateur sleuths new evidence to scour for traces of the pioneering aviator and her plane.

The black-and-white images were published by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand after renewed interest in one of the biggest mysteries of the 20th century, spurred by a US expedition to the Pacific atoll of Nikumaroro in search of new clues.

While some low-resolution copies have been uploaded on blogs, the Air Force Museum of New Zealand said it had received several requests for the photos and had released the full set of 47 images in digital high-resolution format on its website.
The negatives were found more than a decade ago by the archivist Matthew O’Sullivan, the keeper of photographs at the museum in Christchurch.

blocks.caption: One of 47 images released by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand of Gardner Island, now Nikumaroro. Photograph: RNZAF/RNZAF Official

blocks.text: Earhart’s most prominent investigator, Ric Gillespie, described the images as a “goldmine” in his blog, saying they were a complete set of aerial photos taken on 1 December 1938 by an amphibious biplane during a New Zealand survey of Pacific islands that was looking for suitable airbase locations.

What happened to Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan when they disappeared on 2 July 1937 during an attempt to circumnavigate the globe at the equator has been a stop-and-start search over eight decades, and filled with false leads.

A leading theory is that the aviator who broke several records, including becoming the first woman to fly a nonstop solo trip across the Atlantic, ran out of fuel and was marooned on Nikumaroro, then known as Gardner Island.

The hypothesis is that she survived for a while, drinking rainwater and eating fish and turtles, based on signs of a castaway’s campsite and artefacts, including glass from a jar that is thought to have contained cosmetic cream.

blocks.caption: Amelia Earhart standing in front of the Lockheed Electra in which she disappeared in July 1937.  Photograph: Alamy

blocks.text: This week, archaeologists and scientists from Earhart’s former benefactor, Purdue University in Indianapolis, are searching a part of the island for the “Taraia Object”, an elongated shape in a lagoon named after the part of the island where it was first noticed in a 2020 satellite image. Other longtime Earhart explorers, including Gillespie, are not convinced, saying it is probably a fallen tree and not the wreckage of her Lockheed Model 10-E Electra. The small atoll had been visited dozens of times.

In their latest update on Nikumaroro, which is part of the archipelago country of Kiribati, the expedition said “severe weather” had hampered their metal-detecting but that they would release an update within 48 hours.

“Despite Thursday’s weather delay, the expedition remains on schedule, with two more days of field operations planned – and an update on the identification of the Taraia Object expected,” Purdue University said.

“We understand the tremendous interest in what we’re doing at Nikumaroro, and we appreciate everyone’s patience,” said Rick Pettigrew, the expedition lead and executive director of the Archaeological Legacy Institute. “This is a complex scientific process. You don’t simply arrive at a site and immediately identify what’s there. We have to carefully collect the data, analyse it and reach sound conclusions.”
The New Zealand military images are some of the earliest photographic evidence of the island. There is no immediate sign of an object in the Taraia area.

articles.title: British man fined €3,000 for causing two-year-old son’s death in Cyprus
articles.summary:
Joshua Foster pleaded guilty over death of toddler who fell from fourth-floor window of hotel during family holiday

A British man has been handed a €3,000 (£2,500) fine after his…

blocks.text: A British man has been handed a €3,000 (£2,500) fine after his two-year-old son fell nearly 12 metres (40ft) to his death from the fourth floor window of a hotel in Cyprus.
Joshua Foster thought the window was closed when he placed the boy on a sill to show him the view of a waterpark and “lost control” of him, the court previously heard.
The 37-year-old appeared at Paphos district court on Friday for sentencing having pleaded guilty to a charge of causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act.
Foster, an auditor, held back tears as his sentence was read out by the district judge Froso Christodoulidou.
After the 25-minute hearing, Foster hugged his lawyer before embracing his parents.
The boy fell from the fourth floor of the five-star King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort in Chlorakas on 12 July, the first day of the family’s holiday.
The court previously heard that Foster, his wife, two children and in-laws had arrived in Cyprus in the early hours of the morning on the date of the incident.

blocks.caption: The family were on holiday at the  King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort in Chlorakas, Cyprus, when the incident happened. Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PA

blocks.text: After various activities, including visiting the pool, the family returned to their rooms to get ready to go out for dinner.
At about 6pm, Foster, his father-in-law and son walked towards the lift, and his lawyer Alexandros Alexandrou told the court that the defendant was in a “good mood” and was playing with his son.
The court was told that as they approached the lift, the boy noticed a waterpark outside.
It was said that Foster pushed the lift button, placed the child on the windowsill, the boy looked out, and the “inconceivable” unfolded before Foster had a chance to react.
Alexandrou told the hearing, which took place on 6 October, that Foster’s life “changed for ever” from that moment.
It was heard that Foster had not realised that the section of the window was open, and that he thought there was protective glass.
Prosecutor Chryso Pergandi said that at around 6.40pm, police received reports that a child had fallen from the fourth floor of the beachfront hotel under unknown circumstances.
The boy was taken to Paphos general hospital where, despite efforts to resuscitate him, he was pronounced dead.
In a voluntary statement to police, Foster said that when he placed his son on the windowsill, the boy “fell before he had a chance to grab him”.
After the incident, Foster was taken to Paphos general hospital and a blood sample to detect drugs and alcohol was taken.
Tests showed that the alcohol concentration in his blood was an estimated 124mg.
Alcohol consumption did not form a significant part of the case against Foster, and his lawyer said there was no testimony that he was drunk.
The lawyer told the court that Foster had no previous convictions and his remorse “is clear”.
He said he was held in custody for eight days immediately after the incident, adding that while grieving for his child he had to call his daughter from custody to explain what had happened.
The court heard the window was 2.85 metres wide and 1.2 metres high.

articles.title: ‘Opening the lid of a horrible secret’: Jamaicans confront enslavement with taboo-busting stories on screen
articles.summary:
As violent spirits are unleashed in Sky’s Possession, observers see confident creatives reclaiming the island’s narratives in a form of ‘cultural reparation’

A woman opens a 300‑year‑old…

blocks.text: A woman opens a 300‑year‑old box, unleashing a violent spirit – it is the spirit of colonialism and oppression roaring back to life. It is a pivotal scene in Sky’s supernatural series Possession and symbolises a wider shift in Jamaica’s film industry, where directors are increasingly using the landscape to tell Jamaican stories – including those that confront enslavement, trauma and historical memory.

The series is about a biracial British lawyer who travels to Jamaica to investigate a multimillion-pound inheritance dispute, only to uncover a dark, vengeful spirit tied to the plantation’s brutal colonial past.

For the Jamaican director, Storm Saulter, ensuring that the trauma and enduring legacy of enslavement and colonisation were powerfully represented was critical. Caribbean countries are increasingly arguing that centuries of enslavement have left the region at a lasting disadvantage – fuelling renewed calls for reparations.

Dr Lisa Tomlinson, a lecturer in film studies at the University of the West Indies, says the themes in Jamaican films are changing. “They’re now very much connected and reflective of Jamaican stories – stories that were previously taboo or avoided.”

blocks.caption: Mbatha-Raw plays a lawyer who travels from Bristol to Jamaica to handle an inheritance claim over a former slave plantation. Photograph: Des Willie

blocks.text: While Jamaican films are not always explicitly about reparations, she argues that many are engaging with the legacies of enslavement through cultural memory. “Reparation is not just a political act,” she says. “It’s also culture. These African‑derived spiritualities, the historical knowledge – when they come through creative expression, what they do is give us authority to tell our own stories.”

This, she says, is a form of “cultural reparation”, a reclaiming of narratives devalued or suppressed under colonialism, and a way of educating audiences about the past in ways that academics or politicians struggle to do. “The arts play a critical role in how we are educated in public awareness around reparation,” she says.

Jacqueline Jackson, Jamaica’s film commissioner, sees the shift too. She says productions such as Possession and Delroy Lindo’s Jabari’s People – shot entirely in Jamaica – reflect growing confidence and ambition among Jamaican creatives. “We are well established as a destination for international productions,” she says. “But what we want to see more of is local production and international collaboration that enables us to tell our own stories.”

blocks.caption: Delroy Lindo’s directorial debut Jabari’s People (he is pictured here in Spike Lee’s Da 5 Bloods) is shot entirely in Jamaica.  Photograph: Netflix

blocks.text: Both productions, she notes, worked closely with Jamaican talent to ensure authenticity and demonstrate what is possible when international financing and distribution unite with Jamaican creativity. “They show the growing interest in Jamaican stories and their potential for global audiences,” she says.

Tomlinson believes diaspora film-makers are playing a particularly important role in this shift. Unlike foreign productions that often use Jamaica as an exotic backdrop, diaspora directors are “moving away from the tourist‑gaze depictions” and are “capturing Jamaican everyday life”.

Saulter sees his series as part of a broader political awakening. “The mask has slipped … We’ve been told it’s one thing, and that thing is proven to be false. So there’s a seeking of what is true,” he says.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Storm Saulter, Possession’s director, aims to ‘open up the lid of a 300‑year‑old horrible secret’.  Photograph: Bertie Watson

blocks.text: He says the box‑opening scene is not simply a plot device, but a metaphor for something larger: the resurfacing of long‑suppressed histories and the growing willingness among Caribbean creatives to confront the legacies of enslavement, inherited trauma and colonial violence through film.
“Literally, we’re going to open up the lid of a 300‑year‑old horrible secret,” Saulter said. “It’s the spirit of colonial enslavement and oppression coming roaring back.”

That “spirit”, he explains, is embodied in a character who has lived through centuries of brutality – “a witness to history” – whose presence forces the protagonists to reckon with the past they have inherited.
Saulter’s interest in the subject is rooted in his upbringing. “I grew up in the countryside,” he says. “The Obia man, the church … nine nights … I’ve lived through all of those things.”

His experiences inspired him to tell stories that educate and have “real societal political impact”, while remaining thrilling, intriguing and entertaining. That approach, he argues, allows film-makers to tackle difficult histories. “As opposed to doing something that was like talking heads … we’re bringing you on a journey,” he says.
For Dr L’Antoinette Stines, a Yoruba priestess and cultural expert who advised on Possession, the series’ engagement with Afro‑spiritualist traditions is part of a longer history of resistance.

blocks.caption: Sheldon East plays Cudjoe East, the son of a British man who grew up at the Hope Hill plantation in Jamaica. Photograph: Des Willie/©Sky UK Ltd

blocks.text: “Black people have been fighting and using the arts for a very long time. It’s just that there is greater attention on it today,” she says. For decades she has choreographed similar work, she says, and stresses the importance of honouring the academics, poets and creatives who paved the way for today’s boom in authentic Jamaican storytelling.

She praises Saulter’s insistence on authenticity and creating a series that feels both contemporary and deeply rooted, exploring inherited trauma, ancestral memory and the unfinished business of colonialism.

articles.title: Clashes erupt at Argentine student protests against President Milei's austerity policies
articles.summary: Demonstrators clashed with police as President Javier Milei's decision not to release funding for universities brought students and employees to the streets. Protesters say the country's future is at…

image.caption: Police used tear gas and water cannons against the protesters in Buenos AiresImage: Emiliano Lasalvia/AFP

blocks.text: Protesters took to the streets in Argentina's capital, Buenos Aires, to demonstrate against libertarian President Javier Milei's cost-cutting measures for education.
Thousands of students, university staff, trade unionists and opposition supporters crowded outside the parliament, demanding the implementation of a law to finance universities.

While the rally was largely peaceful, clashes also erupted, with reports of masked individuals throwing stones at police, injuring at least eight officers. Some 25 people were arrested, according to the country's National Security Ministry.
Reports said other protesters had tried to push those throwing stones back. Police used water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds.
Security Minister Alejandra Monteoliva said the protesters wanted to "sow chaos," posting on her X account that the right to protest is not "a right to exercise violence."
Milei vetoes law, refuses to release funding

This was the fifth protest over the Milei government's education spending to take place since Milei entered office in 2023.Such a demonstration also took place in May, in which organizers say some 1.5 million people took part.

blocks.caption: Argentinian President Javier Milei was elected in 2023 after promising to dramatically cut the state's costsImage: Juan Carlos Rojas/picture alliance

blocks.text: Milei vetoed a law, passed by Congress in 2025, requiring the government to invest more money in public universities.

The University Funding Law says the state should increase employees' salaries in line with inflation dated to December 2023. It also calls for the restoration of student scholarships and more funding for universities' operations.
Congress subsequently overrode Milei's veto, and several court rulings have instructed the government to release the funds, but it has so far refused to do so.
According to Milei, who was elected after promising wide-ranging cost-cutting measures, justified his veto by saying "there is no money" for inflation-linked spending increases.

blocks.caption: Public universities in Argentina offer studies free of chargeImage: Pedro Lazaro Fernandez/REUTERS

blocks.text: A government spokesperson said the law had been "suspended" due to the government's legal action against it.
The first half of 2026 saw public spending on universities fall by 41% in real terms, according to the Center for National Economic Research of the University of Buenos Aires.
Argentina's education system is considered to be among the best in South America. Study at public universities is free, drawing students from across the region.

articles.title: Who was Eva Mamlok? Berlin square renamed after Jewish anti-fascist resistance fighter
articles.summary: She started taking action against Hitler as a teenager and never stopped until her death in a concentration camp. Berlin's Blücherplatz is now being renamed after her.

image.caption: The only known remaining photo of resistance fighter Eva MamlokImage: Familienarchiv Siemsen

blocks.text: In the history of German resistance to Nazism, some names have become symbols: Sophie Scholl, Claus von Stauffenberg, Dietrich Bonhoeffer and Georg Elser.
Yet many others have remained largely forgotten.
Among them is Eva Mamlok, a young Jewish woman from Berlin whose acts of defiance began in her teenage years and continued until her murder in a Nazi concentration camp.
Now more people will get to know her story as Berlin renames Blücherplatz, a square in the district of Kreuzberg, Eva-Mamlok-Platz on October 16.

"Eva Mamlok was a very remarkable person. As a young Jewish woman from Berlin, her spirit of resistance was particularly striking," says cultural researcher Alexandra Weltz-Rombach, who has worked extensively with the historians' network "Gruppe Eva Mamlok."
'Down with Hitler'

Eva Mamlok was born on May 6, 1918, into a Jewish family in Berlin. They ran a wholesale wine business, and the family belonged to the vibrant Jewish middle class that formed an important part of Berlin's social and economic life during the Weimar Republic.

But Eva came of age just as Germany was descending into dictatorship. When Hitler became chancellor in 1933, she was only 14 years old. She was also a member of the Socialist Workers' Youth (SAJ). Following the suppression of the left-wing political youth organization later that year, she became active in the underground resistance.

According to testimony from Inge Berner (1922-2012), the sole survivor of Mamlok's later resistance group, Eva climbed onto the roof of a department store on Blücherplatz as a teenager and painted the slogan "Down with Hitler."
"She was caught doing that, though she wasn't arrested at that particular moment — that didn't happen until a year later," notes Weltz-Rombach.

blocks.caption: Known as the Tietz department store, the building onto which Mamlok wrote her slogan was renamed Hertie after its 'Aryanization' by the NazisImage: Public Domain

blocks.text: Arrested for honoring socialist icons Luxemburg and Liebknecht

Eva Mamlok first appeared in official records in November 1934, after she was arrested for taking part in commemorations for socialist leaders Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht at Berlin's Friedrichsfelde Cemetery.

Authorities determined that the 16-year-old held "hostile views toward the state" and placed her in "protective custody until further notice" — a euphemism the regime used to justify imprisonment without trial. She was sent to the women's concentration camp at Moringen in Lower Saxony, where she remained until May 1935.
After her release, she continued her anti-Nazi activities despite the increasing danger, facing persecution both as a political dissident and as a Jew.

In these underground circles, she met Pieter Siemsen (1914–2004), and they remained a couple until he emigrated to Argentina in 1937. The only known surviving photograph of Eva comes from his personal archive.

She had a daughter, Tana, in 1939. The father's identity is unknown, however. The child was placed in a Jewish orphanage in Berlin and deported in 1942 to the Auschwitz-Birkenau extermination camp, where she was murdered.

Meanwhile, because she was Jewish, Eva Mamlok was forced to perform compulsory labor at the Berlin firm F. Butzke Schrauben-Industrie in 1940. There she met other women who shared her opposition to Nazism.

Together they formed what later became known as the "Eva Mamlok Group," an informal resistance network of Jewish and non-Jewish women. They distributed anti-Nazi leaflets and wrote slogans critical of Hitler.

They also shared banned books. "They were books that are today part of Germany's educational canon," from Thomas Mann to Lion Feuchtwanger, notes Weltz-Rombach. She adds that the fact that the Berlin Central and Regional Library (ZLB), Germany's largest public library, stands on the new Eva-Mamlok-Platz is a fitting symbol of this act of resistance and the importance of books.
Mamlok and others in her group were arrested for distributing this forbidden literature. On January 13, 1942, she was deported from Berlin to the Riga Ghetto in occupied Latvia.

According to Inge Berner's testimony, Mamlok remained active in the resistance there too. For example, she arranged for a contact still in Berlin to send her a cake with a miniature camera hidden inside it to document persecution in the ghetto.
In October 1944, she was sent to the Stutthof Nazi concentration camp, where she died in December of that year.
Replacing old symbols of Franco-German hostility

Blücherplatz was named after the Prussian field marshal Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher, whose most renowned achievement was leading his army against Napoleon at the Battle of Leipzig in 1813 and the Battle of Waterloo in 1815.
Several places, including streets and parks, have been named after him in Germany.

"There is no shortage of Blücher memorial sites," says Weltz-Rombach. "And perhaps it's also time to put an end to this old Franco-German enmity — which is, of course, inherent in the name Blücher, given its Prussian tradition — and to establish, in its place, a different form of remembrance," she adds.
The square also happens to be the site of the Carnival of Cultures, a multicultural street festival and parade held every year to celebrate Berlin's global diversity.
Role models for a new generation

Having first heard about Mamlok when a Stolperstein commemorating her was laid in 2011, Weltz-Rombach has been researching her biography for the past few years. The Berlin-based filmmaker, producer and curator has also been sharing the resistance fighter's story through various projects, including an exhibition in 2024 and a podcast series with young Berliners.
Since Eva Mamlok was only a teenager herself when she became politically active, the workshop participants can easily relate to her fate.

These teenagers learn about Mamlok's experiences at the actual locations where she was active, helping them imagine what it would be like to be arrested and imprisoned for six months without trial for doing things that normally wouldn't be considered crimes — such as simply expressing an opinion publicly or laying flowers at a commemorative event, explains Weltz-Rombach.
"Above all, she is, of course, a role model — an example of how one would like to act oneself, and how courageous one would like to be."

Women's "resistance was often of a more everyday nature, rather than planting bombs," notes Weltz-Rombach. Their stories offer examples of "forms of resistance that have only recently received more attention." She mentions, for example, a 2024 exhibition and the launch of a database dedicated to female resistance fighters.

Even though many of the eyewitnesses have now died, Weltz-Rombach believes there are still many more of these stories that deserve to be brought into the spotlight: "There are definitely many names we do not know, that are waiting to be further researched."

articles.title: EU promotes sovereign, trusted AI as it struggles to catch US and China
articles.summary: At an international AI summit in Dublin, EU leaders promoted trusted and independent artificial intelligence. Critics question whether the bloc can close the gap with the US and China while…

image.caption: Though Europe is strong in AI research, regulation, supercomputing initiatives and semiconductor equipment, it lags behind in frontier-model developmentImage: Paul Faith/AFP

blocks.text: If supremacy in artificial intelligence was an Olympic discipline, there would only be two serious contenders for gold on current trajectories: the US and China. The European Union, as has been the case in many areas of cutting-edge technology in recent times, is barely in the AI conversation.

Former European Central Bank President Mario Draghi, whose 2024 report highlighted the EU's desperate need to be more innovative to become more competitive, said recently that AI is "perhaps the most promising" route the EU has to raise growth today. However, he decried the fact that the European Union controls little of the value chain.

"Being cut off from AI, once the economy runs on it, would be more like being cut off from the US financial system," he wrote in an opinion piece for the Financial Times. "The effects would be catastrophic."
Draghi's spirit was on full display in Dublin on Wednesday at an international AI summit the Irish government convened as part of its six-month stint hosting the rotating EU presidency.
The summit's motto, "Harnessing AI to Revolutionize Europe's Competitiveness," might as well have been dreamed up by the Italian former prime minister.
AI safety concerns shadow growth agenda

Harnessing AI has become a lot more complicated. A slew of controversies around AI agents going rogue, from the Hugging Face attack in June when 1,200 agents hacked an online platform, to an Anthropic-designed agent sending a fake tip to US police over an unsolved murder, have caused alarm.
Many from within the tech industry, including Microsoft founder Bill Gates and the leading AI frontier labs themselves, have called for a development pausein order for safety measures to catch up.
Trump announces creation of new 'AI Force'

Yet positivity was largely the name of the game at the summit, with tech and AI industry leaders joining Irish and EU politicians to declare AI's transformative economic and societal potential — while also emphasizing the need for strong regulation and safety standards.

Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin made it clear that Ireland was all in on AI. He echoed European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's recent assertion that the technology represented a "tipping point." He also repeatedly highlighted what he sees as the bloc's commitment to safety.

"We are determined to capture the dividend by mitigating the risks," Martin told the event. "In Europe, we have charted our path ... balancing innovation and opportunity with a trustworthy, human-centered approach to AI."
AI critics say key concerns overlooked

Meanwhile, Henna Virkkunen, the European Commission executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, security and democracy, revealed at the event that the EU had begun its first enforcement actions under its new AI Act, requesting information around security and safety from advanced AI model providers.

However, other topics that concern AI's many critics, from those fearing the massive environmental impact of data centers to others warning about possible AI-related job losses, were largely absent from the discussions.

blocks.caption: Protestor Alexandra Day says not enough attention is paid to AI risksImage: Manuel Vering/DW

blocks.text: Outside the venue, a group of protesters led by People Before Profit, a left-wing Irish political party, criticized the summit for not focusing on these issues.
"There is a deliberate blurring of the line here with the type of AI that is being promoted," Alexandra Day, one of the protest organizers, told DW.
"It is really being pushed on workers with very little consent. There's no right for workers to opt out of using AI now that it's coming into the workplace."
Europe faces a widening AI gap

A sense of urgency was palpable from the speakers inside the summit. Executives from some of the world's biggest AI and tech firms talked up Europe's potential. Yet the EU evidently has plenty of ground to catch up on in terms of AI development.
Despite ramping up its data center capacity, it still lags far behind the US and China. It hosts 5% of the world's AI computing capacity compared to around 75% for the US.
Trump proclaims US 'golden age' of science

The EU is conspicuously absent from lists of the leading AI frontier labs, with only French company Mistral coming close to rivaling the top labs. Its production of leading-edge chips is also nowhere near that of the top US or Taiwanese producers.
As part of its plan to make ground on the US and China, the Irish government, in its role as EU presidency host, presented a policy document at the event.
The so-called "Dublin Declaration" outlines political commitments to strengthen Europe's AI capabilities, including infrastructure investment and financial backing for European AI companies.

In keeping with Draghi's calls for Europe to develop its own AI sovereignty, particularly in supply chains and infrastructure, the declaration suggests that European firms reliant on non-EU cloud and computing services may face additional compliance pressures.

blocks.caption: Eddie Wilson, CEO of European airline Ryanair, doubts the EU's capacity to develop AI wellImage: Manuel Vering/DW

blocks.text: Can Europe balance innovation and regulation?
However, not everyone is convinced by the EU's capacity to either ramp up AI capacity or develop effective regulation.
Eddie Wilson, CEO of European airline Ryanair, said he doubted Brussels could regulate AI well without stifling innovation.
"The last thing you want is people regulating this industry who don't know anything about it," he told DW. "That's generally what happens in Brussels."

Ryanair recently made a major deal with Google to use its cloud data system and its AI platform Gemini Enterprise. It's precisely the kind of collaboration with US AI supply chains that the EU says it wants companies to move away from.
"I worry for Europe because these tech companies need to move at speed," said Wilson. He believes the environment in the US is more amenable to innovation.
"If they're not going to do it here, they're going to do it elsewhere. They're going to do it in China and they're going to do it in the US."

articles.title: Bleak outcomes: Half of kids in care don't finish high school, and far fewer complete post-secondary
articles.summary: In the last five years, many post-secondary institutions in Nova Scotia started offering tuition waivers. It’s an effort to change educational outcomes for a group that’s been disadvantaged for…

image.caption: Jacquie Gahagan is the associate vice-president of research at Mount Saint Vincent University and the lead on the Atlantic Tuition Waiver project. (Galen McRae/CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia

In the last five years, many post-secondary institutions in Nova Scotia started offering tuition waivers. It’s an effort to change educational outcomes for a group that’s been disadvantaged for decades, but a researcher studying the program says much more needs to be done.
Atlantic Tuition Waiver project examines how to raise education outcomes for former youth in care
This fall, at least 45 students started post-secondary programs across Nova Scotia funded by tuition waivers specifically for people who were in government care.

In the last five years, many post-secondary institutions in the province started offering the tuition waivers, part of an effort to change educational outcomes for a group that’s been disadvantaged for decades.
But according to a researcher studying the effect of these programs, much more needs to be done to help this group of young people.

“As we look over time, we see the educational attainment of kids from care is not improving,” said Jacquie Gahagan, who leads the Atlantic Tuition Waiver project and is associate vice-president of research at Mount Saint Vincent University.
Gahagan noted that less than 10 per cent of former youth in care go on to finish post-secondary education.
The researcher also said less that 50 per cent of kids from care in Canada even finish high school, a statistic they described as "a problem.”
By comparison, data from the province of Nova Scotia and Statistics Canada show an overall high school graduation rate of over 90 per cent.
LISTEN | A Cape Breton student recalls her journey from foster care and group homes to university:
Information Morning - Cape Breton15:04Students in care need more than tuition help
Tuition waiver programs launched in Atlantic Canada around 2020 and Gahagan saw a chance to study them from inception. They’ve learned waivers help, but more support is required.
This includes mental health support, mentoring, and sometimes food or housing assistance.
Most tuition waiver programs cover school fees but the student is responsible for added expenses such as room, board, textbooks and laptops.
Senate examines issue
Sen. Wanda Thomas Bernard pushed for the Senate to examine outcomes for youth aging out of care in a national report released in December.
Decades of experience as a social worker in Nova Scotia taught her that the system of services has a “patchwork” quality where students who do well in school tend to get more support.
“But I thought, well, what about the ones who aren't doing so well? They need that help more than anyone else,” she said in a recent interview.
Sen. Wanda Thomas Bernard spent decades as a social worker in Nova Scotia before becoming an independent member of the Canadian Senate. (Craig Paisley/CBC)
She believes the child protection and education systems don’t have enough wraparound support to help kids through the trauma of being removed from their family.
She said that trauma often comes out in behaviours at school, and the focus becomes on fixing or controlling the behaviour rather than inquiring about the reason behind it.
“How do you work with those kids who are difficult to work with?” she said. “Doesn't mean we shy away from them. It means we need to work harder to reach them.”
'Directly into poverty'
Gahagan believes changes at the federal level are needed, including better data collection on outcomes and a national child and youth advocate.

They also believe work needs to be done at the provincial level, but they credit Nova Scotia for implementing the Path program, which allows former youth in care to receive biweekly financial support up to age 24. The money can be used for any purpose, including education.

items: N.S. bill aims to extend support for youth in foster care who age out of the system
When it comes to aging out in N.L., the system is ‘leaving a lot of young people behind’

blocks.text: The province did consultation and research before starting Path in 2024, and released some of its work through access-to-information requests earlier this year.
The briefing notes described how youth in care often do not graduate from high school, which means they transition “directly into poverty.”
One note written in 2021 described how in the previous 10 years there were 730 youth who aged out of care in Nova Scotia. The note said nearly 60 per cent sought income assistance at some point.
Experts urge more support for youth in care struggling to graduate
Stability for education
Programs like Path and post-secondary tuition waivers are meant for young people after they turn 19.
Gahagan is calling for more attention to kids’ schooling while they’re still in the care system.
Former kids in care have spoken to CBC about the disruption of bumping between multiple foster care and group home placements. Gahagan said their research shows that’s a big problem.
Why so many kids run from Nova Scotia's group homes
“You start in a new school. You have a new peer group, you're trying to catch up on what you missed out on,” they said.
“That means we're not focusing on educational attainment, we're focusing on moving this person as needed for placements.”

Jill Barkhouse, the Department of Opportunities and Social Development’s executive director of child and family well-being, said a child’s school experience is “crucial” in their development. She said her department works with the education system to share information and try to help kids succeed.
She said an example of this is a dedicated consultant role that’s shared with the Department of Education and Early Childhood Development to help kids make the transition between schools.
Gahagan said former youth in care often express a sense of embarrassment or personal failure about education. But Gahagan does not see it that way.
“This is a symptom of a bigger problem, which is to say: we're not focusing on the educational attainment of kids in care. And we should be doing that.”

EDITOR'S NOTE: They are among society's most vulnerable: children who experience traumatic instability and end up in government care. In this series called “Left Behind,” the CBC Atlantic investigative team explores the challenges and outcomes through the eyes of people who lived through this and those trying to help them.

articles.title: China tells Israel to stop 'forced establishment' of West Bank settlements
articles.summary: Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi spoke to Israeli President Isaac Herzog on the sidelines of a conference.

blocks.text: Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi has told Israel to stop its "forced establishment" of settlements in the West Bank and reverse its actions, his office said.

The "Palestinian question" is "the greatest historical injustice of this century", Wang told Israeli President Isaac Herzog in a face-to-face meeting on the sidelines of a conference in Azerbaijan on Thursday.
Beijing has been a longstanding supporter of the Palestinian cause and has maintained that a "two-state solution" is the "correct direction".
It has also been positioning itself as a mediator for conflicts in the Middle East.

In 2023 Beijing brokered a deal to restore diplomatic ties between Iran and Saudi Arabia after years of hostility. Earlier this year, it was part of efforts, along with Pakistan, to propose a ceasefire in the US-Israel war against Iran.
Beijing's efforts to tackle the war in Gaza have focused on Palestinian unity.

In 2024 Beijing got rival Palestinian factions to agree to form an interim "national reconciliation government" for the occupied West Bank and Gaza after the war with Israel, although it was never implemented.
Now, Wang says the "immediate priority" is to fully open access to Gaza and stop the continued spread of a "humanitarian catastrophe".
China is willing to work with the international community to get the parties to return to dialogue and "seek a political solution to the conflict", Wang said.
In a post on X, Herzog said he was "pleased" to meet Wang and their talk "focused on the relations between our countries and the situation in the Middle East".
"I emphasised Israel's desire for peace in the region, alongside the strategic threats to our security, first and foremost from Iran and its terror proxies," he wrote.
China maintains close ties with Iran and is the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, which had previously come under US sanctions because of Tehran's nuclear programme.
One year into the ceasefire, people in Gaza continue to live under the regular threat of Israeli strikes, displacement and food security challenges.

Although large-scale bombardment has stopped, Israel has continued strikes in Gaza almost every day. More than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli strikes there in the year since the ceasefire started in October 2025.
The US-brokered ceasefire was the first phase of a deal to end the war in Gaza, which had been triggered by a deadly Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.
But progress into the deal's next phase has been stalled, with both Israel and Hamas accusing each other of violating the terms of their agreement.

articles.title: Formula One in Rwanda: Sportswashing claims vs. hopes for African legacy
articles.summary: Formula One will return to Africa for the first time since 1993. There is concern Rwanda are using it as another sportswashing opportunity, but there is also hope the event's legacy can impact wider…

image.caption: Rwanda will welcome back F1 to the African continent from 2030, but what does the move mean?Image: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Rwanda's sports portfolio has grown after confirming it will host Formula One races from the early 2030s. The track is to be built in Bugesera near Kigali International Airport, which Qatar Airways, an F1 sponsor, owns 60% of.

"To be an African and to see it happening in real time, for me in my lifetime because Kyalami [the track in South Africa where F1 was last hosted in Africa] was before I was born, I'm more than happy to have it on the continent," South African presenter and content creator Nqobile Khwezi told Sky Sports.
"To be able to give that taste back to the rest of the world and the audience of Formula One would be an absolute delight."
F1 have also highlighted the benefits for the host nation.

"Through this race we have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to our more than 100 million fans across Africa and firmly believe that sport can be a positive force for good," an F1 spokesperson told The Athletic.
DW contacted Rwanda's Ministry of Sports for comment, but did not receive a promised reply.
Kagame continues ventures into sport

For the country's President, Paul Kagame, another move into sport is hardly a surprise given his ventures into European football and the NBA in recent years. Rwanda even sponsored Bayern Munich, but fan and media backlash over the deal caused the Bundesliga club to drop the commercial element with the country's tourist arm, Visit Rwanda, last year.

blocks.caption: Paul Kagame's sports portfolio now includes F1 after securing the sport's return to AfricaImage: Bright Emoja/AFP

blocks.text: With many critics accusing Kagame and Rwanda of sportswashing, the arrival of F1, a sport valued at approximately $34 billion (€30 billion), according to sports business website Sportico, brings fresh questions.

"This deal may have positive economic and social impacts across Africa, but we should be realistic about circumstances on the ground in Rwanda," Lewis Mudge, Central Africa director at Human Rights Watch, told DW.

"Human Rights Watch wrote to Formula One in February 2025 to ask how it is addressing the human rights impacts of its activities, including regarding Rwanda and other countries’ bid to host a F1 Grand Prix. We did not receive a response," said Mudge, adding that F1 should only approve racing in the country after addressing the human rights impacts of hosting a race there.

"Rwanda, like other countries, has also used high-profile sports deals and races in the past to distract from its abysmal human rights record. Rwanda is currently the power behind the abusive M23 rebel group in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo and its military forces have been implicated in unlawful displacement and deaths of civilians in violation of international humanitarian law."
For Mohamed Keita, returning the sport to Africa is overdue, but the choice of country is telling.

"The fact that F1 excluded the world's second largest continent from its race series for three decades is indefensible in its own right and is actually a stain on a sport which claims to be global," Keita, Senior Policy Officer, Africa, at the Human Rights Foundation told DW.

"The choice of Rwanda, however, is deeply controversial," Keita continued. "Rwanda is a brutal dictatorship. Its regime is under partial US sanctions for its military occupations of territories of eastern DRC. Rwanda is arming and financing a militia involved in rapes, massacres, forced recruitment and violent plunder of natural resources."
Just Rwanda, or will F1 also come to South Africa?

Formula One has history on the continent. In 1958, there was a race in Morocco and more recently, in South Africa, where the last F1 race in Africa took place at the Kyalami racetrack in Johannesburg in 1993. Many previous races in the country were overshadowed by the policy of apartheid.

Despite Rwanda securing the deal first, South Africa believes it will host before them. When Rwanda announced their hosting, South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa sent his congratulations in a social media post, adding: "This contract is a recognition of the capabilities of the Rwandan nation and of our continent more broadly."
South Africa's Sports Minister Gayton McKenzie also congratulated Rwanda, but pivotally added that South Africa "will get F1, even before 2030."
There is no denying that hosting a race in South Africa would cost significantly less time and money, given the existing infrastructure.
Event legacy opportunities also present

In either country, comes a legacy opportunity. Sports such as Formula One, where the majority of decision-makers, drivers, team principles and engineers are white men, are a living example of the unlevel playing field. The hope of racing in Africa is that it will go some way to changing that.

"I think that's the kind of aspirational drive of hosting a Formula 1 race. It's leveraging STEM [science, technology, engineering, and mathematics] education, technology, aspiring young girls or women, leveling the playing fields, if it's for all those other reasons and we can make it work then I say yes to Formula 1 in Africa," Dr. Kamilla Swart-Arries, an expert in South Africa's events industry and the legacy of sports events, told DW in 2024.

blocks.caption: F1 is returning to Africa for the first time since 1993, but it's legacy on the continent goes back as far the 1980sImage: Ronco/HOCH ZWEI/picture alliance

blocks.text: "I hope F1 will consider further investment in developing African talent in motorsport," said Keita. "There's a lot of good that F1 can do if it genuinely wants to grow the sport in Africa, but Rwanda does not make sense at this moment unless you're doing it purely for the benefit of one dictator and the beauty of the hilly terrain."

"The proposition here is to take the world's most expensive sport to Rwanda, which is one of the world's poorest countries. Rwanda is consistently listed among the UN's list of the 25 least developed countries in the world," said Keita.

The return of the fastest show in sports is a huge moment for both Rwanda and Africa. It raises questions about President Kagame's use of sport, but it also offers an opportunity to shape the event's legacy. Unlike the race Rwanda wants to host, this is not about being the fastest but about making the most of the chance.

articles.title: Order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside White House, sources say
articles.summary: Sources say leaders at the Defense Department received a message that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military needed to be slowed

blocks.text: SETTING UP STARLINK. Servicemen of the 68th Oleksa Dovbush Separate Jaeger Brigade of the Armed Forces of Ukraine set up Starlink satellite internet system, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, near the frontline town of Pokrovsk in Donetsk region, Ukraine on April 10, 2025.
Inna Varenytsia/Reuters
Sources say leaders at the Defense Department received a message that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military needed to be slowed

items: The White House is said to have ordered a slowdown of the SpaceX Starshield service used by Ukraine for military communications, impacting drone operations, according to sources.
Ukrainian officials reported that military-grade Starlink receptors faced issues when mounted on fast-moving objects, complicating strike missions against Russian forces.
Relations between the US and Ukraine have deteriorated, with tensions arising over Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries and a recent US diesel deal with Russia.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

The order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine for battlefield communications and drone operations came from inside the White House, according to two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter.
The officials said leaders at the Defense Department received a message that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military needed to be slowed.

The officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, did not specify who in the White House made the decision or who was responsible for implementing the order. The Pentagon is the biggest customer of Starshield, which is the military-grade version of the Starlink service.

Ukrainian officials said this week that military-grade Starlink receptors stopped working in Ukraine when mounted on fast-moving objects, interfering with the performance of ‌Ukrainian drones that rely on them for onboard guidance systems over Ukrainian territory.
A person in Ukraine’s Defence Ministry said on Thursday, October 15, that the receptors were now working when in motion, but only at speeds of up to 100 miles per hour (160 kph).

The move to temporarily restrict the vital communications system came as President Donald Trump has pressured Kyiv to stop its attacks on Russian refineries, which he has blamed for the soaring energy prices that are denting his Republican Party’s prospects in the November midterm elections.
But experts say that surge in energy costs is mainly the result of the US-Israeli war with Iran, which brought Iranian attacks on energy facilities and has largely shut the vital Strait of Hormuz.
In response to a request for comment about the order to limit Starshield, a senior US official said: “No such request was ever made by the president.”
The White House did not respond to questions about whether other administration officials might have made the request.
Starshield was developed by SpaceX specifically for government and national-security customers, particularly the US Department of Defense. Starshield uses the Starlink constellation as its backbone.

Ukrainian officials said the restrictions complicated strike missions against Russian forces and logistics in occupied territory and slowed interceptor drones used to shoot down incoming Russian Shahed drones.

Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, said on X on Wednesday that because Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government, any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military or the president.
SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.
The Department of Defense and the Ukrainian embassy in Washington also did not respond to requests for comment.

Relations between Kyiv and Washington have deteriorated in recent days following a meeting in Miami on October 9 that convened representatives from both countries as well as Europe and the World Bank.

Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, the Trump administration’s Middle East envoy, struck a tough tone with Ukraine in the meeting, according to a separate person familiar with the matter. They told Ukrainian officials that the US was frustrated with Kyiv’s continued strikes on Russian refineries despite repeated requests from Washington to stop.
The US delegation also explained Washington’s decision to strike a diesel deal with Russia, saying the White House hoped it would soften Moscow’s stance on peace talks.

That deal, under which Russia will supply more than 2.25 million barrels of diesel to ​US and global markets, has triggered a backlash from some US lawmakers, who say it will give Moscow cash to pursue its war without forcing Russian President Vladimir Putin to make concessions to end the conflict.

In the days that followed, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy and Trump criticized each other, with Zelenskiy calling the US decision on the Russian diesel deal “weak.” Trump called for elections in Ukraine and Zelenskiy’s ouster.

Behind the scenes, American officials threatened to stop providing intelligence to Kyiv about Russian missile launches that Ukraine uses to thwart attacks, as Reuters previously reported. Trump said on Tuesday Washington was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine.

Following the move to restrict Ukraine’s access to Starshield, the Ukrainians made calls on Tuesday and Wednesday to find answers from senior officials at the White House, State Department and Pentagon, a senior Ukrainian official said, adding that Kyiv was told it was a White House decision.

The Pentagon has spent billions of dollars on the Starlink and Starshield services. It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft ​for missile-warning missions and a spy ​constellation for the National Reconnaissance ⁠Office, Reuters reported in 2024. – Rappler.com

articles.title: EU’s von der Leyen pledges to ‘not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops the war’ as leaders discuss Ukraine – Europe live
articles.summary:
European leaders are meeting in Brussels amid worsening relations between Washington and Kyiv

Irish PM Micheál Martin got asked about Ukraine on his arrival, too.

He…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 4m agoSituation in Ukraine 'really grave' and talks with US are 'very difficult,' EU foreign policy chief warns
9m agoIrish PM calls for 'a European response' to Ukraine's needs and outreach to the US
19m agoMorning opening: EU leaders meet to discuss Ukraine
19m ago'This is no time to withdraw support to Ukraine,' Costa says
19m ago'We will not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops the war,' EU's von der Leyen says
19m agoZelenskyy thanks for support from 'real leaders' as he stresses need to prepare for winter
19m agoIf Europe wants to eat croissants, drink coffee and not think about threats - support Ukraine, Latvian PM says

blocks.text: Situation in Ukraine 'really grave' and talks with US are 'very difficult,' EU foreign policy chief warns
EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas warns on arrival that the situation in Ukraine is “really grave” with “no signs from Russia that they want to stop this war or into any sort of truce or peace.”

blocks.caption: EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas speaks to the press as she arrives to attend an EU summit in Brussels. Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “We need to support Ukraine, also to get through the winter, because winter is going to be harsh,” she warns. “And that’s why we really need to help Ukrainians to survive, to defend their country.”
Kallas says she expects the issue of frozen Russian assets to be raised again today.
She says “we have agreed that we will not return the frozen assets, unless Russia pays reparations for Ukraine.”
She says the EU is “trying to convince also our American partners” that more pressure needs to be put on Moscow.
“But you can see that with our American allies, it’s very difficult at the moment.”
Irish PM calls for 'a European response' to Ukraine's needs and outreach to the US
Irish PM Micheál Martin got asked about Ukraine on his arrival, too.

blocks.caption: Ireland’s prime minister Micheál Martin speaks with the media as he arrives for the EU summit at the European Council building in Brussels. Photograph: Omar Havana/AP

blocks.text: He said “the very severe pressure that Ukraine is under needs a European response,” with the opening of the accession clusters, and the deploying of the EU’s €90bn loan to Ukraine as soon as possible.
He also says there needs to be a “clearer landscape” on what the EU can offer Ukraine in medium term, “whether it’s immobilised assets or other mechanisms.”
“I am conscious on the last occasion, we strongly supported the issue of the seizure, the seized assets and whether they could be deployed. But that came to nought in the end.”
He says Europe needs to “maintain the pressure on Russia.”

But he also notes that he wants to see “a continuing outreach from Europe to the United States,” making representations that “as far as Europe is concerned, Russia has been the aggressor from the beginning.”

“What is happening now is, really, without any sort of regard for innocent civilian life, Russia is simply bombing civilian infrastructure, and endeavouring to kill as many people as possible in Ukraine and to put as much pressure as possible on the civilian population in Ukraine to try and force a Ukrainian climbdown. The stakes are high and the situation is of considerable concern.”
If Europe wants to eat croissants, drink coffee and not think about threats - support Ukraine, Latvian PM says
Latvian PM Andris Kulbergs drops an early quote of the day contender, as he explains the stakes on Ukraine in direct and practical terms:

“It is a super important moment because, well, if we want comfort in Europe and [be able to] eat croissant, drink coffee in the morning, and don’t think about the threats, then we have to support Ukraine.”

blocks.caption: Latvian PM Andris Kulbergs addresses the media in Brussels. Photograph: dts News Agency Germany/Shutterstock

blocks.text: He says Russia “was pulled out from under the water” by Trump’s war in Iran and the crisis in the strait of Hormuz, which increased its oil revenues, “and that is not helping.”
“Ukraine needs financial support and military support in order to have to go through this harsh winter … ahead of us.”
Zelenskyy thanks for support from 'real leaders' as he stresses need to prepare for winter
In what definitely feels like a swipe at some other leaders (*waves across the ocean*), Zelenskyy begins his remarks by saying he is happy to have “huge support” from “leaders, real leaders.”

blocks.caption: Zelenskyy arriving for today’s EU summit Photograph: dts News Agency Germany/Shutterstock

blocks.text: He says Ukraine wants the war to end as soon as possible, but sees “no signals from the Russian side that they are ready to end this war.”
“That’s why we have to prepare for the winter,” both on energy and defence, he says.
'We will not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops the war,' EU's von der Leyen says
Commission president von der Leyen also delivers a pretty unequivocal message, as she blames Russia for violating Donald Trump’s energy ceasefire and says Moscow “escalated” its attacks instead.

blocks.caption: Costa, Zelenskyy and von der Leyen arriving for today’s European Council. Photograph: Yves Herman/Reuters

blocks.text: She makes it clear that the EU will not offer Russia any concessions, despite pressure from the US.
“One thing is absolutely clear: we will not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops the war.”
She says the talks today will also focus on defining Ukraine’s path to the European Union by opening two further “negotiating clusters” as they are known before the end of the year.
The leaders will also discuss how to support Ukraine during the winter.
'This is no time to withdraw support to Ukraine,' Costa says
Arriving with Zelenskyy and von der Leyen, Costa is very clear in his message on Ukraine as he declares the EU’s support to Ukraine “remains as strong as ever.”

blocks.caption: Costa, Zelenskyy and von der Leyen briefing journalists ahead of today’s meeting. Photograph: Geert Vanden Wijngaert/AP

blocks.text: In what feels like a targeted message to Ukraine, Russia, but also the US, he says:
“This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine. This is no time to relieve Russia’s sanctions.”
He adds “this is essential to bring Russia to accept a real ceasefire, to bring Russia to the table of negotiations and to stop this war.”
Costa also signals his intention to move on the accession prospects for Ukraine, saying:
“You can count on us not only to support you in war, but most important for your future as a member of the European Union.”
Morning opening: EU leaders meet to discuss Ukraine

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
EU leaders and Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy are meeting today in Brussels to discuss the latest in Russia’s war against Ukraine amid worsening relations between Kyiv and Washington.

blocks.caption: Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrives to attend a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of an EU summit in Brussels. Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Zelenskyy is expected to arrive any moment now, alongside European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen and European Council president António Costa.
Overnight Ukraine was once again affected by Russian attacks, which killed at least three in the eastern city of Kharkiv. 370,000 people were left without power in the Volyn region bordering Poland.

Today’s talks come at a critical moment as Ukraine increasingly struggles with repelling Russian air attacks as a result of acute shortages of interceptor missiles, with Zelenskyy also involved in a very public series of disagreements with Donald Trump at White House.

The EU leaders will discuss what the bloc can do to support Ukraine during the upcoming winter and beyond and whether any substantial progress can be made on the key issue of its plans to join the European Union.
Separately, the leaders will also talk about migration and foreign policy more broadly.
I will bring you all the key updates here.
It’s Friday, 16 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

articles.title: No kids, no apologies: Why Filipino women are opting out of motherhood
articles.summary: An expert says the 'era of high fertility' that drove the country to overpopulation is over

blocks.text: First of two parts
Rubie Montejo was 24 years old and financially struggling as a call center agent when she first considered not having children.

“I was questioning a lot of my decisions and what direction to take with my career,” she said in a mix of English and Filipino. “And then, I thought to myself, I don't think I wanna involve another human being in this life when I have so many questions and confusion myself.”
She eventually told her mother about her decision and was met with unexpected support. However, things were different outside her home in the province.
Her neighbors voiced familiar warnings — cautioning Montejo that she would face regret, solitude, and lack of support from her would-have-been children in her old age.

“[Not having children] wasn't that normal before, especially if you grew up in the province as I did. Women were expected to, you know, marry at a certain age and then bear children after or before their 30s,” Montejo recalled.
But with her mother backing her choice, she gradually gained confidence. Now a 33-year-old, single, social media strategist, Montejo has fully embraced a child-free lifestyle.
“I could imagine [then] that it would be so much more difficult if a child were involved [in my life],” she said.
32-year-old Bea (not her real name) decided to have one child with her husband of three years and plans to stop there, despite relatives urging them to have one more so the child feels less lonely.

She explained that restructuring their existing savings would be a hassle if they had a second child. “It brings more happiness to be able to provide the comfortable life you can give your child,” Bea said in a mix of English and Filipino.

Although the Philippines remains within the working-age demographic range, its population has begun to resemble those of Asian neighbors such as Japan, South Korea, and Singapore, which are already aging.

Compared to these countries, the Philippines remains in transition. The Commission on Population and Development (CPD) expects the country to become an aging society by 2028, when Filipinos aged 65 and above reach 7% of the population.
The World Health Organization classifies a country as an “aging society” when the proportion of older people reaches this threshold.
Jose Ramon Albert, senior research fellow at the Philippine Institute of Development Studies (PIDS), said this new pattern is gradually displacing the longstanding concern of overpopulation.

“Philippine population policy was built around one fear: that population growth would outrun the economy's capacity to feed, educate, and employ people. The [data] tells us that the era of high fertility is over,” he told Rappler.
Change in socioeconomic status

Myline Quiray, Information Management and Communications Division chief of CPD, enumerated changing marriage patterns, increasing contraceptive use, declining number of desired children, and child health and survival as some of the top reasons for the trend.
However, she pointed to women’s socioeconomic status as the main driver.
“They're employed, they're educated — so the delay in fertility is happening,” she said.
Albert noted that as women have begun to outperform men in schools and stepped into diverse workforce roles, marriage and parenthood may become lower priorities for them.
Jireh Ramos, a 29-year-old law student who has been married for five years, opted for a child-free lifestyle to focus on higher education.
“I'm very intentional with the life I'm building right now. I have a career, I have law school, I have relationships, and I have a lot of things I want to experience in my life,” she said.

Ramos also feels content with their current routine at home: she studies for hours in a separate work room from her husband’s, shoots videos as a content creator on TikTok with 61,000 followers, takes breaks, and catches up with her husband at the end of the day.
Besides the need to focus on their own economic well-being, women also face pressure from rising household living costs, said Albert.

“Can you really blame people for deciding against having children or maybe deciding just to have one child instead of, like, three — when everything is getting more expensive while [salaries] in the Philippines do not keep up with inflation?” said Montejo.
Ramos also echoed the sentiment about costs and said, “Kids, in this economy, right? It’s perfectly valid. It really is expensive [to raise a child].”
Evolving marriage patterns, social media influence
The Philippines also saw a shifting pattern in marriage — or rather, a decreasing need for it.
In the Philippine Statistics Authority’s (PSA) 2025 National Demographic and Health Survey, 42.7% of women aged 15-49 and in childbearing age have never married.

Albert noted that family formation itself has changed — couples now delay marriage, do not marry at all, or cohabit instead. “For many women, marriage is no longer an economic necessity, and childbearing is a choice weighed against other goals,” he said.
In 2020, common-law or live-in marital arrangements among households rose to 14.7% in 2020 from 9.2% in 2015.

As more opportunities open for women, Albert added that entering into marriage could also become less appealing without a “legal exit” such as divorce, so women would rather explore other forms of relationships.
Social media has also broadened exposure to alternative life paths centered on education, career, travel, or other forms of family formation through influencers.

Like Ramos, Montejo also does content on TikTok and openly discusses her childfree lifestyle. In one reel, she talked about the risk of passing down health conditions to children as a valid reason not to have kids.
On the other side of it, she pointed out that online platforms also harbor negative perspectives. She pointed to parents who "openly talk about how they wish they didn't have children."
“You see people talk about it openly like, ‘oh, this is the worst decision I've ever made in my life,’ and that's gonna influence you for sure… we didn't have that before,” she added.
Gaps remain
While the national fertility rate dropped to an all-time low, regional data still paint a different picture.
CPD’s Quiray admitted gaps in expanding education, family planning, and contraceptive use in the country’s poorer households and far-flung areas as possible explanations for the disconnect.
Minimum wage still varies per region, with Metro Manila having a nominal minimum wage of P695 while BARMM, Caraga, Bicol Region, and others are still at the P400 mark as of March 2026.
Experts noted that wage disparities make it more difficult for families in lower-income regions to afford raising children compared to reduction in highly-urbanized areas.

Albert stressed that empowering women in these areas to make informed family planning decisions requires expanding their access to healthcare, education, and jobs. “Invest early and where the children are,” Albert said.
Investing in women's capabilities
A falling fertility rate is not necessarily a bad thing, said the PIDS fellow, as it proves that the Philippines has successfully curbed overpopulation and is taking bold steps for women in society.
Instead of mitigating the decline, Quiray said the CPD is focusing on further increasing women’s capabilities.
“More than the human numbers, it's really the quality of life that matters… We cannot dictate or mandate Filipinos to have children or not to have children,” she said.

The CPD, under the current Philippine Population and Development Plan of Action, listed eight multisectoral objectives, including empowering women in the workforce, promoting healthy aging, responsible parenthood, and others.
When presented with more paths in life, Montejo and Ramos said women are freer to choose a lifestyle that suits them, whether or not with a child.

For Bea, motherhood does not dictate the limits of her potential. “Women today have so many choices regarding what they want to do, aside from being a mother.” (To be concluded) – with reports from Jake Gomez / Rappler.com
NEXT: As Asia grays, can an aging Philippines avoid its neighbors' fate?
